ebnf Module = { Import | Declaration } ; Import = "import", ( Name | "{", Name, { ",", Name }, [ "," ], "}" ), "from", PlainStringLiteral, NEWLINE ; Declaration = [ "export" ], (TypeDeclaration | InterfaceDeclaration | FunctionDeclaration) | Implementation | TestDeclaration ; TypeDeclaration = "type", Name, [ TypeParameters ], ":", NEWLINE, INDENT, (RecordBody | AlternativeBody), DEDENT ; RecordBody = Field, { Field } ; Field = Name, ":", Type, NEWLINE ; AlternativeBody = CaseDeclaration, { CaseDeclaration } ; CaseDeclaration = "case", Name, [ "(", Parameters, ")" ], NEWLINE ; InterfaceDeclaration = "interface", Name, [ TypeParameters ], ":", NEWLINE, INDENT, ContractBody, DEDENT ; ContractBody = OperationSignature, { OperationSignature } ; OperationSignature = "fn", Name, "(", [ Parameters ], ")", "->", Type, NEWLINE ; FunctionDeclaration = "fn", Name, [ TypeParameters ], "(", [ FunctionParameters ], ")", "->", Type, Suite ; Implementation = "impl", NamedType, "for", NamedType, ":", NEWLINE, INDENT, MethodDeclaration, { MethodDeclaration }, DEDENT ; MethodDeclaration = "fn", Name, "(", [ FunctionParameters ], ")", "->", Type, Suite ; TestDeclaration = "test", PlainStringLiteral, Suite ; Parameters = Parameter, { ",", Parameter }, [ "," ] ; Parameter = Name, ":", Type ; FunctionParameters = FunctionParameter, { ",", FunctionParameter }, [ "," ] ; FunctionParameter = Parameter, [ "=", Expression ] ; TypeParameters = "[", TypeParameter, { ",", TypeParameter }, [ "," ], "]" ; TypeParameter = Name, [ ":", Bounds ] ; Bounds = NamedType, { "&", NamedType } ; Type = NamedType | FunctionType | "(", Type, ")" ; NamedType = TypePath, [ TypeArguments ] ; TypePath = Name, { ".", Name } ; TypeArguments = "[", Type, { ",", Type }, [ "," ], "]" ; FunctionType = "fn", "(", [ Parameters ], ")", "->", Type ; A type declares either record fields or alternative cases. An interface declares one or more operation signatures. Mixing these forms is rejected. A nullary alternative uses case Ready, without (). Parameter names and declaration names must be unique within their applicable scope. Function parameters and results always have explicit types. Function declarations and expressions with bodies accept default arguments . Interface signatures, function types, and data fields have no defaults. Variadic parameters, parameter patterns, and anonymous-function type parameters are not accepted. Trusted library/API contracts may define optional named arguments; an omitted API argument is checked against that declared contract.
Imports and declarations may be interleaved; import visibility and declaration resolution do not depend on written order. Import paths and test names are plain text literals: escapes are permitted, interpolation is rejected. export applies to types, interfaces, and named module functions, not tests or implementation blocks. Implementation blocks declare no type parameters. In impl Contract[T] for Data[T]:, T comes from the receiver type declaration; applicable bounds come from the type and interface declarations.
Every parameter used in the interface or method signatures must occur in the nominal receiver application. Contract operations and implementation methods cannot declare their own type parameters. Implementation applicability and overlap follow contracts .
Value types have no intersection/refinement syntax. & is used only to combine generic bounds, such as T: Read & Closeable; bound order does not affect the requirements. Synchronized[T] and SynchronizedGuard[T] are ordinary imported types, and lock scopes use existing with syntax.
There are no module-level executable statements or let/var bindings. Functions and tests contain executable code. A snippet showing local bindings without an enclosing function is a body fragment, not a complete .ms module. Type paths do not introduce wildcard/namespace imports or make a private type accessible; resolution follows module rules .
Statements and patterns# ebnf Suite = ":", NEWLINE, INDENT, Statement, { Statement }, DEDENT ; Statement = SimpleStatement, NEWLINE | IfStatement | WhileStatement | ForStatement | MatchStatement | WithStatement ; SimpleStatement = Binding | Assignment | ReturnStatement | "break" | "continue" | CallStatement ; Binding = ("let" | "var"), (Name, [ ":", Type ] | PositionalPattern | RecordPattern), "=", Expression ; Assignment = (Name | Expression, ".", Name), "=", Expression ; ReturnStatement = "return", [ Expression ] ; CallStatement = Expression ; IfStatement = "if", Expression, Suite, [ "else", (Suite | IfStatement) ] ; WhileStatement = "while", Expression, Suite ; ForStatement = "for", Name, "in", Expression, Suite ; WithStatement = "with", Name, "=", Expression, Suite ; MatchStatement = "match", Expression, ":", NEWLINE, INDENT, MatchArm, { MatchArm }, DEDENT ; MatchArm = CasePattern, Suite | "_", Suite ; CasePattern = CasePath, [ "(", PayloadNames, ")" ] ; CasePath = Name, [ TypeArguments ], { ".", Name } ; PayloadNames = (Name | "_"), { ",", (Name | "_") }, [ "," ] ; BindingPattern = Name | PositionalPattern | RecordPattern ; PositionalPattern = "[", [ BindingPattern, { ",", BindingPattern }, [ "," ] ], "]" ; RecordPattern = "{", RecordEntry, { ",", RecordEntry }, [ "," ], "}" ; RecordEntry = Name, [ ":", BindingPattern ] ; CallStatement must resolve to a call expression; arithmetic expressions or bare names are not standalone statements. Assignment replaces an existing var binding or updates a record field. Collection positions are updated through methods. Only a simple name binding may carry a type annotation. Destructuring patterns infer their types from the checked initializer; annotate an intermediate name first when the initializer needs context. Positional patterns can be empty, selecting an empty fixed result or list. Empty record patterns are rejected because they bind nothing. _ is allowed in match payloads and as a match wildcard, not as an ordinary binding or destructuring elision.
else if is two words; elif is not syntax. Alternative match patterns use exact positional case payloads, not constructor argument labels. On a contract view, the same pattern syntax names a complete concrete record or alternative type and exactly one receiver binding; a final wildcard is required. Their exhaustiveness, wildcard position, and binding checks are in pattern matching . if, match, loops, and with are statements, not value-producing expressions. Local type/implementation/import/test declarations are not accepted. Nested named function declarations are rejected; bind an anonymous function to a local name instead.
The existing with construct supplies its cleanup contract. This grammar does not define a move, borrow, consuming function kind, spawn keyword, or deferred-call construct. Runtime APIs are checked according to their own declarations and may impose more constraints on otherwise ordinary calls and list literals.
Rejected forms# Manuscript let count = 3 # Not a complete module item. fn wrong() -> Int: return 1 # A suite requires four spaces. fn wrong() -> Int: let (first, second) = pair # Parentheses are not a binding pattern. return if true: 1 else: 2 # if is not an expression. Each example is an independent rejected form. A syntax error does not require the parser to continue and produce further type diagnostics for that fragment.
Back to language basics · Expressions and operators

title: Strings and bytes
content:
Strings and bytes# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use String for text and Bytes for raw data. Both are immutable. Strings always contain valid UTF-8 and are available without an import. Import Bytes from @std/bytes.ms when naming that type. A byte sequence may need decoding before it can be treated as text.
String literals# A text literal starts and ends with " and occupies one physical source line, including its interpolation expressions. Raw newlines and raw control characters U+0000 through U+001F are rejected. Other Unicode scalar characters can appear directly. A literal evaluates to String; there are no single-quoted, raw, multiline, or byte literals.
Escape Value \" Double quote \\ Backslash \n LF, U+000A \r CR, U+000D \t Tab, U+0009 \{, \} Literal opening/closing brace \u{H} Unicode scalar with one to six hexadecimal digits H Scalar escapes accept uppercase or lowercase hexadecimal digits. Values above U+10FFFF and surrogates U+D800 through U+DFFF are compile errors. Unknown escapes, an unescaped closing brace, and an unterminated literal are compile errors. A brace inside a scalar escape belongs to that escape, not to interpolation. Null can be written as \u{0}; it remains valid String and is not a string terminator.
Manuscript let quote = "She said \"hello\"." let template = "Literal braces: \{name\}" let lines = "first\nsecond" let symbol = "\u{1F642}" These are function-body fragments. String is stored and compared without implicit Unicode normalization. The single scalar "é" and the two-scalar "e\u{301}" remain distinct values even when they render similarly. UTF-8 encoding uniquely represents their scalar sequences; String equality compares those contents exactly.
Interpolation# An unescaped { opens an embedded expression, and its matching } closes it. Interpolation uses the ordinary expression grammar , including calls and nested text literals. The scanner balances expression delimiters and recognizes text escapes/nested text literals; braces inside a nested literal do not terminate the enclosing expression. Empty expressions, interpolation format suffixes, comments within the embedded expression, and physical newlines inside an interpolated literal are rejected. A function expression with a statement suite consequently cannot appear inside interpolation.
Manuscript let name = "Ada" let count = 3 let greeting = "Welcome, {name}!" let calculated = "Next: {count + 1}" Embedded expressions evaluate once each from left to right. Each result is formatted before evaluating the next embedded expression. Plain surrounding text is concatenated with those formatted results. Result propagation or a fault stops evaluation of the remainder. Interpolation formats values; it does not permit implicit conversions at call, assignment, or return boundaries.
Every value is directly formattable, including records, alternatives, collections, functions, Bytes, interface views, runtime resources, and unconstrained type parameters. Interpolation uses the same conversion as toString().
Converting values to String# Every value has a built-in toString() method with signature fn() -> String. It needs no import or generic bound. A bound method retains its receiver and can be called later:
Manuscript fn text[T](value: T) -> String: return value.toString() test "string conversion": let count = 3 let convert: fn() -> String = count.toString let direct = count.toString() let bound = convert() let embedded = "{count}" Each conversion above produces "3". This follows JavaScript’s convenience of converting any value to text; the exact representations below are Manuscript’s own. Assignment, arguments, and return values still require compatible types: passing an Int to a String parameter requires an explicit .toString().
The built-in method takes precedence over a field or interface operation named toString. It cannot be overridden. Application-specific display functions can return String explicitly. Conversion never invokes user-defined formatting operations or native resource operations; even a closed resource remains printable.
Deterministic formatting# Formatting never depends on locale, host display settings, or a process’s decimal separator.
Type Formatting String Contents unchanged; inserted braces/quotes are ordinary output characters and are not parsed again Bool true or false Unit unit Int Base-ten digits, optional leading minus, no separators or leading zeros Float Shortest round-trip decimal under the rule below; signed zero retains its sign Decimal Exact numerical decimal value, normalized as below; no significance/scale padding Record Type(field: value, ...), with fields sorted by name and values recursively converted Alternative Type.Case for a nullary case; Type.Case(value, ...) for payloads in declaration order List [value, ...] in element order Heterogeneous pack (value, ...) in element order Map Map(key: value, ...) in insertion order Set Set(value, ...) in insertion order Bytes Bytes(byte, ...), with each byte in base ten; no UTF-8 decoding Interface view Conversion of its underlying receiver Function [function], including bound methods; the function is not called Duration Signed nanoseconds followed by ns, such as 2000000ns Instant Instant(tick), with its nanosecond tick in base ten OperationId OperationId(number), with its number in base ten BigInt Base-ten integer digits Timestamp UTC RFC 3339 text with fractional seconds as needed Regex Pattern text Other opaque native values, authorities, and resources [object]; internal state and addresses are not inspected Type names in records and alternatives omit module identities and type arguments. Nested Strings retain their contents without quoting. Empty values use the same delimiters with no items, such as [], Map(), and Type(). These text forms are for display; they are not a serialization or identity format. At nesting depth 64, conversion emits ... for that value, so deeply nested or cyclic adapter values terminate. The outer value starts at depth zero; entering a field, payload, collection item, map key/value, or interface receiver adds one.
For a finite nonzero Float, choose the decimal significand with the fewest significant digits whose numerical conversion to binary64 under round-to-nearest, ties-to-even yields the original value. If several candidates have that digit count, choose the one numerically closest to the exact binary value; if equally close, choose the candidate with an even final significand digit. Remove trailing significand zeros and place the decimal point under the rendering rule below. A zero formats as 0; negative zero formats as -0.
For Decimal, use the exact stored numerical value rather than an intermediate Float conversion. Remove trailing fractional/significand zeros without changing the number, and use the same decimal-point rule. Any Decimal zero formats as 0. Formatting does not round a Decimal to a smaller precision or preserve its source spelling: 1.00d formats as 1.
For either finite numerical decimal, let e be the base-ten exponent of its first nonzero digit in scientific notation. Use plain decimal notation when -6 ≤ e ≤ 20, adding zeros as necessary. Otherwise use one digit before the decimal point, remaining significant digits after it (omit the point if there are none), followed by lowercase e, an explicit + or -, and the exponent magnitude without leading zeros. For example, 0.000001 uses plain notation and an exponent of -7 uses 1e-7; an exponent of 21 uses 1e+21.
Non-finite Float values format as NaN, Infinity, or -Infinity; NaN payloads and signs do not affect that text. The numeric rules define how these values arise; they have no source literal spelling.
Indexing and character boundaries# There is no text[index] or slicing syntax. The data API defines byte length, UTF-8 encoding/decoding, and byte lookup. Scalar and grapheme indexing are unsupported.
A byte position, a Unicode scalar, and a user-visible grapheme are different units. For example, "é" has two UTF-8 bytes; "e\u{301}" has two scalars but can display as one grapheme. Byte lookup alone cannot select a character.
External data# Capability adapters validate UTF-8 when constructing text from foreign values and preserve immutability when transferring buffers. The standard type catalog lists both types alongside the intrinsic and imported standard types.
Previous: Numbers and booleans · Next: Records and nominal types

title: Types and data modeling
content:
Types and data modeling# Core language guide · Design index Choose a type based on the data you need to represent. Use a record for named fields, an alternative for a fixed set of cases, and an interface for operations a caller needs. Generic types let you reuse a model with different element types.
Concept What you will learn Records and nominal types Declare mutable fields and distinguish domain identifiers. Alternatives Represent a fixed set of possibilities with tagged cases. Optional values Represent absence explicitly with some and none. Collections Use mutable lists, maps, and sets with explicit shallow copies. Equality and hashing Understand value comparison and key eligibility. Operation contracts Implement interfaces with concrete or generic blocks and construct explicit contract views. Generics and bounds Apply parameterized types and express required properties. Type compatibility and expected types Check exact types, contextual constructors, and inference boundaries.

title: Records and nominal types
content:
Records and nominal types# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A record groups named fields into one value. Its fields can be changed after construction. Assignment and argument passing retain the same instance; use .clone() when you need a separate copy. Each record declaration creates a distinct type; this is called nominal typing. Use a record when data has a known shape, such as a customer with a name and email.
Manuscript type Customer: name: String email: Optional[String] Records have nominal identity and mutable fields. A resource field retains an ordinary reference to that object.
A record declaration has at least one field; an empty body is not a record declaration. Field types are explicit. Duplicate field names and field default initializers are compile errors.
Construction# Constructors supply every field by name exactly once. Missing, duplicate, or unknown fields are compile errors. Call order may differ from declaration order; field expressions evaluate in written call order. Each expression is checked against its declared field type, including expected-type checking for none and empty lists.
Manuscript let customer = Customer(name: "Ada", email: none) let name = customer.name The constructor states which value belongs to each field. customer.name reads the field. To use the optional email, handle its alternatives as described in optional values .
Manuscript # Rejected: required email is missing. let incomplete = Customer(name: "Ada") # Accepted: let fixes the binding, not the record fields. customer.name = "Grace" Generic records use explicit parameters, such as type Box[T]: with value: T. Box[Int](value: 1) constructs that application; see generics .
Mutation and cloning# A method can update its receiver’s fields without replacing the record:
Manuscript interface Counter: fn increment() -> Unit type Val: val: Int impl Counter for Val: fn increment() -> Unit: self.val = self.val + 1 Field writes keep the declared field type. The receiver expression is evaluated once, before the replacement value. Nested fields, parameters, aliases, and closure captures refer to the same record storage.
.clone() returns a new record with independent field storage. It is shallow: nested records, collections, callbacks, and resource references are retained. Changing a clone’s own field does not change the original; changing a shared nested object affects both.
Record and alternative values and List, Map, Set, and Bytes expose a built-in .clone(). Native file handles, sockets, queues, synchronization objects, guards, pools, and other service handles do not. A record containing a handle can be cloned, but that keeps the same handle and its existing lifetime.
Domain identity# Distinct identifiers such as CustomerId use nominal field types.
Manuscript type CustomerId: value: String type OrderId: value: String The two declarations represent distinct types even though their fields have the same shape. This keeps a customer identifier distinct from an order identifier at function boundaries.
Manuscript let customer_id = CustomerId(value: "42") # Rejected: equal field shapes do not make nominal types interchangeable. let order_id: OrderId = customer_id A nominal identity includes its defining module, declaration, and type arguments. Alternate normalized import paths to the same module do not create new types. Type applications are invariant .
Public data surfaces# Exporting a record exports its constructor and every field. Field visibility modifiers and opaque exports are unsupported. Field types must satisfy public signature closure , including types nested inside Optional or collections. Importing a record does not import the names of its field types.
Recursive data# Direct or mutually recursive inline record/alternative layouts are rejected. Build a layout dependency graph using only types stored inline in record fields and alternative payloads. Optional and Result are inline alternatives, so their stored payload types remain inline dependencies. List, Map, and Set storage is indirect; removing those container storage edges must leave an acyclic inline graph.
Function values and contract values also have indirect representations. Function parameter/result types and contract operation signatures are not inline storage edges and do not introduce a concrete layout cycle merely by mentioning the enclosing type. Generic recursive references still satisfy the separate finite-application rule in generics .
Manuscript type Node: value: Int children: List[Node] type BadNode: next: Optional[BadNode] # Rejected: inline recursion. type DeferredNode: build: fn() -> DeferredNode # Allowed: function value is indirect. Container element/key bounds still apply. A Set[Node] does not become valid just because it guards recursion: its element must be hashable. Generic recursive cycles must preserve the same type parameters; expanding recursion such as Grow[T] containing List[Grow[List[T]]] is rejected. See generic well-formedness and structural equality .
Resource fields# A record containing a resource does not implicitly close it or extend its open lifetime. Cleanup follows explicit resource scopes . Copying a record does not duplicate a referenced native service; each service synchronizes its own state and lifecycle.
A type declaration uses fields or cases. Use alternatives for a choice among cases and interface for operation contracts that declare required behavior.
Previous: Strings and bytes · Next: Alternatives

title: Alternatives
content:
Alternatives# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use an alternative type when a value can be one of several declared cases. For example, a payment can be paid, declined, or pending. Each case may carry its own data, such as a receipt or a reason.
Manuscript type Payment: case Paid(receipt: String) case Declined(reason: String) case Pending(reference: String) Alternatives are tagged and exhaustively matched. Paid, Declined, and Pending are different cases of Payment, even though each carries text.
A declaration has at least one case. Case names are unique within the declaration; payload field names are unique within each case. A case may have no payload, written case Missing. Payload types are explicit and fields have no defaults. Record fields and cases cannot be mixed in one type declaration. Operation signatures belong to interface declarations.
Construction and identity# Manuscript let payment = Payment.Paid(receipt: "receipt-42") let declined: Payment = Declined(reason: "Card rejected") Type.Case identifies a case of that nominal type. Payload constructors supply every payload field by name exactly once; missing, duplicate, and unknown fields are errors. Payloadless cases are values such as State.Ready, without (). Tags do not implicitly convert to integers.
This qualification names a visible type and its case, not a module namespace. Modules import individual symbols; customers.Customer is not a type path introduced by importing a module. Import the nominal type name itself and qualify its case as Type.Case.
Ordinary lexical name lookup happens first. A local binding, ordinary declaration, or imported symbol with the spelling is used before case shorthand is considered. If ordinary lookup finds nothing, an unqualified constructor case name must identify exactly one case among visible nominal alternative declarations (declared or individually imported). If multiple visible types declare it, qualification is required even when an annotation supplies an expected type. An expected alternative application can supply generic arguments after a unique case is resolved. A qualified case inconsistent with the expected type is rejected. Matching payload shapes do not make distinct alternatives compatible.
Qualification still resolves Type through ordinary lookup. A local value shadowing that name does not act as a module namespace or expose the hidden type’s cases.
Manuscript type LeftState: case Ready type RightState: case Ready let left: LeftState = LeftState.Ready # Rejected: two visible Ready cases, even with an annotation. let annotated: LeftState = Ready # Rejected: two visible Ready cases. let ambiguous = Ready # Rejected: a different nominal alternative. let wrong: LeftState = RightState.Ready Inside a scope with let Ready = LeftState.Ready, subsequent Ready expressions refer to that binding rather than retrying ambiguous case lookup. An incompatible expected type rejects the binding’s type; it does not choose another type’s case instead.
Generic qualification includes type arguments: Choice[Int].Found(value: 1). Exporting an alternative exposes every case and payload field. Payload types follow the public surface and recursive layout rules for records.
Type arguments attach to the nominal alternative, never to the case name. Found[Int](value: 1) and Choice.Found[Int](value: 1) are rejected. Unqualified Found(value: 1) may use argument inference or a complete expected Choice[Int] after case lookup resolves uniquely; explicit arguments use the single spelling Choice[Int].Found(value: 1). These rules also apply to qualified standard Optional/Result cases.
Handling a case# A match selects the case and binds its payload. Code handling a payment must account for all three possibilities; adding another case requires the exhaustive matches to be reviewed.
Match patterns resolve cases against the scrutinee’s known alternative type. Payload bindings are patterns rather than named call arguments. Their syntax is specified in pattern matching .
There is no general implicit union construction or nullable reference type. Declare the set of possibilities as an alternative type, or use Optional for absence.
Resource payloads# Payloads retain ordinary values and references. Matching or extracting a resource reference does not invalidate the original value, register cleanup, or extend its open lifetime. See aggregate references .
Previous: Records and nominal types · Next: Optional values

title: Optional values
content:
Optional values# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use Optional[T] when a value may be missing. some(value: ...) contains a value of type T; none means there is no value. Import Optional from @std/optional.ms.
Manuscript let present: Optional[String] = some(value: "Ada") let missing: Optional[String] = none Missing values use Optional. An optional makes absence part of the function’s or field’s declared type.
Optional[T] is an invariant alternative. Qualified cases are Optional[T].some(value: ...) and Optional[T].none. Unqualified forms use an expected optional type, or infer T from a some payload. none carries no evidence for T and needs context or explicit qualification.
Manuscript let inferred = some(value: 1) # Optional[Int] let explicit = Optional[String].none # Rejected: no type determines the absent payload. let unknown = none # Rejected: no automatic wrapping. let wrong: Optional[String] = "Ada" There is no implicit unwrapping or flattening: Optional[Optional[Int]] differs from Optional[Int]. Result[T, E] likewise needs both arguments determined; an expected result type can supply the missing argument in ok(value: ...) or error(cause: ...). See compatibility and expected types .
Handling absence# Manuscript fn display_name(name: Optional[String]) -> String: match name: some(value): return value none: return "Anonymous" The some branch binds the contained text. The none branch chooses what this application should do when no name is supplied. Both branches return String.
Use Result when a failure needs an explanation. An absent value and a failed operation express different contracts. try propagates a Result error; the design specifies no corresponding implicit propagation for an optional.
Data modeling# A record can contain optional fields, such as email: Optional[String]. Manuscript has no nullable reference type: put absence in the declared type and handle it through ordinary pattern matching .
Previous: Alternatives · Next: Collections

title: Collections
content:
Collections# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use List[T] for an ordered sequence, Map[K, V] for key/value entries, and Set[T] for distinct values. The type arguments state the element, key, and value types. All three collections are mutable references. Assignment retains the same instance; .clone() copies its storage.
Import each collection type you name from @std/collections.ms. Ordinary bracket list literals also require the canonical List import.
Type Contents List[T] Elements of type T Map[K, V] Keys of type K and values of type V Set[T] Distinct elements of type T List literals# Brackets construct mutable lists of values:
Manuscript let values = [1, 2, 3] let empty: List[Int] = [] The first literal infers List[Int]. An empty literal gets its element type from an annotation or the expected parameter type. Every element must match the list’s element type; numeric conversions are explicit. Elements evaluate from left to right, and nested lists remain nested.
A function taking values: List[Int] is called as sum(values: [1, 2, 3]) or with an existing list. See collections as arguments .
Element requirements# Collections accept any value type, including functions, contract views, builders, and synchronized services. Map keys and set elements additionally require Hashable.
Resource and service references may be stored freely. Retaining them does not keep the resource open or register cleanup.
List[Contract] stores ordinary contract views. List[fn(value: Int) -> Int] stores functions. Both may be passed between tasks without additional bounds. Coordinate shared mutation and reads with Synchronized.
Collection applications are invariant. List[Int] is not assignable to List[Float]; a list inserts neither numeric conversions nor implicit unions of unrelated element types.
Manuscript let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1, 2]] # Rejected: incompatible Int and Float elements. let mixed = [1, 2.0] # Rejected: no element type can be inferred. let unknown = [] An expected List[List[Int]] propagates to the inner literals. Without context, a nonempty literal infers one element type from independently typed elements and checks every element against it. Context-dependent elements such as none cannot invent a payload type; another element or enclosing context must determine it. For example [none, some(value: 1)] is List[Optional[Int]], while [none] without context is rejected.
Collection storage can guard recursive data . This does not waive element bounds or confer hashing on the container itself.
Iteration# Map and set iteration follows insertion order. A for loop expresses traversal. Ordering within one traversal does not establish an execution order between concurrent operations.
Mutation and copies# append, prepend, with_value, without, with_values, fill, copy_within, and reverse update a list and return the same instance. Append reuses available capacity and grows storage when necessary; it does not copy the full list on each call.
Map with_entry, without, with_default, with_default_from, merge, and clear update the receiver. Set with_value, without, and clear update the receiver. Their return values retain that instance for chaining.
Manuscript let values = [1, 2] let alias = values let copy = values.clone() values.append(3) # alias now contains [1, 2, 3]; copy still contains [1, 2]. Clones have independent outer storage and retain nested references. map, filter, slice, concat, sorted, and set algebra construct new results. Text and Bytes retain their existing nonmutating operations.
A for loop and collection callback traversals snapshot collection membership once; elements retain their references. Adding or removing items inside the body does not change that traversal. Protect shared mutation and concurrent reads with Synchronized; every alias must use the same lock.
Building data# Use the data API for construction, lookup, and updates in place. Builders provide synchronized construction and sealed builder results.
See generics and bounds for type arguments and equality and hashing for key eligibility.
Previous: Optional values · Next: Equality and hashing

title: Equality and hashing
content:
Equality and hashing# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Equality compares eligible values by their contents. Hashing is the additional property needed to use a value as a map key or set element. The compiler checks these properties from the type. Services, resources, and capabilities do not gain equality automatically.
Equality is by value for eligible data types; services, resources, and capabilities have no implicit equality.
Eligibility and value behavior# Bool, Int, Decimal, String, Bytes, Unit, Duration, and Instant support equality and hashing. Never vacuously meets both bounds but has no constructible value. Float supports IEEE 754 equality: NaN compares unequal to every value, including itself, and positive and negative zero compare equal. Float is not Hashable.
String equality compares exact UTF-8 scalar sequences without Unicode normalization. Bytes compare byte sequences. Decimal equality compares numeric value rather than spelling or trailing zeroes. Hashing must agree with equality: equal values have equal hashes, but unequal values may collide. Hash values/algorithms are not a stable serialized format or a public source operation.
Records compare only with the same instantiated nominal type, field by field. Alternatives require the same instantiated type, tag, and equal payload fields. A record/alternative is Equal when every component is eligible for equality, and Hashable when every component is eligible for hashing. Optional and Result follow these alternative rules. Sharing does not grant equality to service/resource references.
Collection Equality Hashing List[T] Same length and equal corresponding elements; requires T: Equal Unsupported Map[K, V] Same key/value associations regardless of insertion order; requires eligible keys and V: Equal Unsupported Set[T] Same members regardless of insertion order; requires eligible elements Unsupported Collections are not Hashable. A record containing a collection can be Equal but cannot automatically become a map key or set element. Function values and contract views have no implicit equality or hashing.
Manuscript let same = [1, 2] == [1, 2] let different = [1, 2] == [2, 1] # false # Rejected at type checking: Float is not Hashable. fn accepts_float_keys(values: Map[Float, Int]) -> Unit: return For guarded recursive data , eligibility is checked over the finite declaration graph. Every nonrecursive leaf must meet the bound; recursive references reuse the requirement already being checked. A cycle does not establish eligibility if a leaf fails it. Equality traverses current field and collection contents structurally and terminates on cyclic data graphs. Containers still block hashing derivation even when they guard recursive layout.
Manuscript type Tree[T: Equal]: value: T children: List[Tree[T]] This tree is Equal for eligible T; its list field prevents hashing. User-defined implementations of compiler bounds cannot override these derivations.
Compiler-defined bounds# Equal and Hashable are compiler-defined bounds. Hashing requires equality. A generic operation can require these properties using a bound , and the compiler checks whether its type arguments meet the requirement.
Use Requirements Value equality Eligible data type with equality Map[K, V] key Hashable, including equality Set[T] element Hashable, including equality Equality and hash consistency# For a Hashable type, equality must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Equal values must hash identically under the same hash configuration. Unequal values may have the same hash; a map or set must resolve every collision by equality rather than accepting a hash match as a key match. Hashes are internal lookup aids, not stable IDs or persistence formats.
Keys and set elements must retain their equality and hash behavior while stored. Do not mutate a stored key or its nested data; remove it before changing it and reinsert afterward. .clone() can separate record field storage, but nested references remain shared. Neither operation depends on a resource’s open state, external authority, insertion order, or current wall-clock time. Float and records containing Float remain equality-comparable with IEEE behavior, but cannot meet Hashable’s equivalence requirement because NaN is not equal to itself.
With structural derivation, every declared field participates. A display label or cached value is not silently excluded. Model a lookup identity as its own record, then use that record as the key:
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" type CustomerKey: id: String type Customer: key: CustomerKey display_name: String test "domain identity is a value": let first = Customer(key: CustomerKey(id: "c1"), display_name: "Ada") let renamed = Customer(key: CustomerKey(id: "c1"), display_name: "Ada Lovelace") if not (first != renamed): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (first.key == renamed.key): return panic(message: "check failed") let names = Map[CustomerKey, String]().with_entry(key: first.key, value: first.display_name) let updated = names.with_entry(key: renamed.key, value: renamed.display_name) if not (updated.length() == 1): return panic(message: "check failed") A domain requiring normalized text identity should construct a canonical key value explicitly. String equality itself remains exact; adding a matching operation name to a type does not change == or key lookup.
Domain values and runtime authority# A nominal record describes domain data. Capabilities describe external authority, and a Background service controls work under a fixed lifetime. Safe concurrent sharing does not automatically grant equality to a service or resource.
The compiler generates equality and hashing operations for eligible types. The design does not introduce arbitrary user-defined operator overloading.
Previous: Collections · Next: Operation contracts

title: Operation contracts
content:
Operation contracts# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index An interface lists the operations a caller needs. This is an operation contract: a concrete implementation must supply those operations with the declared signatures. Use it when callers should depend on behavior rather than a particular data type.
The following contract refers to application-defined Money, Receipt, and PaymentError types:
Manuscript interface Payments: fn charge(amount: Money) -> Result[Receipt, PaymentError] The caller can see the amount accepted, the receipt returned on success, and the expected payment error. The contract uses the same explicit function signature rules as an ordinary declaration.
Explicit implementations# Operation contracts support explicit implementations through impl Contract for DataType; implementations bind self to the receiver. Contracts have no inheritance or default implementations.
An implementation supplies the contract’s operations for the named data type. The implementation relationship is declared explicitly rather than inferred from coincidentally similar operation names.
Manuscript interface Increment: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int type Offset: delta: Int impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int: return value + self.delta self is an implicit receiver binding inside each implementation method, with the concrete receiver type. It is not written as a parameter, is not supplied as a call argument, and cannot be redeclared. The receiver does not add a field to the contract. Methods follow the ordinary mutable-field and reference rules.
An implementation must match the contract exactly. After substituting generic type arguments, check:
every operation appears exactly once; operation names match; parameter labels, their declaration order, and parameter types match; result types match. Missing, extra, duplicate, or mismatched operations are compile errors. An implementation method may add defaults for calls through its concrete receiver; interface-view calls still require the interface signature’s arguments. Neither interface operations nor methods declare their own generic parameters. Parameter labels and order are part of function identity .
Manuscript # Rejected: amount does not match the contract's value label. impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(amount: Int) -> Int: return amount + self.delta The rejected block is an alternative negative example, not a second block to add to the valid example.
Coherence and visibility# An implementation declared in the concrete type’s defining module is available wherever that type is used. An implementation declared for an imported source type is a local extension, visible only within the module declaring the implementation. The interface may be local or imported in either case. No new syntax is needed.
For example, offset.ms exports a record:
text export type Offset: delta: Int Another module can add its own interface implementation:
text import Offset from "./offset.ms" export interface Double: fn doubled() -> Int impl Double for Offset: fn doubled() -> Int: return self.delta * 2 export fn double_view(value: Offset) -> Double: return Double(value: value) Inside this module, Offset(delta: 3).doubled() returns 6. Importing double_view or Double elsewhere does not make doubled available on raw Offset values. Calling double_view(Offset(delta: 3)).doubled() works there because the returned view retains the selected implementation.
Each module sees the receiver’s defining-module implementations plus its own local extensions. Reject duplicate or overlapping receiver/contract pairs within that visible set, including attempts to replace a defining-module implementation. Separate modules may define the same local pair independently; neither extension becomes visible through imports, including transitive imports. Different interfaces with the same operation name still require an explicit view to disambiguate.
Views, bound methods, and specialized generic functions retain the implementation selected where they are created. A generic bound uses the implementation evidence supplied at specialization, including when forwarded to another generic function. Calls on statically concrete types inside a function use that function’s declaring module. Passing a raw concrete value does not carry additional conformance into another module.
Concrete and generic blocks obey the same visibility rules. Receivers must be source-defined nominal records or alternatives; intrinsic and standard-library receivers, interfaces, bare type parameters, specialization, generic operations, and implementation inheritance remain unsupported. Contracts can be generic but cannot have fields, cases, default bodies, associated types, or static operations. A contract declares at least one operation. An implementation does not re-export either its type or its contract.
Exported contracts expose every operation. Types in their operation signatures obey the public surface rules .
Generic implementations# An implementation uses generic parameters from its receiver type declaration. Its receiver must be an application of a local or imported source nominal data declaration. Parameter names in the receiver application come from that data declaration. Inherited bounds retain their original nominal identities; an extending module need not import the names used in those bounds. Only parameters occurring in the receiver application are in scope for the interface and methods; matching the receiver determines all implementation arguments. Concrete and nested receiver applications remain supported. Interface parameter names need not match data parameter names: an application substitutes the receiver parameters positionally. An undeclared name such as U in impl ReadValue[U] for Box[U] is rejected when Box declares only T.
Manuscript interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T type Box[T]: value: T impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value This block implements ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int], ReadValue[String] for Box[String], and every other well-formed application. Methods use the receiver declaration’s parameters but cannot declare their own. Bounds are inherited from the receiver type declaration and, for interface arguments that are receiver parameters, from the interface declaration. The compiler checks the body once under these inherited bounds, with self: Box[T], and checks exact substituted operation signatures.
Inherited bounds must prove that every nested type application and operation in the body is legal. At a use, receiver matching supplies the arguments and those arguments must satisfy the inherited bounds. When a receiver argument is specialized to a concrete type, references to that parameter in other inherited bounds use the concrete type. For example, Pair[A, B: ReadValue[A]] with receiver Pair[Int, B] gives B: ReadValue[Int].
Interface parameter bounds can restrict implementation availability without restricting the data type:
Manuscript interface SameValue[T: Equal]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool impl SameValue[T] for Box[T]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool: return self.value == other A Box[T] with no proof of T: Equal cannot use this implementation. Receiver references may be passed freely; equality remains a separate property.
Two blocks overlap if their receiver and contract applications can simultaneously match the same pair of types. Check this by structurally unifying both pairs, with each receiver’s inherited parameters treated as distinct variables and nominal identities and invariant arguments preserved. Ignore bounds in this check: different bounds cannot select competing implementations. Reject overlap between implementations visible in the same module at declaration checking, even if no current call uses it. There is no most-specific selection or specialization.
Manuscript # Rejected alongside the generic block above: both apply to Box[Int]. impl ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int]: fn get() -> Int: return self.value Implementations of ReadValue[Int] and ReadValue[String] for the same receiver are distinct pairs, but their shared get name still requires an explicit view for dispatch. Generic method calls and specialized implementation dependencies obey the same finite-application rules as generic functions.
Explicit contract views# Create a contract view explicitly with Contract(value: concrete). For a generic contract, use Contract[T](value: concrete). The concrete type must have an applicable declared implementation and satisfy its bounds; a matching method name alone is not enough.
A view keeps the same receiver reference without copying native state or extending its resource lifetime. The receiver retains its concurrency contract: passing a view does not add a lock to a local mutable collection.
Manuscript fn use_increment(operation: Increment) -> Int: return operation.apply(value: 1) let offset = Offset(delta: 2) let view = Increment(value: offset) let result = use_increment(operation: view) # Rejected: conversion is not implicit at a call boundary. let wrong = use_increment(operation: offset) The constructor accepts an implementing concrete value or an existing view of the exact contract application. An existing view is an identity conversion. Different contracts/applications and unchecked contract-to-concrete conversions are rejected. A contract type match can recover a concrete record or alternative receiver after checking its exact nominal identity at runtime.
Write generic view arguments explicitly or supply an expected application of the same contract. Operation names do not infer arguments.
Selecting an operation# A concrete receiver or generic parameter may call an operation directly when exactly one implemented/bounded contract supplies its name. Otherwise select a view, such as Increment(value: offset).apply(value: 1). Arguments and result types cannot resolve operation-name ambiguity. A bound method retains its receiver and has the operation’s ordinary function type.
A contract type satisfies its own exact named generic bound without a source impl. For example, Converter[Int] satisfies T: Converter[Int], but not T: Converter[String]. All such values may be passed between operations.
Manuscript fn invoke[T: Increment](operation: T) -> Int: return Increment(value: operation).apply(value: 1) let from_concrete = invoke(operation: offset) let from_view = invoke(operation: view) Both calls satisfy the same bound; neither inserts an implicit conversion at the call boundary.
Concurrent use# All contract values may be passed between operations; concurrent invocation follows the receiver’s contract. There is one view type, with ordinary spelling such as ReadValue[Int]. Explicit view construction checks the implementation relationship and preserves the receiver reference. No conversion adds synchronization, equality, hashing, cleanup, or lifetime extension. Native services synchronize their internals and lifecycle. Source implementations that need a local mutable queue across concurrent calls keep it behind Synchronized.
Contracts and external authority# A capability can be passed as an explicit input when an operation needs an external service, such as storage or payments. Standard host services are also available through imported accessor functions. Modules and capabilities describes effects, native synchronization obligations, and exported boundary contracts.
Contracts can also appear as generic bounds , where they name the operations required from a type argument.
Previous: Equality and hashing · Next: Generics and bounds

title: Generics and bounds
content:
Generics and bounds# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A generic type describes a family of types using type arguments. The arguments make the element or result types visible wherever the type is used.
Generics use brackets.
Manuscript List[String] Map[String, Int] Optional[String] Result[Decimal, DiscountError] These are type expressions: a list of text, a map from text to integers, optional text, and a decimal result with an application-defined error type.
Bounds# The compiler-defined bounds are Equal and Hashable. They express comparison and key requirements; ordinary behavioral requirements use named operation contracts. Generic declarations use [T, U], with bounds such as T: Equal or T: Read & Closeable.
Bound Required property Equal Type supports eligible value equality Hashable Type supports hashing consistent with equality A named operation contract Type supplies the required operations through an explicit implementation Bounds are checked at every application. Hashable implies Equal for bound satisfaction and body checking. All values may be passed between operations without a sharing bound; this does not add synchronization to mutable objects. Contract types do not gain equality or hashing.
Equal and Hashable are not standalone value types, generic type arguments, view constructors, or implementation targets. Their intrinsic names cannot be redefined by module declarations, imports, or type parameters. Concurrent access requires no compiler-defined bound.
Manuscript # Rejected: a compiler bound is not a parameter type. fn invalid_parameter(value: Equal) -> Unit: return # Rejected: Equal is not a type argument. let invalid_argument = identity[Equal](value: 1) # Rejected: no source view constructor for a compiler bound. let invalid_view = Equal(value: 1) impl Equal for DataType is also rejected; eligibility follows compiler derivation rather than a source implementation. A declaration such as fn invalid[Hashable](value: Hashable) -> Unit: cannot redefine Hashable as its type parameter.
Declarations and applications# Manuscript type Box[T]: value: T fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn same[T: Equal](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right let box = Box[Int](value: 1) let exact = identity[Int](value: 1) let inferred = identity(value: 1) Type parameters are ordered and their names unique. An application supplies exactly one argument per parameter. Default type arguments, higher-kinded parameters, type aliases, and variadic type parameters are unsupported. Records, alternatives, interfaces, and named functions may declare generic parameters. Implementation blocks use the receiver type declaration’s parameters and inherit applicable bounds from the type and interface declarations. Anonymous functions, contract operations, and implementation methods cannot declare their own type parameters. Methods inherit the parameters used in their implementation’s receiver; see generic implementations for receiver matching, bound checking, and overlap rejection.
Applications are invariant: Box[Int] and Box[Float] are distinct types. A generic declaration is not an unapplied type or function value. A generic function passed as a value must be explicitly specialized, for example identity[Int].
Inference from arguments# A function call may omit type arguments only when independently typed supplied argument expressions uniquely determine every parameter. The compiler matches argument types against declared parameter types, including invariant nested applications, then checks bounds and arguments after substitution. Repeated occurrences must determine the same type. No common superclass, implicit union, or numeric widening is inferred.
Manuscript fn choose[T](first: T, second: T) -> T: return first let value = choose(first: 1, second: 2) # T = Int # Rejected: conflicting evidence for T. let mixed = choose(first: 1, second: 2.0) Result annotations do not infer function type arguments. Empty lists, none, and other expressions requiring context cannot independently provide evidence. Once other arguments determine all parameters, substituted parameter types provide context to those expressions. This process does not reorder evaluation.
Manuscript fn count[T](values: List[T]) -> Int: return 0 let known = count[Int](values: []) # Rejected: the empty list does not determine T. let unknown = count(values: []) Generic data constructors follow the same field/payload inference rule, but an expected data application may supply their type arguments before field checking. Thus let box: Box[Int] = Box(value: 1) is valid. A unique complete application must result; a constructor cannot invent an unused type parameter.
Body checking and well-formedness# A generic body is checked once against declared bounds. An unconstrained T cannot be compared with ==, used as a map key, or called through a contract operation. Bounds expose only their declared properties.
Manuscript # Rejected at declaration: missing Equal bound. fn unchecked_same[T](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right type Keys[T: Hashable]: values: Set[T] Every nested application must satisfy its bounds under enclosing generic assumptions. Omitting the bounds from Keys is rejected even if all later uses happen to supply Int.
The same rule checks a generic implementation once under its inherited parameters and bounds. Its method bodies cannot rely on properties absent from the inherited bounds. Matching the receiver determines the implementation arguments; all implementation bounds must hold before its operations or views are available. Bounds may restrict a single implementation’s availability, but are ignored when rejecting overlapping implementations. A concrete implementation cannot specialize a pair already covered by a generic block.
Finite recursive applications# Recursive declarations follow layout rules . Separately, the compiler requires a finite regular family of recursive generic applications. Along a recursive generic cycle, arguments preserve the original parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Tree[T] with children: List[Tree[T]] is allowed. Substituting concrete arguments, reordering them, or expanding them on a recursive cycle is rejected; Grow[T] containing List[Grow[List[T]]] would create an infinite application family. This regularity check follows recursive type references even through function signatures or contracts: an indirect runtime representation does not permit infinitely expanding static instantiations.
The same finite-application requirement covers generic function calls and specialized function values. Follow specialization dependencies through the whole module graph; on a recursive function cycle, the composed substitution must preserve the starting function’s type parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Nonrecursive calls may construct different type arguments. Reject expanding recursive specialization before Go emission, even when the recursive call is unreachable at runtime. This prevents both an infinite monomorphization worklist and generic recursion that the Go backend cannot represent.
Manuscript fn repeat[T](value: T) -> Never: return repeat[T](value: value) # Regular specialization; allowed. fn grow[T](value: T) -> Never: return grow[List[T]](value: [value]) # Rejected: expanding specialization. Apply the check to mutual recursion and references such as grow[List[T]] stored as function values, not only direct self-calls. Include generic implementation method calls and bound methods in specialization dependencies under their inherited receiver parameters. Generated-code compilation errors are not a substitute for a source diagnostic.
Built-in requirements# List[T], Queue[T], Synchronized[T], and collection values accept arbitrary value types, including functions and contract views. Map keys and set elements require Hashable. Equality is independently derived as described in equality and hashing . Sharing does not register cleanup or extend a resource’s open lifetime.
Previous: Operation contracts · Next: Type compatibility and expected types

title: Type compatibility and expected types
content:
Type compatibility and expected types# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index The type you provide must match the type required at that position. This applies to variable annotations, assignments, arguments, returns, fields, and collection elements. For example, an Int cannot silently become a Float, and two records do not become interchangeable just because their fields match.
The exception is an expression of type Never: it cannot produce a value, so it can appear where any expression value is expected. This exception does not make differently declared function types interchangeable.
Exact and nominal identity# Type form Identity and compatibility Built-in Fixed compiler or standard identity Record or alternative Defining module, declaration, and ordered type arguments; matching fields or cases do not establish compatibility Contract view Nominal contract application, plus whether it is plain or shared; conversions are explicit Generic application Exact declaration and every ordered argument; List[Int] and List[Float] are distinct Function Exact parameter labels, declaration order, parameter types, and result type; no variance or label/order adaptation Caller-written argument order affects evaluation without changing function identity. A generic bound grants properties, not subtyping. Shared/plain arguments remain distinct during inference; List[Contract] fails its element bound, while List[Contract] may satisfy it.
Type positions use ordinary name resolution . A value shadowing a type name causes an error, not a second lookup in a hidden namespace. Unqualified cases follow alternative lookup ; expected types cannot override a lexical binding or choose an ambiguous case.
Equal and Hashable are compiler bounds , not standalone value types. Value types have no intersection/refinement syntax; conjunction is available only for generic bounds.
Manuscript fn identity(value: Int) -> Int: return value let exact: fn(value: Int) -> Int = identity # Rejected: amount differs from value. let relabeled: fn(amount: Int) -> Int = identity There are no implicit numeric conversions, optional wrapping/unwrapping, result wrapping, structural record conversions, unions, or nullable references. An integer literal has type Int even under an expected Float; use the explicit conversion API . The type checker does not choose an arbitrary common type for incompatible values.
Propagating context# An expected type comes from the place a value is used: a local annotation, assignment target, return declaration, parameter after generic substitution, record field, or alternative payload.
That type can guide the expressions inside parentheses, list elements, constructor fields, and case payloads. It can supply missing type arguments for a uniquely identified constructor such as none, ok, or error.
Context does not resolve an ambiguous unqualified case name or change a type an expression already determines for itself.
Manuscript type Input: names: List[Optional[String]] let input = Input(names: [none, some(value: "Ada")]) let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1]] let success: Result[Int, String] = ok(value: 1) let failure: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "unavailable") # Rejected: the result error type cannot be inferred from ok's payload. let incomplete = ok(value: 1) The compiler rejects expressions whose type cannot be determined. It does not silently assign a dynamic or unknown type.
Expression without an annotation What can be inferred none or [] Not enough information to determine the payload or element type. ok(value: 1) The success is Int, but the error type is still unknown. some(value: 1) The complete type is Optional[Int]. [none, some(value: 1)] The typed some value supplies enough context for List[Optional[Int]]. A list is rejected if its independently typed elements disagree.
Operators and try do not pass an expected result type backward into their operands. Their operands must determine their own types first. For example, knowing that the value unwrapped by try should be Int does not tell the compiler which error type an incomplete Result constructor should have.
Manuscript fn known() -> Result[Int, String]: let number: Int = try Result[Int, String].ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number) fn unknown() -> Result[Int, String]: # Rejected: the try operand's error type is undetermined. let number: Int = try ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number) Similarly, an expected Bool cannot make [] == [] well typed; neither operand determines a list element type. Explicitly qualify or annotate operands when their types would otherwise be incomplete.
Never operands use the operator candidate rules . Those rules select a required operand type locally; they do not infer it backward from an expected result.
Generic function inference uses supplied argument types only, as specified in generics . An expected return type does not infer missing function type arguments. A generic function value must be explicitly specialized before an expected function type can check it. Anonymous functions still require their own explicit parameter/result types.
Validation boundaries# Every declaration’s referenced types must resolve and every application must satisfy arity and bounds. Generic bodies are checked under declared bounds. Public signatures satisfy public type visibility , and recursive concrete layouts satisfy guarded recursion . These checks precede lowering and do not rely on Go’s structural interfaces or implicit assignments.
Runtime cancellation and resource closed-state errors do not alter static assignability. Their separate contracts remain governed by the existing runtime and reference chapters.
Previous: Generics and bounds · Next: Declarations and calls

title: Functions
content:
Functions# Core language guide · Design index Functions take named inputs and return a declared type. First learn how to declare and call them. Then learn how to pass a function as a value and what it keeps from its surrounding scope.
Concept What you will learn Declarations and calls Write explicit signatures and evaluate arguments in source order. Function values and closures Pass functions as values and understand snapshot captures and resource references.

title: Declarations and calls
content:
Declarations and calls# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A function names its inputs, declares their types, and declares the type it returns. Its body runs in source order. Use return to send a value back to the caller.
Manuscript fn decrement(value: Int) -> Int: return value - 1 let remaining = decrement(3) Function parameters and return types are explicit; local annotations are optional. The caller can infer remaining as Int from the function’s declared return type.
Declarations and resolution# Named functions are module declarations or operations inside an impl. Nested named function declarations are rejected; use an anonymous function bound to a local instead. Every parameter has a unique name and an explicit type, and every function has an explicit result type, including Unit.
The compiler collects module declaration names and signatures before checking bodies. A function can call a later declaration, and ordinary and mutual function recursion are allowed. Duplicate module names and overloaded declarations are rejected. Generic function declarations and applications follow generics .
Parameters belong to the function body’s lexical scope. A local declaration cannot reuse a parameter’s name in that same scope. Each branch, match arm, and loop body creates a nested scope; nested scopes may shadow an outer name.
Argument names# A function with exactly one declared parameter accepts either function(value) or function(name: value). The omitted label resolves to that sole parameter. Functions with more than one parameter require name: value for every supplied argument; the name identifies the declared parameter.
Manuscript fn reduce(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction let remaining = reduce(amount: 10, deduction: 3) let next = decrement(3) let explicit = decrement(value: 3) The rule applies to ordinary functions, methods, function values, and library APIs. Count the callable’s declared parameters, including optional API parameters, rather than the arguments supplied at a particular call. A method’s implicit receiver does not count as a parameter. Constructors and explicit contract views still require labels, including some(value: ...), ok(value: ...), error(cause: ...), and Contract(value: receiver). A zero-parameter function uses ().
parallel receives an ordered pack of zero-argument functions through tasks: [first, second], with options such as timeout: 2.seconds supplied by name. Its heterogeneous results are specified in parallel operations .
Match payload bindings such as some(value): are patterns, rather than calls; see pattern matching .
A parameter with a default may be omitted; every other parameter remains required. An Optional[T] parameter without a default is still required: callers explicitly supply none when absent. Variadic parameters and argument spreading are not supported. Existing trusted library API contracts may explicitly permit omitted named arguments; that permission does not follow from an Optional value type. Unknown labels, duplicate arguments, missing required arguments, and unlabeled arguments to multi-parameter functions are compile errors. Supplying both decrement(3, value: 4) arguments duplicates the sole parameter and is rejected. Supplied values must be compatible with the declared parameter types under type compatibility ; labels do not authorize numeric or contract conversions.
Default arguments# Write = expression after a parameter’s type to supply a default:
Manuscript fn subtract(amount: Int, deduction: Int = 1) -> Int: return amount - deduction fn example() -> Int: let usual = subtract(amount: 5) let explicit = subtract(amount: 5, deduction: 2) return usual + explicit usual is 4 and explicit is 3. A function whose sole parameter has a default also accepts function(). Multi-parameter functions still require labels on every supplied argument, even when only one is supplied. Defaults may appear before required parameters because labels identify arguments.
A default is checked against its explicit parameter type in the function’s lexical scope. It may use imports, module declarations, earlier parameters, and an implementation method’s self. Current and later parameters are not yet in scope. Anonymous functions may use captured outer bindings in defaults; those bindings follow the ordinary snapshot and sharing rules.
Evaluate the callable and all supplied arguments first, in written order. Then evaluate omitted defaults once each in parameter declaration order, before entering the body. Defaults run afresh on each invocation; supplying a value skips its default entirely. Explicit none, unit, false, and zero are supplied values. A failing default prevents later defaults and the body from running. try in a default propagates from the called function under its declared result type.
Named functions, anonymous functions, and implementation methods with bodies may declare defaults. Interface operation signatures, function-type annotations, record fields, and alternative payloads cannot. A method default permits omission through its concrete receiver or inferred bound method value; calls through an interface view follow the interface’s required signature. Defaults do not provide generic inference: omitted arguments supply no type evidence, and a generic default must type-check under the declared bounds.
An inferred immutable local copy of a callable retains its defaults. Explicit function-type annotations, mutable bindings, function parameters and results, fields, and generic forwarding require the full argument list. Defaults are not part of function-type identity; a defaulted function can be passed wherever its complete labeled signature is expected.
Collections as arguments# To accept a variable number of values, declare an ordinary list parameter:
Manuscript fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total let total = sum([1, 2, 3]) let empty = sum([]) The argument supplies one list reference. An existing List[Int] can be passed as sum(existing_values) or sum(values: existing_values). The parameter is required even for an empty list. Function values use the ordinary type fn(values: List[Int]) -> Int, and functions with multiple list parameters require labels on every supplied argument.
See collections for list literals and element requirements.
Evaluation order# Execution and argument evaluation follow source order. When arguments contain calls, those calls run in the order written before the outer function receives their results. Named arguments do not reorder execution to match the parameter declaration.
Evaluate the callable expression, including a method receiver, once before its arguments. Then evaluate supplied argument expressions from left to right in their written order. Arrange those values into declaration order after their evaluation, then evaluate omitted defaults in the called function before its body. A failed or nonreturning supplied expression prevents all later arguments and the outer invocation from running. Constructor fields follow the same rule.
This also matters for concurrency APIs : argument preparation and closure creation happen in the caller before any operation starts.
Unit and Never# unit is the single value of Unit. A Unit function may use return, return unit, or fall through the end of its body. Other functions must return a compatible value on every reachable normal exit; bare return and reachable fallthrough are compile errors. There is no implicit return of a block’s final expression.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn check_positive(value: Int) -> Unit: if not (value > 0): return panic(message: "check failed") fn missing_value() -> Int: return panic(message: "Required value is missing") panic has type fn(message: String) -> Never. Never has no values: a Never expression cannot complete normally and is accepted where any value type is expected. This expression rule does not make List[Never] compatible with List[Int] or change function-type identity.
Return completeness uses a conservative control-flow check:
Construct Reachable normal exits return or evaluation of Never None if without else Branch exits plus a path past the statement if with else or exhaustive match The combined exits of all branches or arms for or while with a condition other than literal true A possible exit, because the body may not execute Literal while true Only a reachable break targeting that loop A nested function’s return or nested loop’s break cannot exit the enclosing function or loop. The check uses no additional constant folding.
Expression evaluation also has no normal successor when a necessarily evaluated subexpression cannot complete. This includes callable/receiver preparation, arguments, constructor fields, list elements, interpolation expressions, unary operands, and both operands of a non-short-circuit operator. A right-hand operand of and or or alone does not remove the possible exit, because it may be skipped; their left operand is always required. Creating a function value does not execute its body.
Track evaluation separately from result typing: 1 + panic(message: "stop") has type Int under the operator rules , but cannot complete normally. A failed initializer accordingly prevents the following statement from being reachable.
Manuscript fn incomplete(active: Bool) -> Int: if active: return 1 # Rejected: the false path reaches the end without returning Int. Unreachable statements remain subject to parsing, name resolution, and type checking, but do not add reachable exits. A Never function must have no reachable normal return or fallthrough. A bare call may be used as a statement and its result discarded; non-call expressions cannot be standalone statements.
Calls that suspend# A potentially blocking library call suspends the current lightweight task. It does not implicitly start another task. There are no async declarations or await annotations.
Manuscript has one function kind. Sequential code remains sequential when a library operation suspends; explicit concurrent execution is specified in concurrency .
For functions used as data and the rules for captured values, continue with function values and closures .
Previous: Type compatibility and expected types · Next: Function values and closures

title: Function values and closures
content:
Function values and closures# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index You can store a function in a local binding and pass it to another function. Write an anonymous function with fn; its type has the form fn(value: T) -> U.
A closure is a function value that keeps values from its surrounding scope. It captures snapshots of the bindings it uses. There is no separate function kind that consumes or transfers those captures.
Manuscript fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) let offset = 1 let decrement = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return value - offset let result = apply(value: 3, transform: decrement) Function types retain parameter names. Calls through values may omit the label when the function type has exactly one parameter; multi-parameter function types require labels on every supplied argument. Labels remain part of function-type identity and compatibility even when a call omits one. Calls have the same suspension and evaluation rules as declared functions. Inferred immutable copies retain default arguments ; explicit function types require all parameters.
Function type compatibility# Parameter names, declaration order, parameter types, and result type are all part of function-type identity. Compatibility is invariant: a different label, reordered signature, or different result type requires an explicit adapter function. Caller-written argument order may vary without changing the function’s declared type.
Manuscript fn subtract_one(amount: Int) -> Int: return amount - 1 fn adapt() -> Unit: # Rejected: amount and value are different function-type labels. let invalid: fn(value: Int) -> Int = subtract_one let renamed = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return subtract_one(amount: value) let result = apply(value: 3, transform: renamed) The rejected binding is a negative example; removing it leaves a valid function. Anonymous functions require explicit parameter and result types and an indented body, exactly as specified in the grammar . An annotation on the receiving variable does not omit those signatures. A generic function must be instantiated before it is stored as a value; identity[Int] is a function value, while a bare polymorphic identity is not. Bound method values have the operation’s function type with the receiver already bound and excluded from the parameter list.
An anonymous function forms its own function boundary for return, try, break, and continue. Its control-flow exits cannot exit the containing function or loop. Capture and sharing behavior remains governed by the separate contracts below.
Snapshot captures# A closure snapshots each referenced local binding when created, including a var’s current value. Later reassignment of that local does not change the snapshot. Assigning to a captured outer local is a compile error; shared mutable local cells are not implicit. Shared mutable state is accessed through synchronized services.
Immutable data is retained by value/reference as appropriate for its representation. A service or resource capture retains a reference to the same object, not a deep copy of the object’s state. Bound methods retain their receiver under the same rules. Retained environments survive through garbage collection; there is no move, borrowed capture, or automatic cleanup on closure invocation/discard.
Resource captures# Manuscript with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let reader = fn() -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError]: return file.read(max_bytes: 4096) callbacks.register(handler: reader) # A later callback invocation reports IoError.Closed. The acquisition fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, IoError]; callbacks is an explicitly supplied registration service. The acquired File and callback are ordinary values.
Capturing a resource does not extend its open lifetime or cancel its with cleanup. Resource methods detect closed state at runtime. This applies equally to resources passed through explicit parameters or retained in records.
Concurrent invocation# Concurrency APIs accept ordinary functions. Function parameters, returned functions, function fields, and generic forwarding work exactly as local function values do. See function sharing . A shared resource can still be closed before invocation.
