Capture request-data snapshots and application services for background work, then acquire job resources within that operation. parallel joins before returning, so an enclosing with remains active while its operations run, unless the resource is explicitly closed elsewhere.
These examples use inferred captures. An explicit capture-list syntax has not been selected and is not required by this design. See parallel , background services , and reference sharing .
Previous: Declarations and calls · Next: Conditionals

title: Control flow
content:
Control flow# Core language guide · Design index Use if for a Boolean decision, match for the cases of an alternative, and loops for repeated work. Leaving a block also runs any cleanup registered in that block.
Concept What you will learn Conditionals Branch on Bool values with if and else. Loops Iterate with for and while, and use break and continue. Pattern matching Handle alternatives exhaustively and bind their payloads.

title: Conditionals
content:
Conditionals# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use if to run a block when a Boolean condition is true. Add else to run a different block when it is false. Only the selected branch runs.
Manuscript fn status(active: Bool) -> String: if active: return "Active" else: return "Inactive" Conditions require Bool. The condition in this example is already a Boolean; numeric and text values do not acquire truth values implicitly.
if is a statement and does not produce a value. Evaluate its condition once; execute exactly one selected branch, or neither branch when the condition is false and no else is present. else aligns with the corresponding if. An additional conditional uses else if, not elif.
Each branch has its own lexical scope. Names declared in a branch are not visible after the conditional; assignments to an outer var affect that existing binding. An else if chain checks conditions in order and stops after selecting a branch.
Manuscript fn classify(value: Int) -> String: if value < 0: return "negative" else if value == 0: return "zero" else: return "positive" if 1: is rejected because its condition is Int. let result = if active: ... is rejected because if is not an expression. Use branch-local assignment to a declared var or explicit returns to select a result. The function return rules determine whether all reachable paths return.
Validating inputs# Validation uses the same ordinary control flow as any other decision:
Manuscript fn nonnegative(value: Int) -> Bool: if value < 0: return false return true The early return exits the function on the negative path. The final return runs on the remaining path. Expected failures uses this structure to reject invalid input with a domain error.
Bindings after a branch# Every binding is initialized at declaration. To select a value for use after the conditional, initialize an outer var and assign to it in the branches. Branch-local names stay inside their branch. See bindings .
Use pattern matching when the decision depends on which case of an alternative value is present.
Previous: Function values and closures · Next: Loops

title: Loops
content:
Loops# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use for / in to visit the values in a collection. Use while to repeat work while a Boolean condition is true. Inside either loop, break ends the loop and continue moves to the next iteration.
Loops are statements, not expressions. Manuscript has no labeled loops, loop-result values, integer-range syntax, or user-defined iteration protocol.
Traversing a list# Manuscript fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total The list contains integers. Each iteration binds an element and updates the accumulator. Addition uses checked Int arithmetic, so overflow is a programming fault .
Iterable types and binding# Evaluate a for’s iterable expression once before entering the loop and snapshot its membership. Mutations to the collection do not change the current traversal; referenced elements remain shared. The loop introduces one immutable identifier per iteration; it does not accept a binding pattern or a type annotation. The closed set of supported iterables is:
Iterable Iteration binding type Traversal order List[T] T Position order Set[T] T Insertion order Map[K, V] MapEntry[K, V] Key insertion order MapEntry[K, V] is a record with fields key: K and value: V. It uses the map’s key/value eligibility requirements. Its type and named constructor MapEntry[K, V](key: key, value: value) are imported from @std/collections.ms; field access is ordinary record access. Iteration infers the entry type without requiring an import of its name. It is not a positional pair. Destructure an entry inside the body when convenient.
Manuscript fn total(values: Map[String, Int]) -> Int: var sum = 0 for entry in values: let {key, value} = entry sum = sum + value return sum for [key, value] in values: is rejected at parsing. Iterating a number, text, optional, function, or arbitrary object with a next method is rejected at type checking. Each iteration creates a new binding and lexical scope. Assigning to the iteration binding is rejected; an outer mutable accumulator can be reassigned.
Repeating while a condition holds# Manuscript fn count_down(start: Int) -> Int: var remaining = start while remaining > 0: remaining = remaining - 1 return remaining The condition is tested as a Bool. Each iteration updates remaining; the loop ends when the comparison is false.
A while reevaluates its condition before every iteration, including after continue. A for continues by selecting its next element and terminates after the last element. An empty iterable executes no body. A false initial while condition also executes no body.
Exiting an iteration# break and continue select the nearest enclosing loop within the same function body. They have no labels or arguments and are rejected outside a loop. An anonymous function inside a loop cannot break or continue that enclosing loop. return exits the current function, including when it appears in a loop body. Unreachable loop-control statements still need a valid enclosing loop.
break, continue, and return leave different control-flow paths, but each runs cleanup for the scopes it exits. Each loop iteration has its own scope. Resources registered with with in an iteration close when that iteration exits. A plain let declaration does not register cleanup. See lexical cleanup for the cleanup order and fault rules.
Cancellation# Each loop back-edge is a cancellation checkpoint, so CPU-bound loops respond promptly to cancellation without explicit calls. See propagation and checkpoints for all runtime checkpoints.
Previous: Conditionals · Next: Pattern matching

title: Pattern matching
content:
Pattern matching# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use match to handle the cases of an alternative type. Each branch can give names to the data carried by its case. For example, a payment may be paid, declined, or pending, and each outcome needs different handling.
A match accepts tagged alternative types, including Optional and Result, and operation contract views. Matching numeric or Boolean literals, guards, ranges, nested case patterns, and combined patterns is rejected. match is a statement; it cannot initialize a binding as an expression. The scrutinee evaluates once.
The following function handles the Payment type declared in alternatives :
Manuscript fn describe(payment: Payment) -> String: match payment: Paid(receipt): return "Paid: {receipt}" Declined(reason): return "Declined: {reason}" Pending(reference): return "Pending: {reference}" Payload patterns# Case payloads bind positions in the declaration’s field order. A pattern must give exactly one identifier or _ placeholder per payload field. Pattern payloads are positional even though constructors always use named fields. Nullary cases use a bare case name without ().
Manuscript type Position: case Point(x: Int, y: Int) case Unknown fn horizontal(position: Position) -> Int: match position: Position.Point(horizontal_value, _): return horizontal_value Position.Unknown: return 0 Point(x: local, y: other): is rejected at parsing. Point(x): is rejected for wrong arity. Repeated binding identifiers are rejected, while _ can occur repeatedly because it creates no name. Each arm’s payload bindings and body share a lexical scope nested inside the enclosing scope.
An unqualified case in a pattern resolves within the scrutinee’s alternative type. A qualified case must belong to that exact type. Other.Point(...) cannot match Position, even when its payload types have the same shape. Constructor-expression name lookup instead follows alternative construction .
Exhaustiveness# Match cases bind data without fallthrough; missing alternatives are compile errors. Wildcard cases must be explicit.
Every case in the example returns its own description. Running the Paid branch does not continue into Declined or Pending. The compiler checks that all alternatives are accounted for.
_: is the wildcard arm. It is permitted once, must be last, binds nothing, and covers every case not already handled. Duplicate cases, unknown cases, an arm after the wildcard, and a wildcard after all cases have been explicitly covered are rejected as invalid or unreachable arms. Qualified and unqualified spellings of the same case count as duplicates.
Manuscript fn paid(payment: Payment) -> Bool: match payment: Paid(_): return true _: return false Adding a case to an alternative invalidates exhaustive matches that lack a wildcard. A match with a wildcard remains exhaustive; its wildcard handles the new case. Return completeness is checked across all reachable arms using the function return rules .
Optional and result values# Optional and Result are also alternative types. Matching an optional distinguishes a present value from absence. Matching a result distinguishes success from an expected failure and lets the caller decide what to do with each.
Contract type patterns# A contract view keeps its concrete receiver. Match that view with ConcreteType(receiver) to handle a particular implementation, followed by _: for generic handling. This is a checked recovery of an existing receiver, not a constructor call.
text import Error from "@std/errors.ms" import JsonError from "@std/json.ms" fn describe(cause: Error) -> String: match cause: JsonError(json): match json: InvalidInput: return "Invalid JSON limits" InvalidData: return "Malformed JSON" LimitExceeded: return "JSON limit exceeded" _: return cause.message() The type must be an imported or local nominal record or alternative with an applicable explicit implementation of the scrutinee’s exact contract. Supply exactly one receiver name or _, including for a payloadless alternative. The binding has the concrete type, so its fields, cases, and implemented operations are available inside the arm. Native opaque receivers can be handled by the wildcard, but cannot be named in a concrete type pattern.
Generic patterns name the complete application, such as MyError[Int](cause); MyError[String] is a different pattern. An in-scope generic parameter may supply an argument, as in MyError[T](cause). Matching uses exact runtime nominal identities and type arguments, with the first matching arm selected. Duplicate statically identical type patterns are rejected. A pattern cannot name a different contract, a bare type parameter, or an individual alternative case.
A final wildcard is required even when every currently known implementation is listed: contracts are open to other implementations. It binds nothing; use the original contract value for generic handling. The scrutinee evaluates once; matching retains the same receiver reference and does not copy it, add cleanup, or catch faults and cancellation. See contract views .
Matching resource references# Matching binds ordinary payload values and references. No binding is consumed, and matching does not register resource cleanup. Destructuring bindings use brackets or braces; alternative match cases retain their Case(payload) syntax. See aggregate references .
Previous: Loops · Next: Expected failures with Result

title: Errors and validation
content:
Errors and validation# Core language guide · Design index Choose the outcome that matches the situation: Result for an expected failure with an explanation, Optional for a missing value, and a fault for a broken programming assumption. These pages show how callers respond to each one.
Concept What you will learn Expected failures with Result Return success or domain errors as ordinary values. Error propagation with try Forward compatible errors without hiding faults or cancellation. Programming faults Check invariants and understand task failure after cleanup.

title: Expected failures with Result
content:
Expected failures with Result# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use Result[T, E] when an operation can either succeed with a value of type T or fail with an expected error of type E. Import Result from @std/result.ms.
Return ok(value: ...) for success and error(cause: ...) for failure. Both are ordinary values. A caller can inspect the result with match or pass the error back with try. Validate runtime input with ordinary conditions before doing the work.
Returning a domain error# Manuscript type DiscountError: case InvalidPrice case InvalidPercent fn discount(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[Decimal, DiscountError]: if price < 0d: return error(cause: InvalidPrice) if percent < 0d or percent > 100d: return error(cause: InvalidPercent) return ok(value: price * (1d - percent / 100d)) The function checks inputs before calculating. It returns an explicit error for each invalid condition and wraps the calculated decimal in ok on success.
Handling the result# The following continues the declarations above:
Manuscript fn discount_message(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> String: let outcome = discount(price: price, percent: percent) match outcome: ok(value): return "Discounted price: {value}" error(cause): return "Discount could not be calculated." This caller chooses a response for either outcome. Another caller could inspect cause with a further match or propagate it with try .
A common error boundary# Import Error from @std/errors.ms when a boundary should accept multiple error domains. It is an ordinary interface declaring message() -> String. Standard errors implement it; user errors can declare an ordinary impl Error in their defining module.
text import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import Error from "@std/errors.ms" import hex_decode from "@std/encoding.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" fn decode(text: String) -> Result[Bytes, Error]: match hex_decode(text: text, max_bytes: 1024): ok(value): return ok(value: value) error(cause): return error(cause: Error(value: cause)) The conversion preserves the original EncodingError case and payload. A caller may handle any error with cause.message(), or select a specific implementation using a contract type pattern . A caller that needs only encoding errors can keep Result[Bytes, EncodingError] and match its cases directly.
Error is explicitly imported and has no special inheritance or exception machinery. Other error values remain legal in Result[T, E]. Conversion at a generic boundary is explicit, and try still requires the same error type .
Results and concurrent execution# Returning error(cause: cause) is normal function completion. In parallel, the domain Result remains the operation’s return value and does not cancel siblings. The outer API result separately reports ExecutionError; see parallel operations . A Background service reports completion-only domain errors through its configured failure observer.
Use Optional for absence without an error explanation and explicit faults for broken programming invariants.
Previous: Pattern matching · Next: Error propagation with try

title: Error propagation with try
content:
Error propagation with try# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use try to continue with a successful Result value or immediately return its error to your caller. This is useful when the current function cannot handle the expected failure itself.
try expression unwraps ok; on error, it returns that error from the enclosing function. The function must return a compatible Result.
The following continues the discount and DiscountError declarations in expected failures :
Manuscript fn discounted_label(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[String, DiscountError]: let value = try discount(price: price, percent: percent) return ok(value: "Discounted price: {value}") Success and failure paths# When discount returns ok, value contains the Decimal payload and the function builds its label. When it returns error, the enclosing function returns that error instead of executing the remaining statements.
The success types differ: the called function returns a decimal, while the enclosing function returns text. Both use DiscountError, so the error can be forwarded unchanged.
Error compatibility# A caller with a different error contract must translate the error explicitly using pattern matching . try does not invent a conversion or combine unrelated error types into an implicit union.
If the called operation returns Result[T, E], the function using try must return Result[U, E]. The success type may change from T to U, but the error type E must be exactly the same. Two error types are not interchangeable just because they implement the same interface. Convert explicitly before constructing the Result that try uses.
A common Error boundary follows the same rule: first match the Result and construct Error(value: cause) on its error branch, then use try on the explicitly converted Result. See common error boundaries .
The expression after try is evaluated once. Try binds more tightly than arithmetic, so try operation() + 1 means (try operation()) + 1.
The compiler rejects try when:
its expression is not a Result; its error type differs from the enclosing function’s error type; the enclosing function or test returns Unit. Inside an anonymous function, try returns from that anonymous function, not from its caller or surrounding function. See expressions and type compatibility .
Cleanup and cancellation# try does not catch programming faults or parent cancellation. A propagated error is a return path and performs lexical cleanup for the scopes it leaves. A programming fault or parent cancellation follows its own unwinding rules.
Previous: Expected failures with Result · Next: Programming faults

title: Programming faults
content:
Programming faults# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A programming fault means an assumption the code relies on has failed. Use ordinary conditional returns to check that assumption. For ordinary invalid user input, use conditions and return a Result error so the caller can respond.
Invariant checks# Use ordinary if and return control flow to check an invariant. Import panic from @std/faults.ms when a violated invariant must produce a programming fault.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn discount_validated(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Decimal: if price <= 0d: return panic(message: "Price must be positive") if percent <= 0d or percent >= 100d: return panic(message: "Percent must be positive and below 100") return price * (1d - percent / 100d) This example expects strictly positive prices and percentages below 100 as preconditions. A violation is treated as a programming fault. Use the validating discount function in expected failures when these values come from ordinary runtime input.
Explicit faults# An explicit panic(message: message) produces a programming fault when code determines that an invariant has failed.
Its source type is fn(message: String) -> Never. It never completes normally; a call can appear where any expression result type is expected, including an Int return position. This does not create a catchable expected-error value or permit normal fallthrough in a non-Unit function. See Unit, Never, and return completeness .
Manuscript panic(message: "Required invariant was violated.") A fault aborts the current operation after cleanup. Programming faults are distinct from expected Result errors.
Cleanup and observation# Cleanup still runs after a fault. A cleanup fault can replace a pending return, domain error, or cancellation, while secondary faults are retained as diagnostics. The full selection and cleanup rules are in lexical cleanup .
An active parallel caller observes an operation fault as ExecutionError.Crashed after siblings are cancelled and joined. Background faults go to the service’s failure observer. A caller’s own fault still unwinds it; try only propagates Result errors. See execution errors .
Previous: Error propagation with try

title: Standard library
content:
Standard library guide# Design index Use this chapter to find standard types and operations. Most names need an explicit import from an @std/...ms module. Start with the type catalog, or choose a task from the sections below. The package pages list exact signatures and explain their limits.
API reference# Browse all implemented modules , including the intrinsic prelude. The reference is generated from compiler definitions; special call rules cover APIs with contextual signatures.
Reading order# 1. Standard types # Core and standard types — Find a type, its meaning, and its import path. Standard imports and API typing — Check exact import identities, callable types, and standard API rules. 2. Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes # Background services — Start work under a service that tracks it and waits during shutdown. 3. Data, state, and I/O # Minimum data operations — Look up the basic methods on collections, text, bytes, and numeric values. Readers, writers, and streams — Read and write bytes, recognize end-of-input, and close streams. Local queues — Use a bounded FIFO locally, or share it through Synchronized. Synchronized values, pools, and leases — Coordinate shared state and acquire a pool lease with scoped cleanup. Builders and immutable snapshots — Construct a value with synchronized mutation, then freeze an immutable snapshot. 4. Application hosts # HTTP request hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. CLI application hosts 5. General-purpose packages # JavaScript built-in coverage — Find method equivalents and semantic differences. Node.js and Go coverage — See what is implemented and what remains outside the library. Common package contracts — Review the errors, limits, and authority rules shared by packages. Expanded library conformance — Find executable checks for package behavior and limits. Runtime facilities# These are ordinary library facilities with effect, sharing, lifetime, and cancellation contracts. They add no concurrency syntax. Host-created requests, sessions, applications, and CLI runs establish fixed execution contexts. Parallel APIs join before returning; background services implement Closeable and join during shutdown.
Standard imports, immutable data, CLI streams, and concurrent APIs have concrete signatures. Queue, pool, builder, HTTP server, and buffered subprocess APIs have concrete contracts. The general-purpose package guide adds executable data, codec, filesystem, cryptographic, networking and HTTP client operations. See outstanding decisions .

title: Standard types
content:
Standard types# Guide index · Design index The catalog tells you what a type means and where to import it. The API-typing page is the detailed reference for how standard names resolve and how concurrent callables and results are checked.
Core and standard types — Find a type, its meaning, and its import path. Standard imports and API typing — Check exact import identities, callable types, and standard API rules.

title: Core and standard types
content:
Core and standard types# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use this table to find a type’s meaning and import path. “Implicit intrinsic” means the type is available without an import. Import other type names from the listed module when you use them in source.
Type Meaning Import from Bool true or false Implicit intrinsic Int Signed 64-bit integer; checked arithmetic Implicit intrinsic Float IEEE 754 binary64 Implicit intrinsic Decimal Base-10, 34 significant digits; round half to even @std/decimal.ms String Immutable, valid UTF-8 text Implicit intrinsic Bytes Immutable byte sequence @std/bytes.ms Unit One value, unit Implicit intrinsic Never No possible value Implicit intrinsic List[T], Map[K, V], Set[T] Immutable homogeneous collections with arbitrary value elements; keys require Hashable @std/collections.ms MapEntry[K, V] Immutable standard record with key: K and value: V; map iteration yields entries @std/collections.ms Optional[T] some(value: value) or none @std/optional.ms Result[T, E] ok(value: value) or error(cause: cause) @std/result.ms ExecutionError Joined-group timeout or crash @std/tasks.ms Background Synchronized service managing work under a fixed lifetime @std/tasks.ms WorkStatus, StartError, BackgroundFailure Background status, admission failure, and failure reports @std/tasks.ms OperationId Identity of a runtime operation, used for diagnostics and Background status/cancellation @std/tasks.ms Synchronized[T], SynchronizedGuard[T] Shared value protected by a scoped mutex guard @std/sync.ms Closeable Standard close() -> Unit cleanup contract @std/cleanup.ms File, ReadStream, WriteStream Resource contracts; all implementations synchronize lifecycle access @std/io.ms Duration, Instant Checked nanosecond duration and monotonic clock instant @std/time.ms Files, IoError File capability contract and expected I/O failures @std/io.ms Clock Monotonic clock capability contract @std/time.ms Functions and closures are ordinary values; runtime tasks are not exposed as source ownership types. Fixed parallel result packs preserve positional types and use bracket destructuring; they are not homogeneous lists.
References do not extend an object’s open lifetime. Use with for deterministic release and Result for expected operation failures. See parallel , background services , and Closeable .
The standard API contract defines visibility, signatures, optional arguments, and pack typing.
General-purpose types# The package guide adds opaque BigInt (@std/bigint.ms), Regex (@std/regex.ms) and wall-clock Timestamp (@std/time.ms); JsonValue/JsonLimits (@std/json.ms); structured format/filesystem/archive records; and package-specific error types (see error contracts ). New capability contracts are FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock and System, available through imported host accessors. TCP/TLS Connection, Listener and DatagramSocket are acquired through the existing Network authority. All names remain individually imported; no additions enter the intrinsic prelude. See coverage for implemented equivalents and remaining gaps.

title: Standard imports and API typing
content:
Standard imports and API typing# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Most standard names must be imported explicitly. Only six intrinsic types and three compiler bounds are available automatically. Native implementation or special compiler support does not make a name globally visible.
This page is the exact reference for standard exports, their identities, and API typing. A trusted manifest may implement these declarations but cannot change their source identities or typing rules.
Names and identity# Every module implicitly sees only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, Never, Equal, and Hashable, as specified by module declarations . The two bounds describe equality and hashing; passing values requires no sharing bound. Ordinary behavior requirements use imported operation contracts.
@std is a reserved directory supplied by the pinned compiler/runtime distribution. Each path below is a standard module, and each name is an individual export. There are no wildcard imports or automatic imports of other exports from the same module.
Module Exports @std/decimal.ms Decimal @std/bytes.ms Bytes @std/collections.ms List, Map, Set, MapEntry @std/optional.ms Optional @std/result.ms Result @std/cleanup.ms Closeable @std/tasks.ms parallel, check_cancelled, ExecutionError, OperationId, Background, BackgroundFailure, WorkStatus, StartError @std/faults.ms panic @std/time.ms Duration, Instant, Clock, clock, wall_clock @std/io.ms Files, File, ReadStream, WriteStream, IoError, stdin, stdout, stderr, files @std/cli.ms arguments, environment Manuscript import Result from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" Imports establish stable nominal identities independent of the application. Imported names follow ordinary collision and shadowing rules; unimported standard names are not reserved. A local declaration with the same spelling never acquires standard operators, cleanup recognition, callback checks, or native members.
The general-purpose package guide documents additional module exports and common errors . Imported accessors provide FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock, System, and Network services. Network includes TCP/UDP/TLS/client/DNS operations. These additions retain explicit imports and nominal identities.
Syntax and compiler support# Some library identities need compiler support while remaining explicit exports:
Ordinary bracket literals require the canonical List import in the module. The tasks literal of the imported parallel binding is a positional pack and does not require List. A d-suffixed literal requires the canonical Decimal import. Decimal arithmetic and interpolation keep their specified behavior. Optional and Result are standard alternatives with ordinary case lookup. try recognizes the canonical Result identity; a user-defined alternative named Result does not qualify. for, collection derivation, and guarded layout recognize the standard collection identities. MapEntry is an exported record; map iteration can infer it without importing its name. with recognizes the canonical Closeable implementation, or an operation contract declaring the exact close signature. A module writing impl Closeable or a Closeable bound imports that name; using an already-typed resource does not require an otherwise unused import. Runtime API special checks attach to the resolved standard callee. A user-defined parallel is an ordinary function and never receives pack rules. A missing or substituted List/Decimal import rejects the corresponding literal during resolution/type checking. Inferred library values may be matched, traversed, or used through their declared members without importing every type in their public signatures. Naming such a type or using its unqualified expression constructors requires its own import. Primitive receiver members in the data API are fixed standard bindings and can likewise produce inferred library values; they add no ambient type names. Importing a type supplies its declaration; imported host accessor functions return services from the current execution.
OperationId is the single opaque identity for runtime operations, whether started by a joined group or admitted by a Background service. It has no source constructor and no implicit equality or hashing, and it grants no scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. A Background service’s status and cancel act only on IDs it admitted. WorkStatus has nullary cases Running, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled, Crashed, and Unknown; qualify these case names when necessary. StartError has Closed and Full. IoError has Closed, InvalidInput, Unavailable, and Failed(message: String). These are ordinary alternatives. Execution errors are defined in joining .
Manuscript fn panic(message: String) -> Never fn check_cancelled() -> Unit These lines specify bindings rather than complete source modules. check_cancelled unwinds the current execution if it has stopped; it returns Unit otherwise.
Joined concurrency# All concurrency names are explicit library exports. The call below requires the parallel import from @std/tasks.ms; no concurrency operation, error type, work identity, or service expands the intrinsic type/bound list. Every concurrency name, including check_cancelled and OperationId, is exported by @std/tasks.ms. Timeouts and scheduling are implemented by library/runtime bindings.
parallel requires tasks and permits only the optional named argument timeout: Duration. Omission means no added limit; an inherited deadline still applies. Negative timeouts fault. Zero-timeout, stop, join, and outcome rules follow joining outcomes .
tasks must be a bracket literal, optionally grouped in parentheses. Each position must independently resolve to a zero-parameter function fn() -> Ri. The binding produces Result[Pack[R1, …, Rn], ExecutionError]. Here Pack is compiler notation, with no source type-name spelling or source constructor. Existing lists are rejected.
Standard concurrency callbacks are ordinary function values. Parameters, fields, collections, and generic forwarding preserve their call behavior. Operations may return functions or services; resource lifetime remains governed by explicit cleanup.
Function values# parallel requires a direct call because its literal pack determines a heterogeneous result shape. The Background constructor also remains a direct constructor call.
background.start and HTTP admission methods may be saved or passed to helpers. Source contracts can expose ordinary callback-taking operations, including wrappers around background submission.
Inferred result packs# A pack can be inferred into a local, carried through an inferred generic type argument, bound in a Result match, returned through a generic T, and destructured with exact positional arity. It cannot be written in an annotation, explicit type argument, field, or named function signature. Nested inferred packs retain their exact shape. Pack identity is the ordered sequence of position types; the empty pack is distinct from Unit and List. Packs may be passed between operations, but have no equality, hashing, iteration, field access, or indexing. An ordinary generic identity function can preserve a parallel pack without a new source syntax.
Background service# Background(limit: Int) constructs a synchronized native service under the current execution context. limit must be positive. Its only optional arguments are reporter: fn(failure: BackgroundFailure) -> Unit, drain: Duration, and history_limit: Int. The defaults are the host diagnostic sink, zero drain, and 128 completed statuses. drain and history_limit must be nonnegative. Retained reporter resources must remain usable through service shutdown.
Manuscript type BackgroundFailure: case Failed(operation: OperationId, cause: String) case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String) # Operations of the native Background service: fn start(operation: fn() -> Result[Unit, String]) -> Result[OperationId, StartError] fn cancel(id: OperationId) -> Unit fn status(id: OperationId) -> WorkStatus fn close() -> Unit start accepts an ordinary callable. This is one operation signature: Operations without domain errors explicitly return ok(value: unit), and operations with domain error types explicitly translate them to String using match. There is no generic method, implicit formatting of arbitrary errors, or overload. Background explicitly implements Closeable in the standard binding.
Failure reporting# The reporter receives Failed for a returned String error and Crashed for a programming fault. Cancellation changes status rather than producing a domain error. Reporter calls are serialized, may suspend, and run outside transition locks under a shielded service context. Shutdown waits for them.
At most limit completion reports may be pending. Capacity exhaustion or a reporter fault sends both the original diagnostic and the reporting failure/overflow diagnostic to the host sink. A reporter fault never invokes the reporter recursively. The sink itself has a bounded buffer; overflow increments a retained counter and emits a host stderr diagnostic. Uncooperative reporters remain subject to host escalation.
Status eviction never reuses an ID for different work. An ID the service did not admit, including one from another service or a joined group, returns Unknown from status and is a no-op for cancellation.
Capabilities and data operations# The host’s authority roots and stream signatures are defined by CLI hosts and streams . Standard collection, byte, text, numeric, and duration members are defined in minimum data operations . Source code cannot add implementations or members to intrinsic or standard-library types. Source types may implement standard contracts in their defining module or through local extensions .
General user type packs, optional source parameters, generic operations, and third-party dependency package imports are unsupported. HTTP host registration follows the bounded request API .
Data services and additional host capabilities# @std/queues.ms exports Queue; @std/sync.ms exports Synchronized and SynchronizedGuard; @std/pools.ms exports Pool, Lease, and PoolError; @std/builders.ms exports ListBuilder, MapBuilder, SetBuilder, BytesBuilder, and StringBuilder. Their exact contracts live in queues , synchronized values and pools , and builders . None is ambient. Opaque constructor parameter names are not source fields.
@std/time.ms also exports sleep(duration: Duration) -> Unit, a sequential cancellable delay. Negative duration faults; zero performs a cancellation checkpoint.
@std/http.ms exports the bounded request host types in HTTP . Network.serve accepts an ordinary handler and may be stored as a bound method. @std/process.ms exports Commands, CommandOutput, and CommandError in streams . Import network() from @std/http.ms and commands() from @std/process.ms to obtain those host services.

title: Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes
content:
Concurrency services# Guide index · Design index Use parallel for a fixed set of operations and Background for work managed by a longer-lived service. Parallel calls wait for their started work before returning. A background service waits during shutdown.
Parallel operations Background services — Start work under a service that tracks it and waits during shutdown.

title: Background services
content:
Background services# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use Background for work managed by an application or component rather than by the caller’s immediate request. Import it from @std/tasks.ms. The service tracks its operations and implements Closeable so shutdown can wait for them.
You can create several services and pass them as ordinary parameters. The API reference defines which callables they accept.
Manuscript with emails = Background(limit: 32): with indexing = Background(limit: 4): serve(emails: emails, indexing: indexing) The constructing host supplies the execution parent. Construct application services under the application lifetime, session services under the session lifetime, and request services under the request lifetime. Calling a service from another context never reparents it.
Starting work# Manuscript import Result from "@std/result.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" type MailError: case Rejected interface Mailer: fn send(to: String) -> Result[Unit, MailError] fn enqueue(emails: Background, mailer: Mailer, address: String) -> Result[OperationId, StartError]: let send = fn() -> Result[Unit, String]: match mailer.send(to: address): ok(_): return ok(value: unit) error(_): return error(cause: "Email delivery failed") return emails.start(operation: send) Start does not wait for capacity. Accepting work, reserving a slot, and checking closure happen atomically. The limit counts accepted operations whose completion has not yet been committed. Accepted work starts without an extra unbounded queue; rejected work never runs.
Completion frees the slot before failure reporting, so a slow reporter cannot hold up new admission. Start does not retry automatically.
Background operations return Result[Unit, String]: explicit ok(value: unit) on success, or a String error after domain-error adaptation. Successful operations produce status; failures reach the reporter. One operation’s failure does not cancel unrelated operations.
The returned OperationId is the same identity used in execution errors, failure reports, and traces. With this service, it supports status and cancellation without transferring shutdown responsibility. The standard API contract defines signatures, status retention, constructor defaults, bounded reporting, and fallback diagnostics.
Closures retain ordinary captured references. Capture a request-data snapshot and application services, then acquire resources inside the operation’s own with blocks. Capturing a request’s resource does not extend its lifetime; use after close returns a resource-specific error. Closure syntax is the ordinary syntax in function values and closures .
Bind the operation’s data in an ordinary closure; there is no function-plus-arguments submission form.
Lifetime and shutdown# Pass Background directly. Its start binding follows the direct-call restriction . Sharing or dropping a service reference or work ID does not change its lifetime or cancel work. Work never transfers between services.
close() -> Unit is idempotent and does not finish until admitted work and its cleanup have ended:
Close admission atomically across all aliases. Allow a configured drain period; the default is no drain delay. Request cancellation of unfinished operations. Join every admitted operation and finish bounded reporting/cleanup. Cancelling a submitting request does not cancel accepted work. Cancelling the service’s fixed parent does cancel its operations, even if a drain period was configured. A service’s close cannot join itself; host/component code outside its operations performs shutdown.
Hosts choose overall budgets, admission/reporting settings, and an escalation policy for uncooperative work. Expiry is not successful joining; the runtime cannot forcibly terminate an arbitrary goroutine safely. Closing a service before closing its application dependencies is required.
This is process-local execution, not durable delivery. Work that must survive restart needs a durable queue. If acknowledgement can be lost during request cancellation, use application idempotency keys to make resubmission safe.
Runtime and library responsibilities# The Go runtime supplies operation start, stop, join, and synchronization. Admission, reporting, and shutdown policy can be implemented over those primitives. The initial implementation may provide the service in Go behind the same imported API. These native primitives are implementation details, not source intrinsics. The compiler validates ordinary callback signatures; service admission, status retention, reporting, drain, cancellation, and joining remain library/runtime behavior.

title: Data, state, and I/O
content:
Data, state, and I/O# Guide index · Design index Choose a facility based on what you need to do: work with data values, read or write streams, pass values through a queue, coordinate shared state, or build a value locally. I/O resources need explicit cleanup.
Minimum data operations — Look up the basic methods on collections, text, bytes, and numeric values.
Readers, writers, and streams — Read and write bytes, recognize end-of-input, and close streams.
Local queues — Use a bounded FIFO locally, or share it through Synchronized.
Synchronized values, pools, and leases — Coordinate shared state and acquire a pool lease with scoped cleanup.
Builders and sealed results — Construct a value with synchronized mutation, then seal the builder and obtain its result.

title: Minimum data operations
content:
Core data operations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index This is the reference for basic methods on standard data types. These methods belong to the canonical intrinsic or imported receiver type. They do not introduce new global names or compiler bounds.
Import standard types when naming them. Ordinary bracket list literals need List. A type inferred from a return value does not need its own import unless you name it in source. Updates mutate records and collections in place. Use .clone() first to preserve their current contents. Transformations such as map, filter, slice, concat, sorted, and set algebra still return new collections. Sizes and indexes use Int; allocation failure is a host failure.
A single-parameter operation may omit its argument label. Multi-parameter operations require the exact labels below.
JavaScript built-in coverage describes the expanded receiver surface and exact differences.
Collections# Receiver or constructor Signature/result List[T] length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[T] List[T] append(value: T) -> List[T]; concat(values: List[T]) -> List[T] Map[K, V]() Empty Map[K, V] Map[K, V] length() -> Int; get(key: K) -> Optional[V]; contains(key: K) -> Bool Map[K, V] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Map[K, V]; without(key: K) -> Map[K, V] Set[T]() Empty Set[T] Set[T] length() -> Int; contains(value: T) -> Bool Set[T] with_value(value: T) -> Set[T]; without(value: T) -> Set[T] All existing element and key bounds apply. An empty Map/Set constructor requires explicit type arguments or a complete expected application; it supplies no inference evidence by itself. List construction uses the existing bracket literal. Negative or out-of-range list indexes return none. A size exceeding MaxInt64 faults.
Maps and sets traverse in insertion order. Replacing an equal map key retains its original key value and first insertion position; adding an existing set element retains its original value and position. Removing an absent key/element is a value-preserving operation. Removing and then adding places the new entry at the end. Equality remains independent of insertion order. A simple implementation may copy storage on update; builder APIs are specified separately once their signatures are settled.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn positives(values: List[Int]) -> List[Int]: var result: List[Int] = [] for value in values: if value > 0: result = result.append(value: value) return result test "dynamic mutable data and explicit copies": if not (positives(values: [3, -1, 2]) == [3, 2]): return panic(message: "check failed") let absent: Optional[Int] = none if not ([1].get(index: 5) == absent): return panic(message: "check failed") let original = Map[String, Int]().with_entry(key: "a", value: 1) let updated = original.clone().with_entry(key: "b", value: 2).with_entry(key: "a", value: 3) if not (original.get(key: "a") == some(value: 1)): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (updated.get(key: "a") == some(value: 3)): return panic(message: "check failed") Strings and bytes# Receiver or constructor Signature/result String byte_length() -> Int; to_bytes() -> Bytes; parse_int() -> Optional[Int] Bytes(values: List[Int]) Immutable bytes; each value must be 0–255, otherwise a programming fault Bytes length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[Int]; concat(values: Bytes) -> Bytes Bytes to_text() -> Optional[String] String.to_bytes uses UTF-8. Bytes.to_text succeeds exactly for valid UTF-8, preserving contents without normalization; invalid bytes produce none. Byte get follows list index behavior and returns the unsigned byte as Int. An empty Bytes(values: []) is valid.
parse_int accepts exactly an optional ASCII + or - followed by one or more ASCII decimal digits and an in-range mathematical value. It permits leading zeros, rejects whitespace, separators, fractions, exponents, and any unconsumed character, and returns none for invalid or out-of-range input. Runtime parsing is distinct from the stricter source literal grammar. Additional scalar indexing, text transformations, collection algorithms, and numeric formatting are described in JavaScript built-in coverage ; the canonical signatures live in the generated reference. Grapheme and locale operations remain unsupported.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" test "explicit byte conversion": if not ("é".byte_length() == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("é".to_bytes().to_text() == some(value: "é")): return panic(message: "check failed") let invalid: Optional[String] = none if not (Bytes(values: [255]).to_text() == invalid): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("-007".parse_int() == some(value: -7)): return panic(message: "check failed") Numeric and time conversion# Receiver Signature/result Int to_float() -> Float; to_decimal() -> Decimal Float truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Decimal to_float() -> Float; truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Int milliseconds, seconds, minutes members producing Duration Int→Decimal is exact. Int→Float and Decimal→Float round once to nearest binary64, ties to even. Decimal→Float may produce signed infinity or signed zero under the Float rules. Truncation discards the fractional part toward zero, then checks the mathematical integer against the exact signed 64-bit limits before conversion. NaN, infinities, or an out-of-range integer yield none; do not compare against a rounded Float representation of MaxInt64 and then use a Go cast.
Duration is a signed 64-bit count of nanoseconds. The three unit members work on any Int expression and multiply by 1,000,000, 1,000,000,000, or 60,000,000,000 with overflow checks. Instant is an opaque monotonic instant in the current run’s clock domain; it has no source constructor. Clock adapters and injected test clocks must preserve a single comparable domain within a run. Cross-domain comparison or subtraction faults. Duration arithmetic and Instant shifts/differences check overflow; these compiler-defined operations are enumerated in the operator table .
Boundary expectations: 1e300.truncate_to_int() is none; converting Float +2^63 to Int is none, while Float -2^63 succeeds. 2.seconds is 2,000,000,000 nanoseconds. Unsupported unit names and mixed arithmetic such as 2.seconds + 1 are type errors.

title: Readers, writers, and streams
content:
Readers, writers, and streams# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A stream reads or writes bytes over time. Its close operation releases the underlying resource. Native hosts and source fakes can both implement the contracts below.
The host supplies synchronized ReadStream, WriteStream, and File views. All stream contract values are safe to share; closing a stream still closes it through every alias.
Manuscript interface ReadStream: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface WriteStream: fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface File: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit Read requires positive max_bytes or returns IoError.InvalidInput. ok(some(bytes)) contains 1 through max_bytes bytes; ok(none) is EOF. Empty chunks never represent EOF. The bound limits each read, not total file size. Write waits until all bytes are accepted or an error occurs; empty writes succeed without I/O. An error may follow a partial external write and supplies no rollback. Internal buffering is bounded with backpressure.
Native wrappers serialize simultaneous reads/writes without holding a lifecycle lock during blocking I/O. Close marks admission closed, interrupts active I/O where supported, waits for admitted I/O to end, and releases the handle once. Later calls return IoError.Closed. Concurrent close callers wait for the same release/fault. A flag check followed by unsynchronized handle use is insufficient. Uncancellable I/O can delay release and requires host escalation; expected completion errors belong to read/write, and unexpected release failures are cleanup faults.
Contract values declaring these exact close operations are eligible for with under Closeable ; cleanup does not require concurrent sharing. Source fakes implement the selected stream contract and explicitly construct contract views when substituting for standard host roots or acquisitions; no native File constructor or contract inheritance is needed. Adapters honor cancellation and undelivered acquisition . The bounded subprocess facility is exported by @std/process.ms. Import commands() -> Commands from @std/process.ms to obtain the host command service:
Manuscript # Commands fn run(program: String, arguments: List[String], input: Bytes, max_output_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[CommandOutput, CommandError] type CommandOutput: exit_code: Int stdout: Bytes stderr: Bytes CommandError has InvalidInput, Unavailable, TimedOut, OutputLimit, and Failed(message: String). Empty/NUL program names, NUL arguments, negative bounds, and negative timeout return InvalidInput. The total stdout plus stderr bound is nonnegative. Nonzero ordinary exit is an ok output with that code. Timeout or output overflow stops and joins the process before returning its error; caller cancellation unwinds after joining. POSIX process groups include descendants in termination.
On platforms without process-group support the wrapper controls the direct process, with bounded pipe completion; descendant supervision needs a platform host contract. Interactive subprocess streams remain separate future contracts; network sockets , streaming HTTP and WebSockets are implemented.

title: Local queues
content:
Local queues# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Queue[T] is a mutable FIFO for single-threaded use. Import it from @std/queues.ms. Omit capacity for an unbounded queue, or supply a positive capacity to bound it. Every operation returns immediately: enqueue returns false when full, and dequeue returns none when empty.
Manuscript import Queue from "@std/queues.ms" import panic from "@std/faults.ms" test "a local queue": let queue = Queue[Int]() queue.enqueue(10) match queue.dequeue(): some(value): if value != 10: return panic("unexpected value") none: return panic("queue is empty") API# Queue[T]() creates an empty, unbounded queue. Queue[T](capacity: Int) creates an empty queue with a fixed positive capacity. A nonpositive capacity is a programming fault. Elements may be any value type, including functions and contract views. The queue is an opaque reference without equality or hashing; aliases and saved methods use the same queue.
Manuscript fn enqueue(value: T) -> Bool fn dequeue() -> Optional[T] fn peek() -> Optional[T] fn length() -> Int fn is_empty() -> Bool enqueue appends at the back and returns true, or leaves a bounded queue unchanged and returns false when full. An unbounded queue grows as needed and always accepts an enqueue. dequeue removes the oldest value; peek reads it without removal. Both return none when empty. Dequeuing frees capacity, and an empty queue may be reused. There is no waiting, close operation, cleanup registration, or end-of-stream state. A queue cannot be a with initializer.
Sharing a queue# For concurrent access, put the queue in one Synchronized[Queue[T]] and hold its guard throughout every operation, including reads. Each caller acquires its own guard from the same wrapper:
Manuscript import Queue from "@std/queues.ms" import Synchronized from "@std/sync.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn make_queue() -> Synchronized[Queue[Int]]: return Synchronized(value: Queue[Int](capacity: 16)) fn enqueue(shared: Synchronized[Queue[Int]], value: Int) -> Bool: with locked = shared.lock(): return locked.get().enqueue(value) fn dequeue(shared: Synchronized[Queue[Int]]) -> Optional[Int]: with locked = shared.lock(): return locked.get().dequeue() The queue itself has no mutex. The compiler allows references to be passed freely and does not enforce this locking discipline. A queue or bound method obtained through locked.get() remains an alias after the guard closes; it must not be used concurrently outside that lock. Wrapping the same queue in two separate synchronized containers does not coordinate them. Store the queue directly in one wrapper and share that wrapper.
Wrapping a queue serializes access; it does not add waiting for values or free capacity. Never wait for another operation to fill or drain the queue while holding its lock. Lock acquisition follows the ordinary Synchronized cancellation and cleanup rules .
Previous: Readers, writers, and streams · Next: Synchronized values, pools, and leases

title: Synchronized values, pools, and leases
content:
Synchronized values, pools, and leases# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use synchronized services for application state shared by requests and background work. A pool supplies leases: acquire a lease in a with block, then return it to the pool through close. Keeping a reference to the lease does not extend its lifetime.
Pool references can be shared by requests and background work. A job acquires its own lease under its own scope. Retaining a lease reference does not prolong its lease lifetime.
Access and closure must be coordinated: close waits for or cancels outstanding operations before allowing reuse, and stale aliases report closed state rather than using a connection assigned to another caller. Supported simultaneous use is explicit in the adapter/service contract.
Synchronized# Import Synchronized and, when an annotation needs it, SynchronizedGuard from @std/sync.ms. Synchronized[T](value: T) is an opaque reference containing one value and one mutex. Aliases share both. Its only operation is lock() -> SynchronizedGuard[T].
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Synchronized from "@std/sync.ms" test "a complete update holds one lock": let counter = Synchronized(value: 0) with locked = counter.lock(): locked.set(value: locked.get() + 1) with locked = counter.lock(): if not (locked.get() == 1): return panic(message: "check failed") lock() waits cancellably for exclusive admission. The guard exposes get() -> T, set(value: T) -> Unit, and close() -> Unit; it has no source constructor and implements Closeable. Use with to release it on normal exit, return, loop exits, propagated errors, faults, and cancellation. The synchronized container itself has no close operation. Neither type has equality or hashing.
The lock remains held across ordinary calls and suspension until the guard closes. Cancellation never forcibly releases an executing critical section: the holder unwinds and performs shielded cleanup first. An acquisition that loses to cancellation before delivery releases the undelivered guard. There is no FIFO or starvation-freedom guarantee.
Guard aliases and saved methods use the same active acquisition. Get/set and release coordinate atomically; after release, get/set fault through every alias, even after another task acquires the container. Close is idempotent and cannot release a later acquisition. A guard may pass through helpers or be captured by concurrent work. Calls through the same guard are individually safe, but sharing it does not serialize complete sequences between those callers; acquire separately for independent critical sections.
Reacquiring a lock held by the current operation or an execution ancestor faults before waiting, including from a nested joined task and shielded cleanup. Cycles between independent operations or different locks remain a programming error; acquire multiple locks in a consistent order. Keep critical sections short and avoid waiting for work that needs a held lock.
Set replaces the stored value immediately. Faults, propagated errors, and cancellation do not roll back committed writes or external effects. Get returns the stored value, including the same mutable record or collection reference. Use .clone() while holding the guard to retain separate outer storage; nested references remain shared. The lock protects access made while held; it does not attach synchronization to every reachable object. A mutable record, collection, or local Queue obtained through get must be used entirely within the guard scope when shared, and all callers must acquire the same wrapper. Put related fields in one record inside one Synchronized to update their invariant together.
Synchronized replaces the former State API. Migrate each get/set/swap sequence to a with locked = value.lock() scope; use guard get/set within that scope. There is no implicit transaction, retry callback, mutable-reference syntax, or sharing bound.
Pools and leases# Import Pool, Lease, and PoolError from @std/pools.ms. Pool[T](resources: List[T]) owns a nonempty fixed collection of distinct resource receivers. T must be a concrete operation-contract view declaring close() -> Unit. Construct views explicitly before pooling; a type variable’s implementation bound does not establish this representation at construction. The supplied resources must remain under the pool’s exclusive lifecycle management.
Manuscript # Pool[T] fn acquire() -> Result[Lease[T], PoolError] fn close() -> Unit # Lease[T] fn get() -> Result[T, PoolError] fn close() -> Unit Acquire waits cancellably for capacity. Closed admission returns PoolError.Closed. Delivery that loses to cancellation releases its lease before unwind. Pool and lease objects are opaque, and eligible for with; they have no equality or hashing.
Get returns a guarded contract view. Calls through that view admit under the lease’s lifetime, including method values saved before release. Closing the view releases the lease. Lease close stops admission, cancels and joins admitted operations, and returns capacity exactly once; concurrent closers join the same release. A later get returns Closed. Stale I/O views return IoError.Closed; stale operations without an I/O error result fault. Release during an admitted operation interrupts it; I/O reports Closed, and other contracts report a programming fault unless caller cancellation already applies.
Pool close stops acquisition, wakes waiters, invalidates every lease, joins its operations, then closes owned receivers in reverse supplied order. It is idempotent; concurrent callers observe the same release fault. A lease or pool cannot join its own active operation. Closing may wait indefinitely for uncooperative native code; shutdown escalation is separate.
See sharing , release , and background resources .

title: Builders and sealed results
content:
Builders and sealed results# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A builder supports mutable construction and returns its result when sealed. Builder aliases are ordinary references; freezing may seal the builder so later mutation reports a runtime error.
Builders synchronize mutation and freeze across all aliases. Freezing seals the object atomically; an append racing with freeze either contributes to the snapshot or faults after sealing. Concurrent appends have nondeterministic order. There is no ownership-transfer or consuming function type.
API# All builder names are exported by @std/builders.ms. They have zero-argument constructors and are opaque references with no equality or hashing. Type arguments can come from an explicit application or a complete expected constructor type.
Type Mutation Freeze result ListBuilder[T] append(value: T) -> Unit List[T] MapBuilder[K: Hashable, V] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Unit Map[K, V] SetBuilder[T: Hashable] with_value(value: T) -> Unit Set[T] BytesBuilder append(value: Int) -> Unit, concat(values: Bytes) -> Unit Bytes StringBuilder append(value: String) -> Unit String freeze() seals the shared local object and returns its result. Repeated freeze returns the same value. List, Map, and Set results are ordinary mutable collections; sealing prevents further builder operations, not mutation through the result. Use .clone() to retain a separate copy. Every builder mutation through any alias after sealing is a programming fault. Byte append requires 0 through 255. Map replacement preserves insertion position; set insertion ignores an already present value. Builders have no implicit cleanup or ownership transfer.
See aggregates and collections .

title: Application hosts
content:
Application hosts# Guide index · Design index A host starts application code and sets its execution lifetime, cancellation, and limits. The CLI host invokes main once; an HTTP host gives each request its own execution context.
HTTP request hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. CLI application hosts

title: HTTP request hosts
content:
HTTP request hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The HTTP host gives each request its own execution context and limits. It controls admission, body sizes, deadlines, disconnect cancellation, backpressure, and fault isolation. Handlers use parallel APIs for joined work and with for request resources.
If the client disconnects, the host cancels the request and its nested groups. Those groups finish joining and registered cleanup runs before the request ends.
Request handlers use parallel for joined work and with for request resources. Client disconnection cancels the request and its nested groups; those groups join and registered cleanup runs before request execution ends.
Streaming responses remain within their request lifetime until streaming finishes. WebSocket/session hosts establish explicit session lifetimes and participate in shutdown; they are not untracked background goroutines.
Application background services are constructed under the application context and passed to handlers. Accepted work uses that service’s context, not the submitting request’s deadline or disconnect signal. Jobs capture request data and application services and acquire their own resources. Admission can race with request cancellation; idempotent submissions are an application concern.
Server shutdown stops request admission, allows a configured grace period, cancels and joins remaining request/session work, closes background admission and drains/cancels/joins those services, then releases application resources. A finite grace period does not guarantee uncooperative work exits; host escalation is separate.
Bounded request API# @std/http.ms exports Network, HttpServer, HttpRequest, and HttpResponse. The imported network() -> Network accessor returns the current execution’s host network service.
Manuscript type HttpRequest: method: String path: String query: String headers: Map[String, Bytes] body: Bytes type HttpResponse: status: Int headers: Map[String, String] body: Bytes # Network fn serve(address: String, handler: fn(request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse, limit: Int, max_body_bytes: Int, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration, grace: Duration) -> Result[HttpServer, IoError] fn close() -> Unit # HttpServer fn address() -> String fn wait() -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> Unit These signatures specify library operations. A complete declaration places the entire function header inside delimiter continuation. serve accepts an ordinary handler, including a function parameter or field, and may be stored as a bound method. limit and timeout are positive; byte bounds and grace are nonnegative. Invalid settings return IoError.InvalidInput; binding failure returns Unavailable; a closed network returns Closed. Port zero permits an OS-selected port reported by address().
The host admits at most limit requests; excess requests receive 503 without invoking a handler. Bodies over the bound receive 413. Each handler gets a fixed timeout/disconnect context, and all work and cleanup in it join before its lifetime ends. Handler faults are isolated as 500 and recorded by the bounded diagnostic sink. Timeout/cancellation yields 504 where the connection still permits a response. Source routes by ordinary branching on method/path; raw query remains encoded. Header values are bytes to preserve non-UTF-8 HTTP input. Header keys are visited in sorted order.
Responses require status 200 through 599, a bounded body, and valid header names/values. Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, and Connection are host-managed and cannot be supplied. Invalid responses yield 500. This API is deliberately a bounded, fully buffered request/response host. Streaming HTTP and reusable clients and WebSocket sessions have separate implemented contracts.
Server close stops admission, waits up to grace, then cancels and joins remaining requests and closes transport. It cannot be called from its own request. Network close joins all its servers. A server also registers with its construction execution lifetime, so omitting a with binding cannot detach server work. Unexpected transport release errors are cleanup faults; uncooperative handlers may delay joining beyond grace.
See background services , cancellation , and conformance programs .

title: CLI application hosts
content:
CLI application hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A CLI application starts at an exported fn main() -> Int. The host creates the execution context and host services, calls main once with no arguments, then waits for work and cleanup before reporting the exit code.
The selected entry module must export exactly one nongeneric main with no parameters and an Int result. Missing or internal main, or a different signature, is a compile error. Other exports are allowed.
Importing host services# Import the accessor for each service an application uses. Accessors are ordinary zero-parameter functions backed by the current execution’s host services:
Import from Accessors @std/cli.ms arguments() -> List[String], environment() -> Map[String, String] @std/io.ms stdin() -> ReadStream, stdout() -> WriteStream, stderr() -> WriteStream, files() -> Files @std/fs.ms filesystem() -> FileSystem @std/http.ms network() -> Network @std/process.ms commands() -> Commands, control() -> ProcessControl @std/time.ms clock() -> Clock, wall_clock() -> WallClock @std/random.ms entropy() -> Entropy @std/system.ms system() -> System Type names and functions still require explicit imports when named in source. Importing an accessor does not add other declarations to scope. Calling it returns the existing service; repeated calls do not construct new roots. Helpers, callbacks, parallel work, and imported modules use the services of their invocation execution. Background services retain their construction execution’s services.
Manuscript import arguments from "@std/cli.ms" import stdout from "@std/io.ms" export fn main() -> Int: let message = "Arguments: {arguments().length()}\n" match stdout().write(data: message.to_bytes()): ok(_): return 0 error(_): return 1 On success this program prints Arguments: N followed by LF and exits 0. Stream signatures are defined in streams .
Arguments exclude the executable name. Environment is a startup snapshot; duplicate OS names are resolved by the host before entry. Invalid UTF-8 in process inputs is a startup failure on native stderr with exit 70 before main runs. Relative file paths on native CLI roots use the live process working directory; explicitly constructed filesystem services can retain a fixed base.
The native CLI grants its ordinary OS filesystem, networking, and subprocess access. There are no per-function dependency declarations, injected replacements, or manifest permission enforcement. Explicit interface parameters remain useful for substituting source fakes in helpers; applications may also call imported host accessors directly.
Resources and tests# The host creates synchronized service implementations behind ordinary contract views. The host closes roots after main and its scoped work finish. Applications register acquired files and other resources with with; retaining a reference does not prolong their open lifetime. Closing a root stream affects every alias in that execution.
Each source test receives fresh host roots with an empty argument list and its own environment snapshot. Imported accessors work in test bodies. Roots close after test work joins, and closing a root in one test does not close another test’s root wrapper. No fake host or API replacement facility is implied by these accessors.
Exit and shutdown# Normal main results must be 0–125; other results fault. An unhandled root or cleanup fault exits 70 after attempted cleanup and reports primary/secondary diagnostics on host stderr. SIGINT/SIGTERM request cancellation; after joining and cleanup SIGINT exits 130 and SIGTERM exits 143. The first accepted stop reason is retained; a fault during joining/cleanup takes precedence and exits 70. Parent cancellation unwinds main rather than becoming a normal Result.
The ms run launcher forwards SIGINT/SIGTERM to the native host and waits for its joined shutdown before reporting that exit status.
Construct application Background services in main with with, inside their dependencies’ scopes. Shutdown stops admission, joins services, then releases roots. Uncooperative work/reporters can require host escalation ; the host exposes its watchdog policy. Escalated exit is incomplete cleanup, not conformance success.
Network services register under their construction execution and join before host roots are released. Network owns acquired TCP/UDP/TLS handles and joins them during host-root shutdown. The bounded HTTP and subprocess contracts are in HTTP and streams . The filesystem, entropy, wall-clock, and system contracts are in general-purpose packages .
The imported control() accessor returns ProcessControl for current-process information and explicit environment, directory, identity, signal, and umask operations. See host package contracts for their process-wide effects and native limitations.

title: General-purpose packages
content:
General-purpose packages# Standard library guide · Package coverage Find a package by the task you want to perform. Read common contracts for shared error and limit rules, and coverage to compare available functionality with Node.js or Go. The signature blocks are reference declarations, not complete programs.
Text, bytes, and collections — Work with text, bytes, encodings, collections, and regular expressions. Numbers and mathematics — Use floating-point functions and arbitrary-precision integers. Serialization and formats — Parse and write JSON, CSV, URLs, and escaped HTML text. Paths and filesystem — Manipulate paths and use an explicit filesystem service. Time and system information — Work with timestamps and query supplied clock or system services. Cryptography and randomness — Hash, authenticate, encrypt, sign, and request random bytes. Networking and TLS — Use destination policies, DNS, sockets, and verified TLS. HTTP clients and streaming hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. WebSocket sessions — Send and receive messages within a WebSocket session lifetime. Subprocesses and terminal I/O — Read terminal streams and run commands through explicit authority. Compression and archives — Compress data and handle archive entries with explicit limits. Logging, testing, and diagnostics Read a signature# For example, fn parse(text: String, limits: JsonLimits) -> Result[JsonValue, JsonError] means:
Call the function with named text and limits arguments. Success returns a JsonValue; an expected failure returns a JsonError. Import the function from the module listed above its signature. Import type names separately if your own annotations use them. A heading such as “FileSystem operations” lists methods on a supplied service. Importing its interface gives you the type; obtain the service value from the host or a function parameter. Read the behavior sections for limits, cleanup, and partial effects.
Filesystem, OS, process, paths, and timers — Node.js 24 API mapping, bounded handles, explicit process authority, timer lifetimes, and platform limits.

title: Resources & cleanup
content:
Resource lifetimes and cleanup# Design index Use with when a file, connection, or other resource must close at the end of a block. The runtime reclaims unused memory, but you must arrange release of external resources. Keeping another reference to a resource does not keep it open.
Reading order# 1. References and sharing# Ordinary references — Understand what another reference does, and why it does not keep a resource open. Concurrent access and resource lifetime — Check whether data or a function can safely be used by concurrent operations. Aggregates and local construction — Store resources inside records or collections without assuming automatic cleanup. Assignment and branches — See what reassignment and branches do to references and registered cleanup. 2. Scoped cleanup# With scopes — Acquire a resource and close it at the end of a block with with. The Closeable contract — Implement the cleanup operation required by with. Scope-exit ordering — Follow cleanup order after a return, error, fault, or cancellation. Shielding and cleanup faults — Understand cleanup after cancellation and what happens if close itself faults. External resource release — Separate closing a handle from successfully completing its work.

title: Common package contracts
content:
Common package contracts# Standard library guide · Coverage · Package index These rules apply across the general-purpose packages. Exact types and signatures live in the pinned Manuscript files under stdlib/. The checker reads those files and verifies that native runtime signatures agree with them.
Imports and callbacks# Import each function or type you name from its module. Standard imports are pinned with the distribution. They add no ambient types, wildcard imports, user-defined generic operations, or automatic imports of host accessors.
Function identity includes the module, so json/parse, bigint/parse, and url/parse remain distinct in generated code. Source import renaming is unsupported; use a helper module if two imports have the same spelling.
Sequential callbacks run under the caller’s execution context and may wait for operations. All callbacks are ordinary values and can also be passed to concurrent APIs.
Errors# Each package returns a named error type from its own module: JsonError from @std/json.ms, EncodingError from @std/encoding.ms, FileSystemError from @std/fs.ms, and so on. Each type contains the cases relevant to that domain; its exact definition is in the generated reference . For example, JsonError has only InvalidInput, InvalidData, and LimitExceeded.
All standard error types explicitly implement Error from @std/errors.ms, an ordinary operation contract with message() -> String. Specific API signatures retain their domain error type. A generic boundary uses Result[T, Error]; use an ordinary Result match and return error(cause: Error(value: cause)). The explicit view preserves the original receiver, case, and payload. See the executable filesystem/random/time example .
Handle a concrete error with its ordinary case match. Handle a generic Error by calling message(), or use a contract type match to recover a concrete error such as JsonError(cause), then match its cases. The final wildcard handles other implementations. Custom errors participate through an ordinary impl Error for CustomError in their defining module. Error does not constrain Result’s error parameter or turn faults and cancellation into expected failures.
try propagates the declared error type; it does not convert unrelated types or implicitly construct an Error view.
