This replaces the former shared LibraryError contract: update imports and return annotations, and qualify cases such as JsonError.InvalidData when multiple imported types define the same case name.
Use specific error cases for classification. message() and Failed(message: String) diagnostics are human-readable text, not stable error codes. A native Failed preserves its diagnostic text; a payloadless native error reports its qualified case, such as JsonError.InvalidData. LogError.Io delegates to its underlying IoError. Command, pool, and task errors also implement Error while retaining their distinct cases and identities.
Situation Behavior Malformed data or unavailable OS service Return an expected Result error. Missing value Use Optional. Illegal collection slice bounds, broken programming assumptions, or explicit invariant violation Produce a programming fault. Parent cancellation Unwind; do not turn cancellation into EOF or a domain error. Local network deadline expires Return Timeout, subject to the operation’s documented error type. If cancellation wins before a newly acquired resource is delivered, native acquisition releases that resource. Delivered socket handles use with and synchronized close admission. Retaining another reference never extends the open lifetime.
Bounds and native limits# Byte, item, and depth limits are nonnegative unless a package requires a positive value. Exceeding a bound returns an error, not a truncated success.
A limit on a function’s output does not bound input already allocated by the caller. Some native operations also allocate before they can check a limit: CSV may parse one record, ZIP may read the central directory, and logging may construct a full record. Bound source reads and consult each package’s behavior section.
Facility Native limit JSON Depth ceiling of 512. HTTP Response headers limited to 64 KiB. Entropy 16 MiB per call. UDP receive At most 65535 bytes. These limits do not form a general memory or CPU sandbox.
Cancellation and partial effects# Native loops check cancellation between bounded chunks. A single math, regex, big-integer, directory, resolver, or OS call may delay cancellation until it returns. There is no forced termination.
Writing, copying, or removing data can fail after changing an external prefix. Cancellation and errors do not imply rollback or a transaction.
Access to external services# Imported host accessors supply filesystem, entropy, wall-clock, system, network, and command services. Source fakes implement the same contracts with explicit contract views.
Pure codec, path, math, and hash functions grant no OS access. Native CLI services use the process’s OS permissions. Filesystem subtree restrictions are not implemented; Network.restrict narrows destination access. Imported host accessors obtain services from the current execution. HTTP and socket operations retain their service interfaces and TLS verification.
Networking includes DNS, Unix sockets, verified TLS, streaming HTTP, and WebSockets. HTTP/3 is outside the supported scope. Native builds bundle pinned dependency sources and licenses rather than fetching packages.

title: References and sharing
content:
References and sharing# Guide index · Design index Several names can refer to the same object. These pages explain what happens when you pass, store, replace, or share those references. Keep two questions separate: is concurrent access safe, and is the resource still open?
Ordinary references — Understand what another reference does, and why it does not keep a resource open. Concurrent access and resource lifetime — Check whether data or a function can safely be used by concurrent operations. Aggregates and local construction — Store resources inside records or collections without assuming automatic cleanup. Assignment and branches — See what reassignment and branches do to references and registered cleanup.

title: Ordinary references
content:
Ordinary references# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Several names can refer to the same object. Passing a reference to a function, putting it in a record, or capturing it in a closure gives another way to access that object. The original reference still works.
Data copies# Record and collection aliases observe updates to the same instance. .clone() creates separate outer data storage and retains nested references. Cloning a record containing a file or socket retains that handle; it does not duplicate, reopen, or extend the resource’s lifetime. Opaque handles do not have a built-in clone operation. See mutation and cloning .
Memory and open resources# Go’s garbage collector reclaims memory that is no longer needed. Releasing a file handle, socket, or other external resource is a separate job. Use an explicit close() call or a with block to arrange that release.
Keeping a reference keeps the object accessible in memory. It does not keep an external resource open. When one reference closes a resource, operations through its other references also see that it is closed. Dropping a reference, closure, or work ID does not itself close anything.
Returning a resource# A factory can return an open resource for its caller to put in with. But a function must not expect a resource to stay open merely because it returns it from inside a local with block. That block still closes the resource before the caller receives it.
What the function does What the caller receives Returns an open resource without registering local cleanup An open resource; the caller must arrange cleanup. Returns a resource registered in a local with block A reference to the resource after that block has closed it. Later use of a closed resource produces its runtime closed-state error.
The compiler does not catch every missing with. Libraries should provide scoped APIs and diagnostics to help callers avoid omissions. Manuscript has no move or ownership-transfer operation.
See Closeable , with scopes , and closures .

title: Text, bytes, and collections
content:
Text, bytes, and collections# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use these modules for text transformations, raw bytes, encodings, collection algorithms, and regular expressions. Import the functions you need from the module above each signature block. Read the behavior sections for indexing, ordering, and limit rules.
@std/string.ms# Manuscript fn contains(value: String, text: String) -> Bool fn ends_with(value: String, suffix: String) -> Bool fn from_scalars(values: List[Int]) -> Result[String, TextError] fn join(parts: List[String], separator: String) -> String fn lower(text: String) -> String fn repeat(text: String, count: Int, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, TextError] fn replace(text: String, old: String, new: String, max_replacements: Int) -> String fn scalar_length(text: String) -> Int fn scalar_values(text: String) -> List[Int] fn slice_scalars(text: String, start: Int, end: Int) -> Result[String, TextError] fn split(text: String, separator: String, max_parts: Int) -> List[String] fn starts_with(value: String, prefix: String) -> Bool fn trim(text: String) -> String fn upper(text: String) -> String @std/bytes.ms# Manuscript fn contains(data: Bytes, value: Bytes) -> Bool fn slice(data: Bytes, start: Int, end: Int) -> Bytes fn values(data: Bytes) -> List[Int] @std/encoding.ms# Manuscript fn base64_decode(text: String, url_safe: Bool, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, EncodingError] fn base64_encode(data: Bytes, url_safe: Bool) -> String fn hex_decode(text: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, EncodingError] fn hex_encode(data: Bytes) -> String @std/binary.ms# Manuscript fn read_float(data: Bytes, offset: Int, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Float, BinaryError] fn read_integer(data: Bytes, offset: Int, width: Int, signed: Bool, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Int, BinaryError] fn write_float(value: Float, little_endian: Bool) -> Bytes fn write_integer(value: Int, width: Int, signed: Bool, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Bytes, BinaryError] @std/collections.ms# Manuscript fn difference[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] fn filter[T](values: List[T], predicate: fn(value: T) -> Bool) -> List[T] fn fold[T, A](values: List[T], initial: A, step: fn(accumulator: A, value: T) -> A) -> A fn intersection[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] fn map[T, U](values: List[T], transform: fn(value: T) -> U) -> List[U] fn map_keys[K: Hashable, V](values: Map[K, V]) -> List[K] fn map_values[K: Hashable, V](values: Map[K, V]) -> List[V] fn reverse[T](values: List[T]) -> List[T] fn slice[T](values: List[T], start: Int, end: Int) -> List[T] fn sort_ints(values: List[Int]) -> List[Int] fn sort_strings(values: List[String]) -> List[String] fn sorted[T](values: List[T], compare: fn(left: T, right: T) -> Int) -> List[T] fn union[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] @std/regex.ms# Manuscript fn compile(pattern: String) -> Result[Regex, RegexError] fn find_all(pattern: Regex, text: String, max_matches: Int) -> Result[List[String], RegexError] fn matches(pattern: Regex, text: String) -> Bool fn replace(pattern: Regex, text: String, replacement: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, RegexError] Text behavior# Text is valid UTF-8. Scalar operations count Unicode code points, rather than bytes or user-perceived characters such as a letter plus a combining mark.
from_scalars rejects surrogate code points and values outside the Unicode range. slice_scalars uses a half-open range: include start, exclude end. Invalid bounds return OutOfRange. trim uses Unicode White_Space. upper and lower use Go’s locale-independent Unicode mappings; they do not normalize combining sequences. split keeps empty parts. It requires positive max_parts; the final part contains any remainder. An empty separator splits Unicode scalars. replace uses literal text. max_replacements must be nonnegative; zero means no replacements. An empty old inserts at scalar boundaries. repeat requires nonnegative count and max_bytes. It checks the size multiplication before allocating. An empty search string succeeds for contains, prefix, and suffix checks. Bytes and collections# Byte and collection slices also use half-open ranges. Negative, reversed, or out-of-range bounds produce a programming fault. values returns each unsigned byte as an Int.
Collection updates mutate their receiver. Algorithms such as map, filter, slice, and sorted return new values. Use .clone() before an update to retain a separate copy; nested references remain shared.
Operation Ordering rule map, filter, fold Callbacks run sequentially in input order, with ordinary cancellation and fault behavior. sorted Sorting is stable. The comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive Int and must define a consistent total preorder. Its call order and call count are unspecified. map_keys, map_values Preserve insertion order. Set intersection and difference Preserve the left set’s order. Set union Keep left order, then append previously absent right values. You may explicitly specialize a generic function and store it as a function value. These operations add no compiler bounds.
Encodings# Hex output uses lowercase. Hex input accepts either case but rejects odd digit counts and whitespace.
Base64 uses padded standard or URL-safe encoding according to url_safe. Decoding rejects whitespace, the wrong alphabet, malformed padding, and nonzero unused bits. max_bytes must be nonnegative; excess decoded output returns LimitExceeded.
Bytes.to_text strictly decodes UTF-8. Invalid text is an error; there is no decoder that silently substitutes replacement characters.
Binary numbers# Integer widths are 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes. Signed integers use two’s complement. An unsigned 64-bit input above MaxInt64 returns OutOfRange.
Invalid widths return InvalidInput. Bad offsets, truncated input, and values that cannot fit the requested representation return OutOfRange. Float reads and writes use IEEE binary64. little_endian: true explicitly selects little-endian order. These functions do not reinterpret unsafe memory or convert numeric types implicitly.
Regular expressions# Regex is an opaque, immutable compiled Go RE2-style pattern. Backreferences and lookaround are invalid; compile failures return InvalidData.
find_all returns whole matches. max_matches must be nonnegative, and exceeding it returns LimitExceeded instead of a truncated success. Go regexp rules govern zero-width and adjacent matches.
replace uses literal replacement text, without $ capture interpolation. It enforces max_bytes and never returns a partial output as success.
The string module also provides bounded Unicode normalization; see JavaScript built-in coverage . Grapheme segmentation, non-UTF-8 codecs, and capture-group match records remain future work.

title: Concurrent access and resource lifetime
content:
Concurrent access and resource lifetime# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Every source value may be passed between concurrent operations. Passing a reference does not synchronize access to the referenced object. Sharing needs no annotation, compiler bound, or callable proof. It does not keep a resource open or register cleanup.
Data and services# Records and collections are mutable. Alternative tags, strings, and bytes retain their value behavior. let fixes a binding, while var permits reassignment; neither freezes a referenced record or collection. Closures snapshot captured bindings, including a mutable local’s current value, and cannot assign to captured outer locals.
Native services and builders synchronize their mutable internals and resource lifecycles. Resource APIs may serialize simultaneous calls or report unsupported overlapping use. Race safety does not make several calls atomic or establish their execution order. Use Synchronized when related reads and writes must run under one lock.
Wrappers coordinate the closed-state check, access to the underlying handle, and closure as one lifecycle protocol. A flag check followed by unprotected I/O is insufficient. A stale lease or lock guard must never access a resource or protected value after release.
A Queue is a local mutable collection with no internal synchronization. When shared, keep it in one Synchronized[Queue[T]] and hold a separately acquired guard for each caller’s full use, including reads. Queue aliases and bound methods must follow that same discipline; the compiler does not track or enforce lock ownership. Records may contain queue references. A shallow record clone retains the same queue reference.
Contract views# Contract(value: receiver) retains the implementing receiver. There is one contract-view type; it can be passed through fields, parameters, returns, and collections and used according to its receiver’s concurrency contract. Generic behavioral bounds require the named operations only. Native service adapters synchronize their receivers and resource lifecycles. A source implementation that holds a local queue must use a synchronized wrapper before exposing concurrent operations.
Function values# Named functions, closures, bound methods, function fields, and function parameters are ordinary values. Copies, generic forwarding, collection storage, and return values preserve their normal call behavior. Concurrency APIs check the function signature, with no separate capture-sharing eligibility or proof-erasure rules. An operation may return another function.
Capture application services and job data for background work, and acquire job resources inside that work’s own with scopes. A resource captured beyond its with scope remains a valid reference, but subsequent operations report closed state. Sharing, resource lifetime, and work lifetime remain separate guarantees.

title: Numbers and mathematics
content:
Numbers and mathematics# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use math for floating-point calculations, numbers for text conversion, and bigint when values exceed the Int range. Numeric conversions are explicit. Read the behavior sections before depending on rounding or overflow results.
@std/math.ms# Manuscript fn abs(value: Float) -> Float fn abs_int(value: Int) -> Int fn acos(value: Float) -> Float fn asin(value: Float) -> Float fn atan(value: Float) -> Float fn atan2(y: Float, x: Float) -> Float fn ceil(value: Float) -> Float fn cos(value: Float) -> Float fn cosh(value: Float) -> Float fn e() -> Float fn exp(value: Float) -> Float fn floor(value: Float) -> Float fn hypot(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn is_finite(value: Float) -> Bool fn is_nan(value: Float) -> Bool fn log(value: Float) -> Float fn log10(value: Float) -> Float fn log2(value: Float) -> Float fn max(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn min(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn pi() -> Float fn pow(base: Float, exponent: Float) -> Float fn remainder(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn round(value: Float) -> Float fn sin(value: Float) -> Float fn sinh(value: Float) -> Float fn sqrt(value: Float) -> Float fn tan(value: Float) -> Float fn tanh(value: Float) -> Float fn truncate(value: Float) -> Float @std/numbers.ms# Manuscript fn format_float(value: Float) -> String fn format_int(value: Int, radix: Int) -> String fn parse_float(text: String) -> Result[Float, NumberError] fn parse_int(text: String, radix: Int) -> Result[Int, NumberError] @std/bigint.ms# Manuscript fn add(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_and(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_or(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_xor(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn compare(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Int fn divide(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn format(value: BigInt, radix: Int) -> String fn from_int(value: Int) -> BigInt fn multiply(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn parse(text: String, radix: Int, max_digits: Int) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn remainder(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn subtract(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn to_int(value: BigInt) -> Optional[Int] Floating-point behavior# Math functions use IEEE binary64 and Go’s domain and overflow rules. An invalid Float domain yields NaN; overflow can yield infinity. The last bits of transcendental results may differ across targets, so tests should use tolerances.
round uses ties-to-even. min and max propagate NaN and preserve signed-zero conventions. abs_int(MinInt64) faults because the positive result cannot fit in an Int. pi() and e() are ordinary zero-argument functions.
Parsing and formatting numbers# Integer radices are 2–36. Input may have a sign and ASCII digits or letters. Parsing consumes the whole input and rejects prefixes, whitespace, and separators. An invalid radix returns InvalidInput when parsing and faults when formatting. An integer outside the Int range returns OutOfRange.
Float parsing accepts signed decimal digits with an optional fraction or exponent. A present decimal point needs at least one digit on each side. It also accepts NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity. Finite syntax that overflows binary64 returns OutOfRange. Formatting uses the existing round-trip Float representation.
Arbitrary-precision integers# BigInt is opaque, immutable, and comparable for equality. Create it with from_int or parse; there is no source constructor, literal, arithmetic operator, or hashing guarantee. Arithmetic functions leave both operands unchanged. Conversion between Int and BigInt is explicit.
Operation Behavior Parse max_digits is positive and counts digits excluding the optional sign. Divide Truncates toward zero; division by zero returns InvalidInput. Remainder Has the dividend’s sign; a zero divisor returns InvalidInput. Compare Returns -1, 0, or 1. Convert to Int Returns none outside the signed 64-bit range. Bit operations Use mathematical two’s-complement semantics. A very large native arithmetic operation can delay cancellation until it returns. Bound input magnitudes where that matters. Decimal keeps its existing 34-digit contract; extended Decimal parse and format APIs remain future work.

title: Aggregates and local construction
content:
Aggregates and local construction# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Records, alternatives, collections, and closures can hold resource references. Storing a resource inside one of these values does not arrange for it to close or keep it open. Arrange cleanup for the resource itself.
Closing a registered resource affects all aliases, including aliases nested in aggregates. Dropping an aggregate does not recursively close its fields. A library object that deliberately manages several resources can implement Closeable and explicitly close them in its implementation.
Collections may retain any value, including resource references and functions. Sharing is universal and does not provide a resource lifetime guarantee.
Builders follow the same reference rules; mutation and freeze are synchronized. Destructuring extracts fields and positions without changing cleanup.

title: Serialization and formats
content:
Serialization and formats# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use these modules to parse and write JSON, CSV, and URLs, or escape HTML text. Choose explicit limits for input size and nesting. Each format has its own validation rules, described after the signatures.
@std/json.ms# Manuscript fn parse(text: String, limits: JsonLimits) -> Result[JsonValue, JsonError] fn stringify(value: JsonValue, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, JsonError] @std/csv.ms# Manuscript fn parse(text: String, options: CsvOptions, max_rows: Int, max_cells: Int) -> Result[List[List[String]], CsvError] fn stringify(rows: List[List[String]], options: CsvOptions, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, CsvError] @std/url.ms# Manuscript fn decode_component(text: String) -> Result[String, UrlError] fn encode_component(text: String) -> String fn format(value: Url) -> Result[String, UrlError] fn format_query(entries: List[QueryEntry]) -> String fn parse(text: String) -> Result[Url, UrlError] fn parse_query(text: String, max_entries: Int) -> Result[List[QueryEntry], UrlError] fn resolve(base: Url, reference: String) -> Result[Url, UrlError] @std/html.ms# Manuscript fn escape(text: String) -> String Data records# Manuscript type JsonLimits: max_bytes: Int max_depth: Int max_values: Int type JsonValue: case Null case BoolValue(value: Bool) case NumberValue(text: String) case StringValue(value: String) case ArrayValue(values: List[JsonValue]) case ObjectValue(values: Map[String, JsonValue]) type CsvOptions: delimiter: String line_ending: String type QueryEntry: key: String value: String type Url: scheme: String host: String port: Optional[Int] path: String query: String fragment: String JSON behavior# JSON numbers keep their exact valid token text, including integers larger than 2^53. They are not automatically converted to Float. stringify also validates NumberValue text because an application can construct that case directly.
Parsing accepts one document. It rejects trailing values, duplicate decoded object keys, and unpaired surrogate escapes. Object order follows Map insertion order. There is no reflection-based record serialization or execution hook.
JsonLimits uses nonnegative limits:
Limit What it counts max_bytes UTF-8 input bytes. Stringify separately limits output bytes. max_depth Container nesting; a root container has depth one. max_values All values, including the root. Object keys are not counted as values. Both parsing and stringify enforce a native depth ceiling of 512. Malformed data returns InvalidData; exceeded limits return LimitExceeded.
Stringify produces compact JSON and uses Go’s escaping for HTML-sensitive characters. It is not a canonical format for signing.
CSV behavior# The delimiter must be one non-NUL ASCII byte other than quote, CR, or LF. line_ending is LF or CRLF. Row, cell, and output limits must be nonnegative; max_cells counts every returned cell.
Go’s encoding/csv quoting rules apply: quotes are doubled, values are not trimmed or converted to other types, rows may have different widths, and blank lines are ignored. CRLF is normalized, including inside quoted cells. Serialization ends every row with the selected terminator. Formula-like spreadsheet values are left as supplied.
Exceeded limits return LimitExceeded. The input String is already in memory, and the parser reads one record before checking its row and cell limits. Bound the source read before parsing untrusted CSV.
URL behavior# parse requires an absolute hierarchical URL and rejects user information. Scheme and host become lowercase. The optional port is in the range 0–65535.
The path keeps escaped separators, the query stays encoded, and the fragment is decoded. resolve follows Go’s net/url rules. Url is an ordinary record, so format and resolve validate values constructed by application code too. Unsupported opaque URLs return InvalidData.
Query entries retain duplicates and order. A bare key has an empty value; + represents a space. Component encoding preserves only ASCII unreserved characters. Decoding rejects invalid UTF-8.
IDNA normalization, a distinction between absent and empty queries, and browser WHATWG URL compatibility remain future work.
HTML escaping# escape handles text and quoted attribute contexts. It does not sanitize HTML or encode JavaScript, CSS, or URL contexts.

title: Assignment and branches
content:
Assignment and branches# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Reassigning a var replaces its value or reference. It does not close the previous object or invalidate other references to it. A let prevents reassignment.
A with binding is immutable and registers the initialized object itself. Reassigning another variable that references the object cannot change which object’s close() will execute. Closing early is permitted because close() is idempotent.
Every binding is initialized at declaration. Branch-local names stay inside their branch; assignments to an outer var keep its declared type. Closures snapshot the current value of a local binding at creation; they do not share mutable local cells.
See bindings , closure captures , and with scopes .

title: Paths and filesystem
content:
Paths and filesystem# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Path functions manipulate path text without accessing disk. FileSystem methods read or change files through a supplied service. A path string or an import alone does not grant filesystem access.
@std/path.ms# Manuscript fn basename(path: String) -> String fn dirname(path: String) -> String fn extension(path: String) -> String fn is_absolute(path: String) -> Bool fn join(parts: List[String]) -> String fn normalize(path: String) -> String fn relative(base: String, target: String) -> Result[String, PathError] @std/fs.ms# FileSystem operations# Manuscript fn read_file(path: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, FileSystemError] fn write_file(path: String, data: Bytes, replace: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn stat(path: String, follow_links: Bool) -> Result[FileInfo, FileSystemError] fn list(path: String, max_entries: Int) -> Result[List[DirectoryEntry], FileSystemError] fn create_directory(path: String, recursive: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn remove(path: String, recursive: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn rename(source: String, destination: String) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn copy_file(source: String, destination: String, replace: Bool, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn canonicalize(path: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] fn read_link(path: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] fn create_link(path: String, target: String) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn temporary_directory(prefix: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] Authority and records# Import filesystem() -> FileSystem from @std/fs.ms to obtain the current execution’s filesystem service. The native FileSystem root uses the live process working directory for relative paths and the CLI process’s native OS permissions. It is not restricted to a sandboxed subtree. The existing Files capability remains read-only.
Importing a type or constructing a path string grants no file access. Source fakes can implement the same contract. NUL paths return InvalidInput; filenames that cannot be represented as text return Unsupported. A temporary directory must be explicitly removed; dropping its path string does not remove it.
Manuscript type FileInfo: name: String size: Int directory: Bool symlink: Bool modified: Timestamp type DirectoryEntry: name: String directory: Bool symlink: Bool Reads, writes, and replacement# read_file limits cumulative bytes and closes its handle on every exit. write_file with replace: false creates exclusively; replace: true may truncate existing data. copy_file bounds input before writing and uses the same replacement rule.
Writes and copies are not transactional. An error can leave a destination prefix. Default creation permissions are 0600 for files and 0700 for directories, subject to platform behavior.
Directories, links, and errors# Directory lists are sorted by byte-lexical order. Excess entries return LimitExceeded, rather than a truncated success. stat uses follow_links to choose link or target metadata.
rename follows the native platform’s replacement and atomicity behavior, including cross-device errors. It does not fall back to copying and deleting. Recursive remove does not intentionally follow symlinks and checks cancellation between entries; it is not transactional.
Temporary-directory prefixes must be nonempty and contain no slash, backslash, or NUL. OS failures map to NotFound, AlreadyExists, PermissionDenied, or Failed(message: ...).
Path functions# Pure path functions use the target platform’s Go filepath rules. join and normalize do not access disk. Cleaning path text does not prove that a path stays inside an authorized directory.
relative requires absolute paths and may return InvalidInput for incompatible roots. Basename, dirname, and extension follow Go filepath behavior, including treating .profile as an extension.
Seekable files, metadata mutation, watchers, secure subtree provisioning, and archive extraction remain future work. Existing Files and stream APIs provide bounded sequential reads.

title: Scoped cleanup
content:
Scoped cleanup# Guide index · Design index A with block registers a resource to close when the block ends. Cleanup also runs after early returns, errors, faults, and cancellation. Start with with scopes, then read the exact rules for close and exit order.
With scopes — Acquire a resource and close it at the end of a block with with. The Closeable contract — Implement the cleanup operation required by with. Scope-exit ordering — Follow cleanup order after a return, error, fault, or cancellation. Shielding and cleanup faults — Understand cleanup after cancellation and what happens if close itself faults. External resource release — Separate closing a handle from successfully completing its work.

title: Time and system information
content:
Time and system information# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use Timestamp for wall-clock time and Duration for a time interval. Access the current wall clock, environment, system information, and random bytes through explicit services supplied by the host.
@std/time.ms# Manuscript fn difference(left: Timestamp, right: Timestamp) -> Result[Duration, TimeError] fn format_timestamp(value: Timestamp) -> String fn nanoseconds(value: Timestamp) -> Int fn parse_timestamp(text: String) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn shift(value: Timestamp, duration: Duration) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn timestamp(seconds: Int, nanoseconds: Int) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn unix_seconds(value: Timestamp) -> Int @std/system.ms# @std/random.ms# Manuscript fn secure_int(entropy: Entropy, min: Int, max_exclusive: Int) -> Result[Int, RandomError] fn uuid_v4(entropy: Entropy) -> Result[String, RandomError] WallClock operations# Manuscript fn now() -> Timestamp System operations# Manuscript fn info() -> SystemInfo fn working_directory() -> String fn environment(name: String) -> Optional[String] Entropy operations# Manuscript fn bytes(count: Int) -> Result[Bytes, RandomError] Services supplied by the CLI# Import wall_clock() from @std/time.ms, system() from @std/system.ms, and entropy() from @std/random.ms to obtain those host services.
Timestamp represents wall time and is opaque, immutable, and comparable for equality. Instant remains a monotonic time value; conversion between them is not implicit. Existing Clock and sleep keep their signatures and error/cancellation rules. Wall-clock changes do not affect monotonic deadlines.
Timestamp rules# Construction accepts UTC years 1–9999 and nanoseconds 0–999999999. Parsing uses strict RFC 3339: an explicit offset, uppercase T/Z, at most nine fractional digits, and no leap seconds.
Formatting uses UTC. It omits a zero fraction and removes trailing fractional zeroes. shift checks the resulting calendar range. difference returns OutOfRange if its nanosecond result cannot fit in Duration.
There are no Timestamp operators or source constructor. Use the named functions; unix_seconds and nanoseconds expose the components explicitly.
System information# SystemInfo has os: String, architecture: String, and cpu_count: Int. This is a native runtime snapshot. CPU count does not reserve resources.
working_directory on the native root returns the live process working directory. environment returns none if the variable is absent or its value cannot be represented as UTF-8. The CLI environment() accessor returns a startup snapshot. Importing System supplies its interface; calling the imported system() accessor obtains the service. The imported ProcessControl service provides explicit process-wide directory and environment mutation; see host contracts .
Randomness# Entropy.bytes returns exactly the requested number of bytes from Go’s crypto/rand. Count must be 0–16777216 per call. It never falls back to a deterministic generator.
secure_int samples uniformly from a nonempty interval that includes min and excludes max_exclusive. Rejection sampling avoids bias, including for interval widths above MaxInt64. uuid_v4 returns a canonical lowercase RFC 9562 version-4 UUID with the correct variant.
A source fake must return the exact requested byte count. Malformed fake output returns Failed.
Timezone and calendar conversion, tickers, seeded generators, and environment mutation remain future work.

title: Cryptography and randomness
content:
Cryptography and randomness# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Choose a cryptographic function by its purpose: hashing, keyed authentication, key derivation, encryption, or signatures. These transforms use supplied bytes. Random material comes from an explicit Entropy service.
@std/crypto.ms# Manuscript fn constant_time_equal(left: Bytes, right: Bytes) -> Bool fn derive_key(password: Bytes, salt: Bytes, iterations: Int, length: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn hmac(key: Bytes, data: Bytes, algorithm: String) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn open(key: Bytes, nonce: Bytes, ciphertext: Bytes, associated_data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn public_key(seed: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn seal(key: Bytes, nonce: Bytes, plaintext: Bytes, associated_data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn sha256(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sha384(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sha512(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sign(seed: Bytes, data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn verify(key: Bytes, data: Bytes, signature: Bytes) -> Bool Choose the operation# Cryptographic transforms are pure functions. Obtain random keys and nonces through an explicit Entropy service.
Task Operation and algorithm Hash bytes sha256, sha384, or sha512. Authenticate bytes with a key HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512. Unsupported algorithm names return Unsupported. Derive key bytes from a password derive_key, using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256. Encrypt and authenticate seal / open, using AES-256-GCM. Sign and verify Ed25519 with sign / verify. Hashing checks cancellation between chunks. Key derivation checks it periodically.
Key derivation# derive_key requires positive iterations and a length from 1 to 1048576. The application chooses the salt and work factor. The function does not define a password-storage policy.
Authenticated encryption# AES-256-GCM requires a 32-byte key and 12-byte nonce. seal appends a 16-byte authentication tag to the ciphertext. open authenticates before releasing any plaintext. The associated data must match exactly.
A nonce must not be reused with the same key. The runtime does not detect that reuse. Invalid key or nonce sizes return InvalidInput; a wrong key or tampered ciphertext returns AuthenticationFailed.
Signatures and key material# sign and public_key take a 32-byte Ed25519 seed. verify takes a 32-byte public key and signature bytes. It returns false for invalid signatures or wrong key/signature lengths. Use Entropy to generate seed material.
These APIs expose keys as Bytes, so garbage collection cannot guarantee erasure of retained copies. They provide no weak-algorithm menu, implicit randomness, automatic private-key diagnostic redaction, or certificate issuance. Verified TLS belongs to the Network and HTTP APIs.

title: With scopes
content:
With scopes# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use with to acquire a resource and close it when an indented block ends. The name introduced by with cannot be reassigned.
Manuscript with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let chunk = try file.read(max_bytes: 4096) This fragment belongs inside a function returning Result[U, IoError]. The function receives files as an explicit capability. Files.open returns a shared File view. The read result is Optional[Bytes]: match it to distinguish bytes from end-of-input.
What happens, step by step# Evaluate the initializer once. Here, that means opening the file. If initialization fails, leave through the initializer’s error or fault path. No close action has been registered. If initialization succeeds, register the resource’s close operation before the next cancellation checkpoint. Run the block. Close the registered resource when execution leaves the block. Cleanup runs for every exit: reaching the end, break, continue, return, an error forwarded by try, a fault, or cancellation. Nested scopes close from inner to outer.
Which values can use with?# The compiler must be able to identify a valid close operation:
Value’s type Required evidence Concrete type An explicit implementation of standard Closeable. Contract view A declared fn close() -> Unit operation. Generic parameter A bound proving one of those operations. See Closeable for the exact checks.
Keep the lifetime tied to the block# A resource acquired inside a loop closes at the end of that iteration. Returning it or capturing it in a closure does not remove its registered cleanup. An ordinary let binding does not register cleanup.
The file, transaction, or background service supplies its own close behavior. with adds no custom enter hook or error-suppression hook.
For compiler contributors: Go’s function-level defer lasts until the function returns, so it cannot by itself implement Manuscript’s nested block lifetimes. The compiler generates explicit cleanup for those scopes. See exit order , cleanup lowering , and the Go defer specification .

title: Networking, DNS, and TLS
content:
Networking, DNS, and TLS# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use an explicit Network service to resolve names and open sockets. Connections, listeners, and datagram sockets must close when their work ends. The sections below explain destination restrictions, cancellation, and verified TLS.
@std/net.ms# Manuscript fn contains_ip(cidr: String, address: String) -> Result[Bool, NetworkError] fn parse_cidr(text: String) -> Result[String, NetworkError] fn parse_ip(text: String) -> Result[String, NetworkError] @std/tls.ms# Manuscript fn parse_certificates(pem: String, max_certificates: Int) -> Result[List[CertificateInfo], TlsError] fn verify_certificates(chain_pem: String, roots_pem: String, server_name: String, now: Timestamp) -> Result[Unit, TlsError] Connection operations# Manuscript fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn shutdown_write() -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] fn local_address() -> String fn peer_address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn read_timeout(max_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn write_timeout(data: Bytes, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn tls_info() -> Result[TlsInfo, TlsError] Listener operations# Manuscript fn accept() -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] fn address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn accept_timeout(timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] DatagramSocket operations# Manuscript fn send(data: Bytes, address: String) -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] fn receive(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Datagram, NetworkError] fn address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn receive_timeout(max_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Datagram, NetworkError] fn send_timeout(data: Bytes, address: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] Authority and restrictions# Import network() -> Network from @std/http.ms to obtain the current execution’s network service. Acquired Connection, Listener and DatagramSocket views are individually imported from @std/net.ms, closed with with, and also owned by Network. Network.close stops admission, cancels and joins in-flight DNS/dials/HTTP acquisition, closes owned services and handles, and waits for admitted I/O. Concurrent close callers join the same shutdown. Repeated accessor calls return the same host root.
Narrowing destination access# Use restrict to create a child Network with narrower access. The child cannot grant access its parent denied. Host entries are exact DNS names, compared without case and ignoring a trailing dot. CIDR entries authorize numeric address ranges. DNS-name dialing requires the name to be allowed. If CIDRs are supplied, every chosen resolved destination must also belong to those CIDRs; raw IP dialing never bypasses a host-only restriction. Empty hosts/CIDRs deny all outbound destinations.
allow_listen permits binding explicitly allowed numeric addresses; inbound listener peers are not an additional outbound grant. Restricted roots reject Unix socket acquisitions. Redirect hops retain the same policy. Restrictions are enforced on actual resolved addresses at dial time, not by URL string prefixes.
Choosing a resolver# with_resolver provisions a child with an explicit numeric DNS server address. The parent policy must authorize that server. Resolver configuration is scoped to the child; it does not mutate process-wide DNS. Lookup/resolve and UDP destination resolution use cancellable native resolver calls. Parent shutdown closes child capabilities. An unrestricted CLI root retains ordinary OS network authority; restrictions are explicit opt-in narrowing.
Records# Manuscript type Datagram: data: Bytes sender: String type DnsRecord: kind: String value: String priority: Int weight: Int port: Int type TlsOptions: server_name: String roots_pem: String certificate_pem: String private_key_pem: String alpn: List[String] require_client_certificate: Bool type CertificateInfo: subject: String issuer: String dns_names: List[String] not_before: Timestamp not_after: Timestamp der: Bytes type TlsInfo: version: Int cipher_suite: Int alpn: String peer_certificates: List[Bytes] verified: Bool DNS result fields# Resolve accepts A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, PTR and SRV. PTR takes a numeric address; SRV takes the full service name. CNAME returns the native canonical-name result. MX fills priority; SRV fills priority/weight/port; other numeric fields are zero. TXT joins the native record’s fragments. If results exceed max_records, the call returns an error rather than a truncated successful list. TXT/domain text that is not valid UTF-8 returns InvalidData rather than constructing an invalid String. The native resolver does not expose TTL; the API does not invent TTL values. Parse_ip/parse_cidr normalize numeric addresses/prefixes, and contains_ip checks prefix membership without DNS or authority.
Socket lifecycle and deadlines# Connect/listen addresses use native host:port notation, with port zero selecting an ephemeral local port on bind/listen. Unix methods use native Unix-domain paths. Read and write use separate synchronization gates, allowing one of each to progress together. Calls in the same direction are serialized. Closing a handle interrupts blocking I/O and waits for admitted operations. Metadata remains readable after close. A half-close ends writing while leaving reads available. It is supported for TCP, Unix, and TLS connections. Read follows the existing IoError/Optional Bytes contract: positive bounded chunks, none for EOF, and Closed for stale aliases. Writes accept all bytes or return an error after a possible external prefix.
Accept and handshake cancellation# Listener accept cancellation uses an interruptible deadline and restores it before releasing the accept gate. Cancellation and accept_timeout do not destroy the listener: it can admit another accept afterwards. A TLS listener additionally bounds each handshake; shutdown cancels admitted handshakes. Accepted handles retain Network ownership. Unix socket availability follows the target OS, not a separate deferred API.
Datagrams and operation timeouts# UDP preserves message boundaries, including empty messages. Receive accepts max_bytes 1–65535 and returns LimitExceeded on an oversized consumed packet, never a truncated success. UDP name resolution responds to caller cancellation and Network/socket closure. Timeout variants take nonnegative durations: zero is an immediate deadline. Expected local timeouts return NetworkError.Timeout; Connection timeout variants retain IoError and use Failed with a timeout diagnostic. Parent cancellation always unwinds. Operation deadlines are cleared under the direction gate before the next operation starts.
TLS and certificates# TLS supports 1.2 and newer with native authenticated ciphers. connect_tls uses system trust plus a required server_name; connect_tls_config accepts explicit trust PEM, client certificate/key, and ALPN. listen_tls uses a server certificate/key and can require verified client certificates. Empty roots select system trust for clients; supplied roots replace that client trust store. There is no insecure-skip-verification switch or retry. Configured names are checked against certificates; chain validation and expiration remain enabled. ALPN values must be nonempty protocol tokens of at most 255 bytes.
Hostnames and certificate helpers# HTTP/WebSocket clients validate each URL hostname; the generic client TLS server_name field does not override subsequent origins. Private-key PEM is explicit input, not an imported ambient secret. Parse_certificates validates PEM/DER syntax with a certificate count bound and exposes metadata. Verify_certificates takes an explicit PEM chain, trust roots, a nonempty name and Timestamp for pure deterministic chain/hostname/expiry validation. Tls_info exposes negotiated version/cipher/ALPN and peer DER certificates, without exposing private keys.
HTTP/3 is intentionally excluded at the user’s request. The HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSocket contracts are in their own pages.
Network operations# Manuscript fn lookup(name: String, max_records: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[List[String], NetworkError] fn connect(address: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] fn connect_tls(address: String, server_name: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] fn listen(address: String) -> Result[Listener, NetworkError] fn bind_datagram(address: String) -> Result[DatagramSocket, NetworkError] fn restrict(hosts: List[String], cidrs: List[String], allow_listen: Bool) -> Result[Network, NetworkError] fn with_resolver(address: String) -> Result[Network, NetworkError] fn resolve(name: String, kind: String, max_records: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[List[DnsRecord], NetworkError] fn connect_unix(path: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] fn listen_unix(path: String) -> Result[Listener, NetworkError] fn connect_tls_config(address: String, options: TlsOptions, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection, NetworkError] fn listen_tls(address: String, options: TlsOptions, handshake_timeout: Duration) -> Result[Listener, NetworkError]

title: The Closeable contract
content:
The Closeable contract# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Closeable is the standard cleanup contract. Import it from @std/cleanup.ms to name or implement it. A with block checks the identity of that standard contract, so an unrelated interface with the same spelling does not replace it. Its declaration is:
Manuscript interface Closeable: fn close() -> Unit For a concrete value the compiler requires its explicit Closeable implementation, resolves that method, and registers a call to it. A contract value is also eligible when its own declaration explicitly contains the exact operation fn close() -> Unit; register that declared operation without a contract-to-contract conversion. A similarly named concrete method without impl Closeable remains insufficient. This rule lets standard File, ReadStream, and WriteStream contracts expose cleanup and admit source test fakes without inheritance. It has no special knowledge of a particular file or transaction. Libraries can implement the same cleanup contract for their own managed objects.
A generic parameter with a Closeable bound also supplies the implementation proof needed by with; dispatch its bound close operation directly without constructing a view or adding a sharing bound. A generic bound naming a contract that explicitly declares the exact close signature is likewise sufficient. An unconstrained type parameter or a merely similarly named method is insufficient.
close() is idempotent, may suspend like any other function, and finishes the object’s release/shutdown obligation before returning. Repeated or concurrent calls do not release an underlying handle twice. An implementation must coordinate ongoing access with closure and ensure that later accesses report closed state.
Expected failures that application code needs to handle belong to explicit operations such as commit(), flush(), or finish(), returning Result. The automatic close hook returns Unit; an unexpected release failure is a programming/cleanup fault, not a discarded error value.
A close failure does not skip other registered actions. Implementations must leave the object unusable or safely quarantined after a failed release rather than exposing an invalid/reused native handle. Faults and remaining release obligations are reported to the host.
General user defer syntax is unsupported. Custom scope cleanup can be packaged in a library object implementing Closeable.
See with scopes , cleanup faults , and operation contracts .

title: HTTP clients and streaming hosts
content:
HTTP clients and streaming hosts# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use HttpClient for reusable outbound requests and HttpExchange for streaming request handling. Response bodies are resources: read them in chunks and close them. A received HTTP error status is still a response you can inspect.
@std/http.ms# HttpClient operations# Manuscript fn send(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: Bytes, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ResponseBody, HttpError] fn send_stream(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: ReadStream, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ResponseBody, HttpError] fn close() -> Unit ResponseBody operations# Manuscript fn status() -> Int fn headers() -> Map[String, List[String]] fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit HttpExchange operations# Manuscript fn method() -> String fn path() -> String fn query() -> String fn headers() -> Map[String, List[String]] fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn send_headers(status: Int, headers: Map[String, List[String]]) -> Result[Unit, HttpError] fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn upgrade(allowed_origins: List[String], subprotocols: List[String], max_message_bytes: Int) -> Result[WebSocket, WebSocketError] fn close() -> Unit Compatibility# The original bounded buffered HTTP host and Network.request remain supported. The new reusable client and streaming host provide HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 without changing those existing record types. HTTP/3 is excluded by user instruction.
Configuration# Manuscript type HttpClientOptions: max_redirects: Int max_idle_connections: Int max_header_bytes: Int idle_timeout: Duration decompress: Bool cookies: Bool tls: TlsOptions type HttpServerOptions: max_requests: Int max_body_bytes: Int max_response_bytes: Int max_header_bytes: Int timeout: Duration grace: Duration tls: Optional[TlsOptions] Option limits# Client redirect counts, idle capacity, and timeouts must be nonnegative. The header limit must be positive, and idle capacity cannot exceed 65536. Server request capacity is 1–65536. Header limits and timeout must be positive. Body and response limits and grace must be nonnegative. With no TLS configuration, the server uses plain HTTP/1.1. With TLS configured, native ALPN negotiation selects HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. Credentials/trust come from explicit TlsOptions. No ambient HTTP proxy is read.
Client lifetime# Create a shared HttpClient through Network.http_client. It implements Closeable, so keep it in a with scope. It owns a pooled transport and optional public-suffix-aware cookie jar. Idle connections and lifetime are explicit options. Close stops admission, cancels in-flight requests, closes outstanding response bodies, joins their upload/read work and releases idle connections. Network close owns and joins clients too.
Reading a response# send returns a ResponseBody that you read incrementally. Reads follow the stream contract. max_response_bytes limits the cumulative decoded output. Status and duplicate headers remain available as metadata. Close before EOF cancels/discards the body; consumed bodies can reuse the pooled connection. Timeout covers DNS through body lifetime; parent cancellation unwinds. Gzip decoding is enabled only with decompress and remains subject to the expanded-byte bound. Invalid UTF-8 header values are rejected before constructing source Strings.
Streaming an upload# Send_stream borrows an explicitly shared ReadStream for the upload and does not close it. The response owns the upload work until response closure/completion: keep the input’s scope open through the response scope. Under HTTP/1.1, streaming server responses enable full duplex so a response does not silently drain/close the outstanding upload. Upload faults retain source fault identity, not a generic transport success. Redirects requiring replay are returned to the caller for streaming bodies; immutable Bytes sends can follow configured redirects. A consumed prefix cannot be rolled back after failure.
Redirects and HTTP status# Redirects honor max_redirects (zero returns the redirect response), reject TLS downgrade, recheck the Network policy on every destination, and remove explicit Authorization/Cookie/Proxy-Authorization when the origin changes. Automatic cookies are selected by the destination jar rather than copying source-origin headers. HTTP 4xx and 5xx statuses are returned responses, rather than transport errors. Header names/values reject injection and callers cannot set host-managed framing fields.
Streaming request host# Network.serve_stream accepts an ordinary handler and may be stored as a bound method. The handler signature is fn(exchange: HttpExchange) -> Result[Unit, HttpError]. The server establishes a fixed request execution context, bounded admission, body/output/header limits, disconnect cancellation and timeout. The handler may read incrementally, emit headers once and write/flush bounded output, or upgrade to a WebSocket session. Source routes by ordinary method/path branching.
Response ordering and limits# Read and write have separate synchronized gates. Send_headers accepts status 200–599 and ordered duplicate header values; it rejects repeated headers emission, CR/LF/NUL values, and caller-supplied framing. Write requires headers first, counts cumulative output bytes, applies native backpressure and disallows bodies for HEAD/204/304. Body bound failures return IoError.Failed with a limit diagnostic. Before headers, handler faults/domain errors produce a generic 500, or 504 for timeout where possible; after headers the host aborts transport rather than returning a misleading complete body. Returning success without headers produces 204.
Request and server lifetime# HttpExchange belongs to its request: retained aliases report Closed once request cleanup ends. Server shutdown stops admission, waits grace, cancels remaining requests/sessions and joins them before returning. Hijacked WebSocket transports are explicitly included in request cleanup and joining. A server or Network cannot close from its own handler. Streaming source code needs no new function kind or detached task syntax.
Network operations# Manuscript fn request(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: Bytes, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ClientResponse, HttpError] fn http_client(options: HttpClientOptions) -> Result[HttpClient, HttpError] fn serve_stream(address: String, handler: fn(exchange: HttpExchange) -> Result[Unit, HttpError], options: HttpServerOptions) -> Result[HttpServer, HttpError]

title: Scope-exit ordering
content:
Scope-exit ordering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index When a scope ends, the runtime runs the cleanup registered by with. It closes inner resources before outer ones. Another reference to a resource, including one stored in a record, does not register another close action.
Evaluate the pending return value or select the initiating error, fault, or cancellation. Finish any active joined API call: it cancels unfinished operations if needed and joins them before unwinding into the caller’s cleanup. Call registered close() methods in reverse registration/nesting order. A Background.close() performs its own service cancellation and joining here. Deliver the pending return/error, unless cleanup selected a programming fault; otherwise propagate the selected fault or cancellation. A cleanup fault suppresses a pending normal return or domain error. The unreturned value is released for garbage collection; it is not recursively closed. Resource factories retain explicit responsibility for resources acquired but never delivered.
Returned references do not bypass registered cleanup. A returned file registered in the exiting scope is already closed when the caller receives it. There is no staged ownership transfer or result escrow.
Register dependencies outside the background service’s with scope so that service shutdown finishes before those dependencies close. See background services and fault selection .

title: Shielding and cleanup faults
content:
Shielding and cleanup faults# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Cleanup still runs when cancellation or a fault ends ordinary work. It ignores the cancellation signal and expired work deadline that caused the exit. This is called shielding. Cleanup keeps the original access to external services and may wait for operations to finish.
If close itself faults# Every registered close action is attempted once during scope exit. A fault in one action does not skip the rest.
Outcome before cleanup If cleanup faults If cleanup succeeds A programming fault is already pending Keep the original fault as primary; record cleanup faults as secondary diagnostics. Keep the original fault. A normal return, expected error, or cancellation is pending The first cleanup fault becomes primary; record later faults as secondary diagnostics. Keep the pending outcome. A concurrency API reports an operation fault as ExecutionError.Crashed. A background service reports it through its failure observer. Root hosts isolate and report request failures.
Cleanup can outlast a timeout# Shielding gives cleanup a chance to release resources; it cannot force uncooperative code to finish. Hosts set cleanup watchdogs separately from request timeouts. If close or join cannot finish, the host may need process-level escalation . A timer expiring does not mean cleanup completed.
If an operation can fail in an expected way, handle that through an explicit fallible completion method before leaving the scope. For example, commit a transaction before relying on close to release it. See Closeable , timeouts , and resource release .

title: Subprocesses and terminal I/O
content:
Subprocesses and terminal I/O# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use stream helpers for bounded reads and copies, and Commands for buffered subprocess execution. The caller supplies the streams or command service. Helpers do not acquire authority or close the streams for you.
@std/io.ms# Manuscript fn copy(input: ReadStream, output: WriteStream, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Int, IoError] fn read_all(input: ReadStream, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, IoError] fn read_line(input: ReadStream, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[String], IoError] Running commands# Commands.run uses the imported commands() host accessor. Supply the program, arguments, input, aggregate output bound, and timeout. It waits for execution and returns captured exit_code, stdout, and stderr. A nonzero exit is returned data. Running a shell must be explicit.
Stream helpers# These helpers use shared stream views without closing them. Keep the streams’ own cleanup scopes open for the whole call. All helpers cooperate with cancellation and enforce cumulative byte limits.
Helper Behavior copy Returns the number of bytes copied. An error may occur after a prefix was written; there is no rollback. read_all Returns all bytes only on success. read_line Reads one byte at a time so it does not consume the next line. It strips LF and a preceding CR, and accepts a final line without a terminator. read_line returns none only if EOF occurs before any data. Its positive max_bytes includes terminator bytes. Invalid UTF-8 returns InvalidData; overflow returns LimitExceeded and may consume a prefix plus one boundary byte. Copy and read_all allow a zero limit for an empty source.
Source streams must return nonempty chunks within the requested size. A malformed stream implementation causes Failed.
Expected stream failures preserve their original IoError case and payload. Invalid UTF-8 returns IoError.InvalidData; an exceeded byte bound returns IoError.LimitExceeded. Helpers do not flatten Result or catch cancellation and faults. Convert a File view explicitly to ReadStream when required by the contract-view rules.
Interactive subprocess handles, terminal raw mode and secret reads, REPL/history, and richer child environment or working-directory options remain future work. Buffered Commands is the current subprocess API; there is no new Process/Child hierarchy.

title: WebSocket sessions
content:
WebSocket sessions# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts A WebSocket session sends and receives complete text or binary messages over a connection. Client sessions come from Network; server sessions come from an HTTP upgrade. Keep each session inside its cleanup and host lifetime.
@std/websocket.ms# WebSocket operations# Manuscript fn receive() -> Result[Optional[WebSocketMessage], WebSocketError] fn send(data: Bytes, text: Bool) -> Result[Unit, WebSocketError] fn ping(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, WebSocketError] fn subprotocol() -> String fn close() -> Unit Acquiring a session# Network.web_socket acquires a client WebSocket for an explicit ws/wss URL, headers, subprotocols and WebSocketOptions. HttpExchange.upgrade acquires the server session inside an admitted request. Both return contract views with synchronized operations and explicit close. Wss retains hostname/chain verification, explicit TLS roots/client certificates and destination restrictions.
Manuscript type WebSocketOptions: max_message_bytes: Int timeout: Duration tls: TlsOptions compression: Bool type WebSocketMessage: data: Bytes text: Bool Message limits and errors# Client max_message_bytes and handshake timeout must be positive. Clients negotiate permessage-deflate only when compression is explicitly enabled. Server upgrade currently accepts uncompressed messages. Bounds apply to decompressed message data as well as wire frames. receive returns one complete text or binary message, or none when the peer closes normally. Oversized messages return LimitExceeded and terminate transport; invalid text UTF-8 returns InvalidData. Repeated reads after a protocol failure return Closed rather than spinning inside the protocol implementation. Send validates text UTF-8 and bounds outbound message bytes. Ping limits control payloads to 125 bytes.
Concurrent calls and protocol rules# One read and one write can run concurrently. Two reads, or two writes, are serialized. Fragmentation, masking, control frames and close codes follow RFC 6455 through the pinned Gorilla implementation. Subprotocol tokens are validated and the selected protocol is observable. Client callers cannot override Sec-WebSocket handshake/framing headers. Server upgrade accepts absent Origin, and by default same-host origins; an explicit allowed_origins list authorizes exact http/https origins, never a wildcard implicit grant.
Session lifetime# The server session remains inside the HTTP request lifetime. Disconnect, request timeout and server/Network shutdown interrupt blocking receives/writes, close the hijacked socket and join the handler’s nested work. Close is idempotent, attempts a normal close control frame with a short bounded write deadline, then releases the handle and joins admitted operations. Source must not retain a session as detached work outside the request. Client sessions remain owned by their Network and lexical with scope. HTTP/3 is unrelated to the supported WebSocket transport and is excluded from this expansion by user request.
Manuscript fn web_socket(url: String, headers: Map[String, String], subprotocols: List[String], options: WebSocketOptions) -> Result[WebSocket, WebSocketError]

title: Compression and archives
content:
Compression and archives# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use compress for a byte stream and archive for named file or directory entries. Both operate on data in memory. Set limits on expanded output; unpacking an archive does not write its entries to disk.
@std/compress.ms# Manuscript fn compress(data: Bytes, format: String, level: Int, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CompressionError] fn decompress(data: Bytes, format: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CompressionError] @std/archive.ms# Manuscript fn pack(entries: List[ArchiveEntry], format: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, ArchiveError] fn unpack(data: Bytes, format: String, limits: ArchiveLimits) -> Result[List[ArchiveEntry], ArchiveError] Compression behavior# Supported format strings are gzip, zlib, and deflate; others return Unsupported. Compression levels are 0–9, and output limits must be nonnegative.
Decompression validates checksums and rejects trailing bytes that do not belong to the format. Concatenated gzip members share one cumulative output limit. Chunk processing checks cancellation. Excess expanded output returns LimitExceeded before the decoder retains output beyond max_bytes.
Gzip output has a zero timestamp and no platform or name metadata.
Archive records and limits# ArchiveEntry contains path: String, data: Bytes, and directory: Bool. ArchiveLimits contains max_entries: Int, max_entry_bytes: Int, and max_total_bytes: Int. All limits are nonnegative and count expanded content.
Pack and unpack support zip and tar, with regular files and directories. Names must be UTF-8 portable relative paths. They reject absolute roots, backslashes, colons, NUL, and empty, dot, or dot-dot components. Duplicate normalized paths are rejected. Directory data must be empty.
Encrypted archives, devices, sparse files, links, and non-UTF-8 names are unsupported. ZIP supports stored and deflated entries and validates checksums. Pack preserves entry order with deterministic metadata: TAR uses the epoch and ZIP uses its 1980 minimum date.
Problem Error Unsupported entry type Unsupported Malformed archive or decoded path InvalidData Invalid source entry InvalidInput Unpacking does not write files# unpack returns separate data entries. It performs no filesystem writes and grants no filesystem access. Automatic extraction is future work.
Bound compressed input reads as well as expanded output. ZIP parses central-directory metadata before checking max_entries. TAR uses native header validation; it makes no canonical guarantee about arbitrary trailing padding or metadata.
An application can validate entries and write them through an explicit FileSystem service. Secure extraction into an existing directory still needs a trusted containment adapter; a lexical path check alone is insufficient. Brotli and Zstd remain future work.

title: External resource release
content:
External resource release# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Files, sockets, stream bodies, transactions, and pool leases need explicit release. Their object memory is garbage collected, but their external handles or activity are released through close() or a with block. These resource objects implement Closeable.
Object Automatic close behavior File, socket, stream body Release the external handle Transaction Roll back if not committed; then release its lease Connection lease Return the connection only after outstanding access has ended Background service Stop admission, cancel as configured, and join work Closing is shared state: all aliases see the same closed object. Resource methods return resource-specific errors such as IoError.Closed after closure. The wrapper must synchronize access and close; checking a flag before accessing a native handle is not sufficient. Old lease references must never access a connection reused for another caller.
Cleanup is not successful completion. Explicit commit, finish, or flush operations expose expected errors with Result. Unexpected release failures become cleanup faults. A plain let, function call, aggregate, or closure does not add implicit close behavior.
Factories close newly acquired native resources when cancellation or an error prevents delivery. A with initializer registers successful acquisition before cancellation can unwind it. See completion and acquisition , sharing , and Closeable .

title: Concurrency
content:
Concurrency guide# Design index An ordinary function call finishes before the caller moves on. Use a concurrency API when operations should run at the same time. Every function can wait for work; there is no separate async declaration.
Choose how the work ends# Need Use When it finishes Run a fixed set of functions together parallel Before the call returns, including on failure. Start work under a longer-lived service Background The service tracks it and waits for unfinished work during shutdown. Parallel APIs join: they wait for every started operation to finish its body and cleanup. A timeout requests a stop; it does not let the call return with work still running.
Start with parallel operations for a complete example. Then read joined groups for error outcomes and cancellation for stopping and time budgets. Runtime contracts contains the implementation details.
Concurrency APIs accept ordinary function values, including functions passed through parameters or stored in collections. Closures keep snapshots of the surrounding bindings they use. Keeping a resource reference does not keep the resource open; see sharing .
Sharing values and updating state# All values may be shared freely, including functions, interface views, collections, and builders. Records and collections are mutable references; local var bindings are snapshotted by closures. Services and builders synchronize their internals. Shared records, collections, and local Queue instances require an explicit lock around conflicting access. For a complete shared update, import Synchronized from @std/sync.ms:
Manuscript import Synchronized from "@std/sync.ms" let counter = Synchronized(value: 0) with locked = counter.lock(): locked.set(value: locked.get() + 1) The guard holds the lock until scope exit. Read the synchronization contract for cancellation, aliases, and reentry. For a shared FIFO, store a Queue[T] inside one Synchronized and hold its guard for every access; see local queues . Sharing does not extend a resource’s open lifetime.
Importing concurrency APIs# Concurrency adds no intrinsic names or compiler bounds. Import each API or type that the module names:
Manuscript import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms" import Duration from "@std/time.ms" These are independent imports, not a required bundle. Importing one does not expose the others. Work status and failure reporting are also explicit standard exports; the standard API contract lists their paths. Ordinary Result annotations and error-adaptation helpers use their own imports from @std/result.ms.
Scheduling, cancellation, joining, time budgets, and service shutdown belong to these library/runtime APIs. The compiler checks callback signatures and the fixed parallel pack shape by the resolved standard binding identity. Its hidden execution context is an internal calling convention and carries host roots used by imported accessors; it is not a source type. A user function named parallel remains an ordinary function.
Fixed lifetimes# Every operation starts under a fixed execution lifetime. That relationship is chosen before work starts and does not change while it runs.
API Execution lifetime Ordinary call Current execution context parallel Joined group nested under the caller Background.start The chosen background service’s fixed host/component lifetime A helper may call parallel and return its completed result. It cannot return running work for another scope to adopt. Background work is started directly through the chosen service.
Passing a Background reference shares access to that service. It does not prolong the service’s lifetime, move its existing work, change its cancellation parent, or reset deadlines. The creating scope registers shutdown with with; aliases reject admission after closure.
A request can submit work through an application background service, but accepted work uses the service’s execution context. Request resources captured by that work can still close when the request exits; later use reports the resource’s closed-state error. Pass request data and application services, and acquire the operation’s resources inside it.
There is no task adoption, task reparenting, source-level detached work, or dynamic ownership graph. Scoped resources and ordinary references follow resource lifetimes .
Reading order# Parallel operations : calling parallel, argument preparation, and typed results Joined groups : the normative stop, join, and outcome contract for parallel Cancellation and budgets : cancellation requests, checkpoints, timeouts, and deadlines Synchronized values : lock scopes, complete updates, aliases, and reentry Runtime contracts : atomic transitions, resource acquisition, adapter contexts, and host escalation The standard library describes background services .

title: Logging
content:
Logging# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Write structured logs to an explicit output stream. Logging returns expected errors. Tests use ordinary conditional returns to check their results.
@std/log.ms# Manuscript fn write(output: WriteStream, level: String, message: String, fields: Map[String, String], max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Unit, LogError] write emits one compact UTF-8 JSON line to the supplied shared WriteStream. It contains level, message, and fields. Allowed levels are debug, info, warn, and error. Fields are a Map[String, String], sorted by the native JSON serializer.
max_bytes must be nonnegative and includes the final LF. Excess output returns LimitExceeded; it is not truncated. Stream failures become Failed. Writes use the stream’s existing synchronization, backpressure, and cancellation behavior.
The caller chooses the output and sensitive fields. The function provides no implicit stderr access, arbitrary object inspection, automatic redaction, or recursive failure logging. Serialization may allocate a complete record before checking the byte limit, so bound untrusted inputs too.
Tests# Tests use ordinary if/return guards; see semantic conformance tests . No expected-fault-catching syntax or authority injection is added. Heap/CPU profiling and richer runtime metrics remain future work. Existing inspect, diagram, and debug metadata contracts are unchanged.

title: Node.js and Go coverage
content:
Node.js and Go coverage# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts This table maps common Node.js and Go tasks to Manuscript facilities. It tells you what runs today and what remains future work. The mapping is about functionality, not compatibility with those platforms’ APIs.
Node.js / Go capability Manuscript option Availability Buffer, bytes, encoding/hex/base64/binary Immutable Bytes, strict UTF-8/hex/base64, binary Int/Float Implemented strings, Unicode scalar operations, regexp Text functions and opaque RE2-style Regex Implemented; normalization implemented; graphemes/locale/legacy encodings deferred Array/Map/Set, slices/maps/sort Immutable receiver methods, searches, map/filter/flat_map/fold/stable sort, grouping, set relations, builders Implemented Math, strconv, math/big Float math, strict number conversion, BigInt, existing Decimal Implemented; extraction/Brotli/Zstd deferred events/sync/channels/context/worker_threads Local Queue wrapped in Synchronized, guards, Pool/Lease, joined parallel and Background contexts Implemented; no JS worker VM or detached tasks console/log/testing Explicit streams/structured JSON log, conditional checks, existing runner Implemented; no sandbox VM equivalent claimed The canonical callable surface lives on the linked package pages. Existing host/service APIs retain their identities. Deferred entries stay explicit; future implementations should add declarations to the Manuscript standard library sources and matching native implementations, semantic/boundary tests, and source-level compiler conformance fixtures together. The distribution remains self-contained with pinned vendored Go dependencies; native builds need no downloads.
For method-level equivalents and semantic differences, see JavaScript built-in coverage .

title: Parallel operations
content:
Parallel operations# Guide index · Design index Use parallel to run a fixed set of operations at the same time. Pass functions in the named tasks argument. The API starts them and waits for every started operation, including cleanup, before returning. Passing a function call would execute it before parallel starts.
