Calling parallel# Manuscript import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" type User: id: Int type Order: id: Int type UserError: case Missing type OrderError: case Unavailable interface Users: fn get(id: Int) -> Result[User, UserError] interface Orders: fn for_user(user_id: Int) -> Result[List[Order], OrderError] type Summary: user: User orders: List[Order] type LoadError: case Execution(cause: ExecutionError) case UserFailure(cause: UserError) case OrderFailure(cause: OrderError) fn load(user_id: Int, users: Users, orders: Orders) -> Result[Summary, LoadError]: let first = fn() -> Result[User, UserError]: return users.get(id: user_id) let second = fn() -> Result[List[Order], OrderError]: return orders.for_user(user_id: user_id) match parallel(tasks: [first, second]): error(cause): return error(cause: LoadError.Execution(cause: cause)) ok(results): let [user_result, orders_result] = results match user_result: error(cause): return error(cause: LoadError.UserFailure(cause: cause)) ok(user): match orders_result: error(cause): return error(cause: LoadError.OrderFailure(cause: cause)) ok(user_orders): return ok(value: Summary(user: user, orders: user_orders)) Preparation# Before parallel starts anything, the caller evaluates arguments, task-pack entries, receivers, and captured values in written order. In this example, creating first and second captures snapshots of user_id and the shared services. Their bodies run later, after preparation succeeds and parallel starts the operations under its group execution context.
If preparation fails, no operation has started. Preparation may have external effects; the runtime does not undo them. Resources acquired during preparation require their own with scopes or acquisition API contracts.
Passing users.get(...) instead of a function executes that call during preparation; it is not a way to schedule the call concurrently, and it is a type error when the result is not callable. Ordinary calls inside a function remain sequential unless another concurrency API is invoked.
Concurrent scheduling and external effect order are nondeterministic. Sharing a resource does not imply that simultaneous operations on it are semantically valid; its API must serialize access or report unsupported concurrent use. See closures and resource sharing .
Ordered, typed results# A literal task pack is a fixed set of positions, each holding a zero-argument function. Positions may have different return types. The result preserves both their types and their input order. Here, user_result is Result[User, UserError] and orders_result is Result[List[Order], OrderError], whichever operation finishes first.
The brackets do not force these different types into a homogeneous List[T]. Fixed positional packs require type-system support for heterogeneous inputs and outputs; parallel itself remains an API call, with no special concurrency keyword. Ordinary list literals outside a positional-pack contract keep their homogeneous list rules.
Pack arity is preserved: parallel(tasks: [first]) returns a one-position successful result, destructured with let [resA] = ...; an empty pack returns an empty successful result and starts no work. Destructuring a fixed positional result with the wrong number of positions is a compile error. Parenthesized binding patterns such as let (resA, resB) = ... are not supported. See destructuring bindings .
Return values and errors# parallel returns an outer Result[Pack, ExecutionError]. The outer Result describes execution of the whole group. Each operation’s return value is preserved unchanged at its position:
Function returns Result position contains String String Result[Stock, OrderError] Result[Stock, OrderError] Optional[String] Optional[String] A returned domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion. It does not stop sibling operations and is not flattened into the outer Result. In the example, match handles each Result and translates its error into LoadError. Use try when the enclosing function has the same error type; see error compatibility . There is no source task-result wrapper beyond the outer Result.
No operation remains running after parallel exits, on any path. An operation fault or an expired timeout stops and joins the group; caller cancellation joins the group and then unwinds the caller. The complete rules are in joined groups .
Results follow the ordinary reference rules ; returning a resource does not keep it open. Unreturned references become eligible for garbage collection; the runtime does not recursively close arbitrary results or captures. Resource cleanup comes from with or an acquisition-specific delivery contract. See completion and acquisition .
The optional named timeout argument shortens the inherited deadline; it never waives joining. See timeouts . Callbacks and results are ordinary values; no sharing bound or callable proof is required. Use Synchronized when callbacks must coordinate a complete read/modify/write update. The standard API contract fixes the callable/result mapping and legal uses of inferred packs; general source declaration syntax for packs is unsupported.

title: Expanded library conformance
content:
Expanded library conformance# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts These executable checks exercise package behavior through the compiler and native runtime. Use the listed fixtures and tests to verify data handling, limits, errors, and cleanup.
tests/e2e/testdata/accept/library*.ms: compiler-to-native execution for exact JSON numbers, duplicate-key/depth failures, codecs, hashes, binary range limits, compression, ZIP, and generic sequential callbacks/function values. runtime/library_test.go: malformed strict encodings/numbers, signed 64-bit binary boundaries, surrogate/duplicate-key JSON validation, PBKDF2 vector, AEAD tampering, Ed25519, compression trailing bytes/bombs, ZIP/TAR paths/limits, exclusive filesystem writes, symlink-safe removal, HTTP duplicate headers/status/redirect/limits, and TCP half-close/round-trip, empty/oversized UDP datagrams, socket close/cancellation, and Network close interrupting active HTTP requests. tests/e2e/testdata/projects/library/main.ms: native CLI acquisition/use of FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock/Timestamp and System roots, including exclusive creation and removal. compiler/library_test.go: every registered function is importable, and opaque BigInt/Regex/Timestamp constructors are rejected. Existing host, service, compiler/cache and e2e tests remain required. The runtime embeds all new implementation sources for standalone builds and content pinning; test sources are excluded from the runtime bundle. Run go test ./..., go test -race ./runtime ./checker ./compiler ./tooling, and go vet ./... with Go 1.25 or newer. Native platform limitations are documented per package rather than inferred from a familiar module name. Written future requirements are not counted as passed tests.
Networking checks additionally cover scoped host/CIDR policy (including raw-IP bypass rejection), custom DNS records, listener reuse after timeout, Unix half-close, cancellation during acquisition, pooled cookies/redirects, HTTP/2, custom trust/hostname validation, mutual TLS, duplex streamed upload/response, decompressed WebSocket bounds and shutdown joining hijacked sessions. tests/e2e/testdata/projects/networking/main.ms exercises HTTP streaming and WebSocket echo through the compiler and an offline native build.
Host compatibility checks additionally cover runtime/library_host_parity_test.go (Node-generated path/glob fixtures, exclusive opens, positional/vector I/O, line bounds, stream adapters, metadata, tree-copy symlinks, directory EOF, temporary cleanup, watch/timer close and cancellation, OS/process information, and environment parsing; native watch event retention/overflow, copy filters/clone/timestamps, glob exclusions/link cycles, exact stat metadata/numeric flags, after/every restart and shutdown, native constants, and signal streams). scripts/node-stdlib-fixtures.cjs refreshes the offline oracle with Node.js 24. The native CLI fixture exercises the new capabilities through Manuscript source. compiler/node_host_coverage_test.go checks every inventory mapping against the current declaration surface; a live Node.js 24 check verifies module exports and returned FileHandle/Dir/Timeout methods against the complete inventory. Runtime-specific facilities stay classified separately. Linux/macOS/Windows CI runs native compatibility checks with CGO disabled. Platform helpers are included in NativeDependencies for standalone builds and the compiler/runtime content pin.

title: JavaScript built-in coverage
content:
JavaScript built-in coverage# Standard library guide · Package coverage · Implemented signatures The inventory follows MDN’s JavaScript reference , particularly Array , String , Map , Set , and Number . Rows identify runnable equivalents; names and contracts follow Manuscript’s type system. Deprecated HTML string wrappers and prototype machinery are excluded from the useful data API.
List / Array# Import List for bracket literals. All updates return new values. Callbacks run sequentially and may suspend.
JavaScript surface Manuscript equivalent Contract length, indexed access, at length(), get(index:), at(index:) get rejects negative indexes; at counts from the end; missing values are Optional concat, push, unshift concat(values:), append(value:), prepend(value:) Append/prepend mutate; concat returns a new homogeneous list pop, shift last() / first() plus without(index:) Retrieval and removal are explicit operations includes, indexOf, lastIndexOf contains(value:), index_of(value:), last_index_of(value:) Element type must satisfy Equal; missing indexes are none find, findLast, findIndex, findLastIndex find, find_last, find_index, find_last_index with predicate: Short-circuit search; reverse search visits from the end some, every some(predicate:), every(predicate:) Empty list produces false / true respectively filter, map, flatMap filter(predicate:), map(transform:), flat_map(transform:) Map may change the element type; flat_map flattens one level flat imported flatten(values:) One level of homogeneous nested lists; compose for deeper flattening reduce, reduceRight fold(initial:, step:), fold_right(initial:, step:) Always supply an initial accumulator; accumulator type may differ from element type forEach for_each(operation:) Callback returns Unit reverse, toReversed reverse() Returns a reversed copy sort, toSorted sorted(compare:) Stable, explicit comparator returning negative / zero / positive Int slice slice(start:, end:) Strict half-open bounds; faults for invalid bounds splice, toSpliced with_values(start:, delete_count:, replacement:) In-place replacement; clone first to preserve the source; start/count must describe a valid range with with_value(index:, value:) Negative indexing supported; out-of-range update faults fill, copyWithin fill(value:, start:, end:), copy_within(target:, start:, end:) In-place updates; strict bounds; overlap-safe copy truncates at the destination end keys, entries, values, iteration keys(), entries(), ordinary for over the list Eager lists; entries are ListEntry(index:, value:) records join List[String].join(separator:) Requires strings; formatting other types is explicit Array.of, Array.from bracket literals; set.values(), map.entries(), text.scalar_values() Construction follows the source type, without dynamic array-like coercion Repeated-value construction, numeric sequences imported filled(value:, count:, max_items:), range(start:, end:, step:, max_items:) Bounded Result; range excludes end and accepts either step direction Map.groupBy, Object.groupBy list.group_by(key:), imported group_by(values:, key:) Hashable keys; first-seen group order and original order within each group new Set(array) list.to_set() Requires Hashable; deduplicates in first-seen order Multi-parameter calls require argument labels; single-parameter methods and callbacks may omit the call label. Callback declarations retain their parameter names: fn(value: T) -> U, fn(value: T) -> Bool, or fn(accumulator: A, value: T) -> A. For an index-aware callback, use list.entries() and its typed ListEntry values. There is no implicit this, sparse slot, callback arity coercion, default comparator, or heterogeneous list.
Native methods introduce only their own output/accumulator variables. Inference uses supplied arguments rather than the surrounding expected result. Specialize a generic method when saving it as a value:
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" fn label(value: Int) -> String: return "item {value}" test "receiver methods compose": let labels = [1, 2].map(transform: label) if not (labels.join(separator: ", ") == "item 1, item 2"): return panic(message: "check failed") let convert = [3, 4].map[String] if not (convert(transform: label) == ["item 3", "item 4"]): return panic(message: "check failed") Generic operations in these pinned native declarations do not add generic operation syntax to application-defined interfaces or implementations.
Map and Set# Import Map / Set when naming or constructing them. Keys and set elements satisfy Hashable. Enumeration returns separate lists in insertion order. Collection equality is independent of insertion order.
JavaScript surface Manuscript equivalent Contract Map.size, get, has, set, delete length, get, contains, with_entry, without Updates mutate; missing lookup is Optional Map.clear, keys, values, entries, forEach clear, keys, values, entries, for_each Entries are MapEntry(key:, value:); callback is fn(key: K, value: V) -> Unit Map.getOrInsert with_default(key:, value:) followed by get(key:) Returns the updated map; an existing value is preserved Map.getOrInsertComputed with_default_from(key:, create:) followed by get(key:) Callback receives key: and runs exactly once if absent new Map(entries), Object.fromEntries imported map_from_entries(entries:) Duplicate keys keep first insertion position and use last value Map/object merging map.merge(other:) Right values replace matching entries in place; new keys append Set.size, has, add, delete length, contains, with_value, without Insert/delete mutate; length and contains read Set.clear, values, keys, entries, forEach clear, values, values, entries, for_each Set keys and values share one spelling; entries contain [value, value] union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference union(right:), intersection(right:), difference(right:), symmetric_difference(right:) New sets; left traversal order, then right-only values where applicable isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, isDisjointFrom is_subset_of(right:), is_superset_of(right:), is_disjoint_from(right:) Boolean relations; arguments are typed sets Use Map[String, T] for a dynamic string-keyed object. Statically declared records retain named fields and nominal identities. Prototype lookup, property descriptors, dynamic record reflection, WeakMap, WeakSet, and finalization registries have no corresponding data API.
String# String methods need no additional import. The same algorithms are available as individually imported @std/string.ms functions. Strings are valid UTF-8; indexes and lengths below count Unicode scalars, not JavaScript UTF-16 code units or user-perceived graphemes.
JavaScript surface Manuscript equivalent Contract length, at, charAt, charCodeAt, codePointAt scalar_length(), at(index:), scalar_at(index:) Scalar text / scalar integer in Optional; negative indexes count from end includes, startsWith, endsWith contains(text:), starts_with(prefix:), ends_with(suffix:) Literal substring operations indexOf, lastIndexOf index_of(value:), last_index_of(value:) Scalar index in Optional; empty search finds start / end slice, substring slice(start:, end:), substring(start:, end:) Slice clamps relative bounds; substring clamps nonnegative bounds and swaps reversed endpoints Strict scalar extraction slice_scalars(start:, end:) Existing Result returning OutOfRange for invalid bounds split split(separator:, max_parts:) Positive maximum; final part retains the remainder; empty separator splits scalars concat concat(values:), interpolation Concatenates text explicitly trim, trimStart, trimEnd trim(), trim_start(), trim_end() Unicode whitespace toLowerCase, toUpperCase lower(), upper() Go Unicode simple case mapping; not locale-sensitive full case expansion repeat repeat(count:, max_bytes:) Existing bounded Result replace replace(old:, new:, max_replacements:) Literal replacement; zero replacements preserves text; empty old inserts at scalar boundaries replaceAll replace_all(old:, new:, max_bytes:) Literal replacement, including empty old; output limit checked before each append padStart, padEnd pad_start(target_length:, padding:, max_bytes:), pad_end(...) Scalar length, complete scalar truncation of padding, bounded output; empty padding preserves text normalize normalize(form:, max_bytes:) NFC, NFD, NFKC, NFKD; bounded output, Unicode stream-safe handling of long combining runs String.fromCodePoint imported from_scalars(values:) Rejects surrogates and invalid scalar values match, matchAll, search, regexp replacement Regex.matches, find_all, replace; imported regex functions RE2-style patterns; explicit match/output limits; captured-group/index records remain a gap UTF-8 conversion to_bytes(), Bytes.to_text() Invalid UTF-8 decoding yields none Locale collation/case mapping (localeCompare, locale case methods, Intl), grapheme segmentation, capture-rich regex results, and search start-position options remain gaps. Manuscript valid UTF-8 makes lone-surrogate repair (isWellFormed / toWellFormed) unnecessary. Legacy substr and HTML wrapper methods are intentionally omitted.
Other built-ins# JavaScript facility Manuscript option Coverage / difference Number string formatting Int.to_string(radix:), Float.to_string(), to_fixed(digits:), to_exponential(digits:), to_precision(precision:) Precision methods return Result, permit 0–100 fraction digits / 1–100 significant digits, retain signed zero, and round ties to even Number predicates / parsing Float.is_nan(), is_finite(), imported strict number parsers; truncate_to_int() No partial parsing or silent coercion; isInteger can compare truncation or use @std/math.ms BigInt Imported constructor/parser and add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, compare, bit methods, to_int, to_string receivers Division errors are values; integer exponent/shift operations remain gaps Typed byte array / Buffer Bytes with at, get, contains, index_of, last_index_of, prefix/suffix tests, slice, reverse, with_value, concat Immutable byte storage; imported binary functions provide signed/unsigned integer and Float reads/writes Math @std/math.ms Existing elementary math, trigonometry, rounding, constants; random authority is explicit JSON @std/json.ms Existing parse/stringify with exact decimal number text and explicit limits Promise aggregation ordinary suspending functions; parallel, Background Joined work and lexical cleanup; no detached Promise or microtask compatibility Date / timers @std/time.ms, explicit Clock / WallClock capabilities Timestamp parse/format, shifts/differences, monotonic timers; calendar/timezone/locale formatting remains a gap ArrayBuffer / DataView Bytes, @std/binary.ms No shared raw memory, typed numeric views, or Atomics; use Synchronized for shared updates Object / Reflect / Proxy / Symbol Records, alternatives, maps, explicit contracts Dynamic prototypes, property traps, metaprogramming, boxed primitive methods, and VM reflection are outside the typed data API See Node.js and Go coverage for files, networking, streams, crypto, processes, compression, and other application facilities already present. The table records functional breadth without claiming JavaScript source or runtime compatibility.

title: Joined groups
content:
Joined groups and execution outcomes# Guide index · Design index A parallel call waits for all the operations it started, including their cleanup. This waiting is called joining. A failure or timeout first asks unfinished work to stop, then waits for it. This page defines the exact lifecycle and which outcome the caller receives.
Terms# Term Meaning Operation One invocation of a function passed to a concurrency API: a tasks position or one Background.start submission Group The operations started by one parallel call Caller The execution that called the API; its context is the group’s fixed parent Joined Every started operation has finished its body and scope cleanup Execution errors# ExecutionError is exported by @std/tasks.ms; import it when naming the result type. Its Crashed payload uses OperationId, also exported by @std/tasks.ms. The standard declaration is:
Manuscript type ExecutionError: case TimedOut case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String) OperationId identifies runtime work for diagnostics; it does not grant scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. Secondary faults are retained in runtime diagnostics associated with the primary outcome.
Group lifecycle# Prepare. The caller evaluates arguments in written order. If preparation fails, no operation starts. See preparation . Start. An empty pack returns ok immediately and starts no work, whatever the timeout. A zero timeout on nonempty input stops the group before any operation starts. Otherwise parallel starts every position. Stop. The first of these triggers stops the group: an operation faults, the group’s timeout expires, or the caller’s context is cancelled or reaches its inherited deadline. Stopping prevents further starts and requests cancellation of unfinished operations. Returning a domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion and never stops the group. Join. The API waits for every started operation, including its cleanup. Joining is not bounded by the timeout; uncooperative work falls to host escalation . Report. After joining, the caller observes the first matching row: Condition after joining Caller observes The caller’s own context was cancelled or reached its inherited deadline The caller unwinds; no Result is delivered. Operation faults become secondary diagnostics An operation faulted, in its body or cleanup error(cause: Crashed(...)) for the primary fault The group’s timeout expired before every operation committed error(cause: TimedOut) Otherwise ok(value: ...) with each operation’s exact return value in input order The first row is checked against the caller’s context, not the group’s derived context. Both can report an expired deadline; only the group’s own timer yields TimedOut, and only to a caller that is still active.
The primary fault is the first fault committed to the group’s outcome. When operations fault concurrently, which one is primary depends on scheduling. Successful value order never does. Commitment of an operation’s outcome and acceptance of a stop are atomic; an operation that committed before the stop keeps its outcome. See atomic transitions .
Faults are isolated at the group boundary# An operation fault becomes Crashed rather than unwinding the caller. This is intentional and matches how hosts isolate a failed request: the faulted operation has already unwound through its own cleanup, its siblings have been cancelled and joined, and the caller is the only remaining place that can respond. No faulted state is resumed. The caller’s own faults still unwind it; try propagates only Result errors.
No per-operation cancellation# No source or adapter API cancels a single operation of a joined group. An adapter that ends a foreign call early reports that through the operation’s declared return value, such as an IoError; it is not a fault. Joined APIs therefore have no separate cancelled outcome. Background work, which can be cancelled individually, reports cancellation through WorkStatus.Cancelled.
See parallel operations , cancellation , and scope cleanup .

title: Cancellation and budgets
content:
Cancellation and budgets# Guide index · Design index Cancellation asks work to stop. It does not mean the work has already stopped; code must reach a checkpoint, leave its scopes, and finish cleanup. Request work follows the request’s execution lifetime. Accepted background work follows its background service’s lifetime.
Requests# Hosts signal requests, joined groups signal their operations, and background services expose cancellation of admitted work:
Manuscript let id = try background.start(operation: work) background.cancel(id: id) The submission fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, StartError]; work must have the standard API contract callable type. Other application error types need explicit adaptation.
Successful Background.start admission yields an OperationId through Result[OperationId, StartError]. cancel(id: id) returns Unit, is idempotent for an admitted ID, and requests cancellation without joining. Dropping an ID has no effect. The service retains responsibility for work until it finishes or service shutdown joins it. IDs the service did not admit, including IDs from other services or from joined groups, and IDs whose status has been evicted are harmless no-ops; an ID never identifies unrelated work.
cancel, status, and close are receiver operations of the imported Background service; there are no ambient cancellation or join functions. Using an already-typed service does not require importing its otherwise unused type name. background.close() is the waiting boundary: it stops admission and performs the configured drain, cancellation, and joining sequence. A closed service stays closed through all aliases.
Late cancellation cannot overwrite an already committed completion. For background work, the first accepted stop reason determines WorkStatus, except that a programming fault during cleanup takes precedence and reports Crashed. Joined groups have no per-operation cancellation; their caller-visible outcomes are defined in joined groups .
Propagation and checkpoints# Cancellation is cooperative: stopped work unwinds at its next checkpoint. These are checkpoints:
runtime operation entry and completion; blocking I/O and other adapter calls; each loop back-edge, before the next iteration of for or while starts; an explicit check_cancelled() call. Loop checkpoints make CPU-bound loops respond promptly without source changes; they cost one poll of the context’s stop signal per iteration. check_cancelled() remains available for long straight-line work. It is an imported standard function, not a language intrinsic:
Manuscript import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms" Importing it supplies the operation declaration; the runtime supplies the current execution context when it is called. Cleanup runs under a shielded context, so checkpoints inside cleanup do not observe the initiating cancellation. No checkpoint occurs between with acquisition and cleanup registration; see completion and acquisition .
Cancelling a request or current operation cancels its nested groups. Each group joins its operations, each operation runs its registered with cleanup, and the caller unwinds.
Background service cancellation reaches the work admitted under that service. Cancellation of a submitting request does not cancel accepted work, because the background lifetime was selected at admission. Cancellation before admission must not start work. Admission and acknowledgement can race with request cancellation; callers must use application idempotency keys if a retried submission must not duplicate work.
Completed external writes remain completed. Cancellation does not provide rollback; a transaction’s explicit resource contract does.
Cleanup is shielded from the initiating cancellation and expired work deadline. It may exceed that deadline; it retains capability authority and remains subject to host escalation . See foreign cancellation and cleanup faults .
Waiting for a synchronized value# Synchronized.lock() waits cooperatively and observes cancellation. If cancellation wins before the guard is delivered, the runtime releases that acquisition. Use with locked = cell.lock() so a delivered guard is registered for cleanup before another checkpoint.
Cancellation of a lock holder unwinds its with scope and closes the guard. It never releases the lock while the holder is still running. Updates already made through locked.set() remain committed; releasing the guard does not roll them back. Guard cleanup is idempotent and shielded from the initiating cancellation. See synchronized values .
Timeouts# Timeouts are named library arguments, not syntax annotations. Duration values come from the standard time API; naming Duration requires its own import from @std/time.ms.
parallel(tasks: [first, second], timeout: 2.seconds) sets one budget for the group’s execution, starting on API entry after argument preparation. timeout is the only budget argument; there is no absolute deadline argument.
Argument validation is part of the standard API contract ; zero-timeout and empty-input behavior is in joined groups . On expiry, the group stops, joins, and reports as defined in joined groups . Results are never delivered while work remains outstanding.
A timeout bounds ordinary work, not cleanup or joining. Foreign code that does not cooperate can delay joining indefinitely; host escalation is the final fallback. An API must not report successful joining merely because its timer expired.
To share one budget across several steps, put the steps in one function and give that function the budget. Nested groups inherit the deadline:
Manuscript let sync = fn() -> Result[Unit, SyncError]: try download_all(sources: sources) try upload_all(targets: targets) return ok(value: unit) let [outcome] = try parallel(tasks: [sync], timeout: 2.seconds) This fragment requires an enclosing Result[U, ExecutionError] function; outcome is the unchanged Result[Unit, SyncError]. Any parallel inside download_all or upload_all inherits the same deadline.
Deadlines# Hosts establish deadlines for application, session, CLI, and request execution contexts. Every operation inherits its fixed parent’s deadline. A joined group can only shorten it with timeout; nothing in source can extend an inherited deadline. The effective deadline is the earliest of the inherited deadline and any group timeout.
Budgets use the runtime’s monotonic timer, not a Clock capability or calendar time. A test runner may virtualize that timer; a fake Clock value does not affect execution budgets.
When the caller’s own deadline expires, the caller unwinds after its groups join; it does not receive TimedOut. Only a group’s own timeout produces TimedOut.
Background work inherits the service’s fixed execution context, including that context’s deadline. It does not inherit the submitting request’s deadline. A service cannot revive cancelled work or extend its host’s deadline. Its context is selected at construction, not at each call to start.
Deadline configuration is a host operation. There are no source task handles to mutate, deadline annotations on functions, or absolute deadline arguments. See background services for drain budgets and adapter contexts .

title: Filesystem, OS, process, paths, and timers
content:
Filesystem, OS, process, paths, and timers# Coverage · Common contracts · Conformance These capabilities cover the native application tasks in Node.js 24’s fs/promises, os, path, process, and timers packages. They use Manuscript names, explicit capabilities, owned results, bounded reads, and lexical cleanup. Filesystem, path, process, system, and timer errors use their package-specific Error implementations; combine different error domains through explicit matching and an Error view. They are not drop-in JavaScript APIs. The tables below distinguish functional equivalents, native OS limitations, and facilities specific to Node’s VM and event loop. The baseline is Node.js 24.19.0: 181 module exports and returned-resource methods, including timers/promises. An adapted mapping supplies the native operation through Manuscript’s bounds, types, authority, or execution lifetimes; runtime_specific records Node facilities outside that execution model. The checked inventory in compiler/testdata/node-host-coverage.json records every public export in the baseline; it does not claim that recording an API establishes identical behavior.
Files and directories# Import filesystem() from @std/fs.ms for path operations. Acquire handles inside with. This fragment belongs in a function returning Result[Unit, FileSystemError]:
Manuscript with file = try filesystem().open(path: path, flags: "r+", mode: 384): let written = try file.write_at(offset: 0, data: "HELLO".to_bytes()) let bytes = try file.read_at(offset: 0, max_bytes: 5) let synced = try file.sync() These calls run in the native CLI conformance fixture tests/e2e/testdata/projects/library/main.ms. 384 is decimal for Unix permission bits 0600. Opening accepts r, r+, w, wx, w+, wx+, a, ax, a+, and ax+. x makes creation exclusive. Permission arguments accept 0..4095 (07777), including setuid, setgid, and sticky bits where the native OS supports them. open_flags accepts numeric native flags from fs.constants(); these numbers are host-specific. Paths use the native filesystem dialect, reject NUL, and use host OS permissions. Relative paths on CLI roots use the live working directory; embedded capabilities constructed with a directory retain that base. Imports confer no filesystem authority.
Node.js facility Manuscript operation access FileSystem.access; access-mode constants from fs.constants() appendFile, writeFile, readFile append_file, write_file, bounded read_file; strict codecs are separate chmod, lchmod, chown, lchown chmod, chmod_link, chown(follow_links: ...) copyFile, cp copy_file, copy_tree, and bounded copy with CopyOptions and an optional filter mkdir, mkdtemp, mkdtempDisposable create_directory, temporary_directory, scoped temporary open, opendir, readdir open/open_flags, open_directory, bounded sorted list stat, lstat, statfs stat(follow_links: ...), stat_filesystem link, symlink, readlink, realpath hard_link, create_link, read_link, canonicalize rename, rm, rmdir, unlink rename, remove(recursive: ...) truncate, utimes, lutimes truncate, set_times(follow_links: ...) glob glob, or typed glob_entries with GlobOptions and an optional exclusion callback watch Native watch_native, or polling watch; both are scoped and cancellable constants fs.constants() exposes native access, mode, open, and copy flags FileHandle supports sequential read/write, positional read_at/write_at, bounded read_file, write_file, append_file, read_vectors/write_vectors, read_lines, seek, stat, truncate, chmod, chown, set_times, sync, data_sync, and idempotent close. A chunk read returns up to 64 KiB; sequential EOF is none, positional EOF is empty Bytes. read_vectors accepts each size up to 64 KiB and a combined size up to 16 MiB. Vector offset -1 uses the current position. Seek origins are 0 (start), 1 (current), and 2 (end). read_file, write_file, and read_lines start at the current position. Line reads validate UTF-8, remove line terminators, and enforce both byte and line limits.
reader() and writer() adapt the same handle to the existing stream contracts, translating FileSystemError into IoError. Closing an adapter closes the handle and every alias. flush synchronizes the file; this is stronger than flushing a userspace buffer. Operations serialize shared file positions. Close prevents new calls, interrupts pollable I/O, and joins admitted calls. Parent cancellation unwinds; it is not EOF. Acquisition releases a resource when cancellation wins before delivery. Regular-file OS calls can delay cancellation until they return.
Directory cursors expose their native path() and return one DirectoryEntry or none and require close. Temporary resources recursively remove their directory at scope exit. FileInfo.mode contains POSIX type and permission bits; permissions contains only permission/special bits. The record supplies size, modified/accessed/changed times, optional created birth time, block size/allocation, device/inode/link count, owner IDs, and regular/symlink/directory/FIFO/socket/device classifications. exact contains arbitrary-precision numeric metadata and nanosecond timestamps. Native fields absent on a host are zero; unavailable birth time is none. Accessed/changed times fall back to modified time when unavailable, including the current Windows adapter.
copy accepts CopyOptions: recursive traversal, replacement, error-on-existing, dereferencing, timestamp preservation, verbatim symlinks, clone policy (none, try, or force), and shared entry/byte budgets. An optional filter runs sequentially for each source/destination pair and can prune directories. Without dereferencing, links are copied as links; relative targets are resolved against the source unless verbatim copying is requested. Dereferencing detects ancestor cycles. Copy rejects copying a tree into itself and traversing a destination symlink as a directory. Existing directories merge; collisions skip, fail, or replace according to the options. Native cloning uses Linux reflinks or macOS clonefile; try falls back to byte copying and force reports an OS error when unavailable. Windows has no clone adapter. The root and descendants share max_entries; all copied data shares max_bytes. Copying and writing can leave a partial prefix after an error.
watch_native retains OS events while the caller is busy. It bounds directory watches with max_entries and buffered events with max_events; overflow policy error returns LimitExceeded, while ignore drops excess events. Recursive watches admit newly created directories and do not follow directory symlinks. Events use rename for creation/removal/rename and change for writes/metadata changes. OS backends can coalesce events, report a containing directory, or overflow; event names and granularity are platform-dependent. Close stops the backend and joins its worker and admitted waiter. Cancellation during acquisition releases the backend.
Polling watch compares bounded snapshots after each requested interval. They report sorted FileEvent records with rename for appearance/disappearance and change for changed metadata. A vanished root reports disappearance. Recursive watches do not follow symlinks. Polling can coalesce or miss transient changes between snapshots; this is not a native OS event stream. Close and parent cancellation interrupt a waiting next without leaving a worker running.
Paths# Import pure path functions from @std/path.ms, or use posix()/win32() for a dialect independent of the host. No path operation reads cwd or touches files.
Node.js facility Manuscript operation basename(path, suffix) basename, basename_without dirname, extname, normalize, isAbsolute, join dirname, extension, normalize, is_absolute, join parse, format parse, format, PathParts resolve, relative resolve(base: absolute_path, parts: ...), relative with absolute inputs sep, delimiter, posix, win32 separator(), delimiter(), posix(), win32() toNamespacedPath to_namespaced_path for absolute Windows drive/UNC paths; relative paths pass through matchesGlob matches_glob Windows parsing preserves the spelling of separators. Normalization emits backslashes. UNC and drive roots remain distinct; relative comparisons are case-insensitive for Windows. Drive-relative components use an earlier explicit absolute base on the chosen drive; an unknown drive base returns InvalidInput, since resolving it would require ambient per-drive cwd. Later absolute components supersede earlier paths. Relative identical paths produce an empty string. PathParts.directory and base take precedence over root, name, and extension when formatting.
Globs support segment wildcards, character classes, **, brace alternatives, numeric brace ranges, and @, +, ?, *, ! extended groups. Hidden segments require an explicit leading dot. Patterns are limited to 4096 bytes; numeric ranges have at most 1025 entries and endpoints within -100000..100000. Use / between filesystem glob segments on every host. Brace alternatives can cross directory separators; alphabetic and padded numeric ranges are supported. Basic filesystem glob returns sorted relative paths without following directory symlinks; its max_entries bounds matched output. glob_entries accepts multiple patterns, pattern/callback exclusions that prune traversal, optional link following with cycle prevention, and separate visited-entry/result limits. Results are sorted, deduplicated PathEntry records. Absolute and parent-relative patterns can visit outside the supplied base, within the authority granted by the filesystem capability.
OS and current process# Import system() from @std/system.ms for OS queries, and control() and commands() from @std/process.ms. system() supplies OS queries. control() supplies current-process authority; commands() continues to run bounded, joined child commands. CLI arguments() and environment() retain startup snapshots; request a fresh environment through the control capability after mutation.
Node.js facility Manuscript operation os.arch, platform, availableParallelism System.info, System.metrics.available_parallelism type, endianness, EOL, devNull Pure os_type(), endianness(), end_of_line(), dev_null() homedir, tmpdir, hostname, userInfo home_directory, temporary_directory, hostname, user_info cpus, freemem, totalmem, uptime, loadavg cpus, metrics networkInterfaces network_interfaces, one record per address release, version, machine os_release, os_version, machine getPriority, setPriority, constants get_priority, set_priority, system.constants() process.pid, ppid, argv, argv0, execPath, platform, arch, identity getters ProcessControl.info, arguments() env, loadEnvFile environment, set_environment, bounded load_environment cwd, chdir working_directory, change_directory memoryUsage, cpuUsage, resourceUsage, uptime, hrtime memory_usage, cpu_usage, resource_usage, uptime, monotonic_time (nanoseconds), or host monotonic Clock getgroups, identity setters, setgroups, umask groups, set_identity, set_groups, initialize_groups, umask execve, title, constrainedMemory, availableMemory replace, title/set_title, constrained_memory, available_memory kill send_signal and scoped watch_signals with native signal numbers stdin, stdout, stderr, openStdin Explicit process stream fields exit, exitCode Return an exit code from main, after scoped cleanup and joins Architecture names follow Go (amd64, arm64), rather than Node (x64, arm64). memory_usage describes the Go heap; it is not a V8 heap report. metrics.available_parallelism queries native usable processors, including Linux affinity and Windows processor groups. CPU accounting is in microseconds for processes and milliseconds for CPU records. The environment loader accepts an optional export prefix, quotes including multiline values, and comments outside quotes. It validates all entries before writing; existing variables win. Changing cwd/environment/identity/umask is process-wide authority and affects subsequent host operations. umask returns the previous mask; permission and priority changes can fail under OS policy.
CPU, memory, uptime, OS release/version, and resident-process memory use native Linux, macOS, and Windows queries through pinned, vendored adapters. Windows load averages are three zeros. User shell comes from native macOS user records or local Linux passwd entries; it is empty on Windows or when no local Linux shell is available. Linux and macOS implement filesystem statistics, process CPU/resource accounting, priorities, identities, groups, umask, and descriptor timestamp updates. Linux no-follow chmod is unsupported, as in Node; macOS supports no-follow chmod and timestamps. Windows implements filesystem statistics, descriptor timestamps, process CPU/resource usage, console titles, and native priority-class mapping. Windows identity/group/umask changes, exec replacement, and no-follow metadata updates return Unsupported. Windows permission bits express its native read/write policy rather than POSIX ownership. system.constants() flattens native signal, errno, dlopen, and priority names; Linux catalogs are compared against Node in tests. Constants are host-specific; only supported native values are exported on other hosts.
watch_signals returns a scoped SignalStream with a bounded delivery buffer. OS/Go signal delivery can coalesce or drop repeated signals; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be observed. The CLI still treats SIGINT/SIGTERM as cancellation, and an observer does not override joined shutdown. Unix send_signal accepts signed PIDs for process groups and signal zero for existence checks. Windows supports existence checks and forced termination for its INT/KILL/TERM mapping; other signals return Unsupported.
Node-only process facilities (VM configuration/version information, JavaScript module loading, V8 reports/profiling hooks, source maps, promise rejection/exception hooks, JavaScript finalization, IPC integration, EventEmitter events, and ref/unref of an event loop) have no direct equivalent. nextTick scheduling is replaced by explicit ordinary calls, yield_now, joined tasks, or Background. Immediate abort and VM-thread CPU accounting remain outside Manuscript execution lifetimes. Process titles use Linux kernel names (at most 15 UTF-8 bytes), macOS program names, or Windows console titles. They do not rewrite argv. Linux constrained-memory queries inspect the current cgroup v1/v2 memory controller; zero means no known limit. Available memory is the lesser of host available memory and the remaining known cgroup budget. On other hosts, constrained memory is zero (unknown), and available memory uses the native host query. initialize_groups resolves a user’s supplementary groups and applies them under native privilege checks. Unix replace supplies an explicit argv and environment and replaces the executable; success never returns and bypasses scoped cleanup, just as native exec does. Use ordinary Commands.run when the caller must retain its execution lifetime. The inventory records these differences explicitly.
Timers and scheduling# Use the existing @std/time.ms module. Ordinary code sleeps sequentially; after and every start concurrent operations and return the same scoped Timer contract.
Manuscript import after from "@std/time.ms" import sleep from "@std/time.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import TimeError from "@std/time.ms" fn operation() -> Result[Unit, String]: return ok(value: unit) fn example() -> Result[Unit, TimeError]: sleep(duration: 10.milliseconds) with timer = try after(duration: 20.milliseconds, operation: operation): sleep(duration: 30.milliseconds) let restarted = try timer.restart() return ok(value: unit) The native CLI fixture exercises these operations and cleanup. after accepts a nonnegative duration; every(interval: ..., operation: ...) requires a positive interval. Zero-duration after schedules work immediately. Both accept ordinary fn() -> Result[Unit, String] operations, matching Background. Synchronize mutable captures explicitly.
Timer has three operations: close, restart, and status. Creation arms the deadline. Restart begins the original duration again, including after completion or an expected failure. Status uses the existing WorkStatus. Expected failures are reported and pause the timer until restart. Repeating callbacks run sequentially; a slow callback can consume one pending tick, and missed ticks never accumulate an unbounded queue. Close cancels and joins an active operation and is idempotent across aliases. The construction execution’s fixed work lifetime also cancels and joins scheduled work at shutdown. Acquire dependencies outside the timer’s with scope so they outlive its callbacks.
A sequential delay needs no resource: call sleep, then return the desired value. A paced loop calls sleep each iteration; use Background when that loop should run concurrently. yield_now belongs to @std/tasks.ms, where it performs a cancellable scheduler yield. There is no JavaScript event-loop phase ordering or ref/unref lifetime.
Node.js facility Manuscript operation setTimeout after(duration: ..., operation: ...) setInterval every(interval: ..., operation: ...) setImmediate Zero-duration after, or yield_now for a sequential yield clearTimeout, clearInterval, clearImmediate, disposal Scoped Timer.close Timer refresh Timer.restart Promise timeout and its value Ordinary sleep, then return the value Promise interval Sequential sleep loop, optionally managed by Background scheduler.wait, scheduler.yield sleep, yield_now

title: Runtime contracts
content:
Runtime concurrency contracts# Guide index · Design index This page is for runtime implementers. The runtime provides the mechanisms to start, stop, join, and synchronize work. Library objects decide whether to accept work, how to report failures, and how shutdown proceeds.
Source programs use standard concurrency APIs . The compiler checks their types, callback signatures, and cleanup contracts. Internal contexts and scheduler mechanisms add no source names or compiler bounds.
Atomic transitions# Each runtime operation has a stable OperationId, a fixed execution parent, a stop signal, an effective deadline, and one completion outcome. Cancellation acceptance and completion commitment have atomic linearization points. There is no reparenting or task-transfer transaction.
Background admission, closing admission, and reserving capacity must be coordinated atomically. If admission wins, the service tracks the accepted operation even if the submitting request stops before receiving its ID. If closure or cancellation wins before admission, the operation never starts. Capacity reservations are released exactly once: on rejection, or when the operation’s completion commits. Pending failure reports have their own bound and do not hold admission capacity.
Completion is not published until registered cleanup and nested joins have finished. A pending cancellation accepted before commitment prevents an ordinary successful outcome from being delivered. Already committed outcomes are stable.
User callbacks, failure reporters, resource cleanup, and joining run outside transition locks. Shutdown is idempotent; concurrent calls to close() observe one shutdown sequence and all wait for it to finish.
An operation must not join itself or an execution ancestor. Closing its own background service, including from nested parallel descendants or reporter callbacks joined by that service, faults before initiating shutdown. Check the fixed execution-parent chain, not just the current operation ID. Hosts close services from outside their admitted work. Cross-service cyclic shutdown is invalid library usage and must be avoided by host shutdown ordering.
The conformance suite uses controlled barriers and race stress for admission versus closure, cancellation versus completion, and concurrent shutdown. See semantic tests .
Completion and resource acquisition# Completion records an operation’s outcome after its body, nested concurrency groups, and registered cleanup finish. Cancellation and completion commitment race atomically; a late stop does not overwrite a committed outcome.
Parallel results are ordinary values, with references to existing objects where appropriate. If the group fails, unreturned references are released for garbage collection. The runtime does not recursively call close() on arbitrary result fields or closure captures: those references may alias resources still used elsewhere. Cleanup responsibility comes from explicit with registration or an acquisition API’s delivery contract, not a result-ownership escrow.
A native acquisition API must close a newly acquired resource if cancellation or a fault prevents it from being delivered. Successful acquisition and registration by with form one protected sequence: no cancellation checkpoint may occur between delivery to the binding and registration of its close() action.
Race outcome Required handling Cancellation wins before delivery Acquisition adapter closes the undelivered resource with acquires successfully Register cleanup before exposing cancellation Cancellation arrives after registration Unwind the scope and run registered cleanup Closure/result retains a resource reference after scope exit The reference remains valid memory; operations report that the resource is closed A source helper returning an open resource must handle resources it acquires but fails to return. Its resource factory/delivery contract is explicit. Merely returning a resource reference cannot cancel a with registration or keep the resource open.
Background operations have no resource-valued result delivery; each operation manages acquisitions through its own scopes. See adapter acquisition and resource release .
Adapter execution contexts# Generated calls carry a hidden execution context. An adapter observes the current operation’s fixed parent context, cancellation signal, deadline, and cleanup mode.
Parallel operations derive contexts from their caller. Background operations derive contexts from their service’s construction-time context. The runtime does not substitute the submitting request’s context merely because start was invoked from that request.
Fixed parent relationships can use Go context derivation directly; there is no movable cancellation ancestry or separate ownership graph. Operation IDs support diagnostics and traces. Go context documentation Cleanup receives a shielded context that ignores the initiating cancellation and expired ordinary-work deadline. It preserves authority; a host cleanup/escalation policy is separate from the request budget. Adapters must support safe resource closure and must not return from a cancelled operation while its foreign work is still outstanding.
See blocking adapters , deadlines , and runtime/library layering .
Host escalation# Joining and cleanup wait for work to actually end. The runtime cannot safely terminate an arbitrary goroutine, so work that ignores cancellation can delay a join forever. Escalation is the host’s last resort for that case. It ends the process; it never reports the stuck work as joined.
Each host runs one watchdog. It starts when the host begins shutdown or receives a stop request, such as SIGINT, SIGTERM, or server shutdown. Ordinary timeouts and request deadlines do not start it. Once started, it covers every waiting boundary: group joins, Background.close(), with cleanup, and resource close.
Setting Default Grace period after the stop request 30 seconds A second stop request during the grace period Escalates immediately Hosts may configure a different grace period. A zero grace period escalates on the first stop request whenever work is still outstanding.
On escalation the host:
writes one diagnostic per outstanding operation to host stderr, containing its OperationId, the source location of its current suspension, and its accepted stop reason; writes any retained primary and secondary fault diagnostics; terminates the process without running further cleanup. The CLI host exits 70 and labels the exit as incomplete cleanup. Conformance treats an escalated exit as a failure of the program, not as successful shutdown. See CLI exit and shutdown , HTTP shutdown , and cleanup faults .

title: Modules and capabilities
content:
Modules and capabilities guide# Design index Organize code into files, choose what each file exports, and pass external services into the functions that need them. A capability is an object that grants access to a service such as files or the network. Adapter pages explain the planned bridge to foreign code.
Reading order# 1. Module boundaries # Modules, exports, and imports Boundary contracts 2. Authority and effects # Explicit capability authority — Make file, network, and other external access visible in function inputs. Inferred effects and call relationships — Follow external behavior through a function and the functions it calls. 3. Foreign adapter contracts # Adapter manifests — Declare a foreign adapter API and the facts the compiler trusts. Foreign values and the trust boundary — Validate foreign values before they enter Manuscript. Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition — Arrange for foreign calls and resource acquisition to respond to stopping.

title: Module boundaries
content:
Module boundaries# Guide index · Design index Each .ms file is a module. Import individual declarations from other files and use export for declarations other modules may use. Boundary contracts describe the data and operations those modules expose.
Modules, exports, and imports Boundary contracts

title: Modules, exports, and imports
content:
Modules, exports, and imports# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Each .ms file is a module: a group of declarations with its own boundary. Use export to make a declaration available to other files and import to bring an individual exported declaration into the current file. Resolved file paths identify modules. There is no module declaration, wildcard import, or cyclic module dependency.
Names and declaration order# Import multiple symbols with import { Name, OtherName } from "./module.ms". The braces contain a nonempty, comma-separated list; a trailing comma and multiple lines are permitted. Each name selects an export and enters the same module namespace as a single-symbol import. Duplicate names and collisions are errors. Single-symbol import Name from "./module.ms" remains supported.
Types, interfaces, module functions, and imported symbols share one ordinary module namespace. Duplicate names, import/declaration collisions, and function overloading are rejected. Imports and declarations may appear in any order: collect names and signatures before checking bodies, so forward references and mutually recursive functions work. Type layout cycles follow the separate recursive data rule , not module-cycle rules.
The intrinsic core type names are only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, and Never. They cover primitive literals, ordinary arithmetic, and function/control-flow typing. The compiler bounds Equal and Hashable also have fixed identities. A module declaration, import, or type parameter cannot redefine these names. They are resolved names rather than lexical keywords. Ordinary local bindings may shadow outer names, but a shadowed value name cannot be used as a type.
All other standard declarations are explicit imports from the compiler-supplied @std directory, including Decimal, Bytes, collections, Optional, Result, Closeable, and runtime/host APIs. The standard imports and API typing page lists their modules. These names are ordinary exports: without an import, a module may declare its own Result, List, or parallel. Import/declaration collisions still fail. Compiler support follows the canonical standard declaration identity, never its spelling. Optional/Result case shorthand becomes visible when its alternative type is imported and follows ordinary lookup and ambiguity rules; qualify Result[T, E].error when a local spelling shadows it.
An unqualified case shorthand is considered only when ordinary lexical name lookup finds no binding or declaration of that name. The candidate cases come from visible alternative types declared in the module or imported by name. Exactly one candidate is required; an expected type cannot choose among multiple candidates. Type.Case explicitly selects the nominal alternative. Match-pattern case lookup uses the scrutinee type, as specified by pattern matching .
Import renaming, namespace imports, re-exports, and wildcard imports have no syntax. A dotted type path does not create a module namespace; callers import each needed exported type by its own name. Qualified alternative constructors remain supported. Module-level executable statements and bindings are rejected; local-value examples elsewhere are function-body fragments.
A visible contract# The file src/domain/customers.ms exports a nominal identifier type:
Manuscript export type CustomerId: value: String The file src/main.ms imports the individual symbol:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms" Exporting a type makes it part of the module boundary; an internal declaration stays within that boundary. A relative import resolves from the importing file’s directory. Paths include the .ms extension and identify a file, with no implicit directory entry or extension lookup.
Public signature closure# An exported function, data type, or contract cannot expose an internal nominal type through a parameter, result, field, case payload, generic bound, or operation signature. Check the transitive public type surface through nested applications and exposed data members. Exported types from other modules may appear in a public signature without automatically re-exporting their names. Generic parameters themselves are not private nominal declarations.
Manuscript type PrivateToken: value: String # Rejected: callers cannot name the internal result type. export fn issue() -> PrivateToken: return PrivateToken(value: "token") Exporting a record exposes every field and its constructor; exporting an alternative exposes every case and payload field; exporting an interface exposes every operation. Opaque exports and selective member visibility are unsupported. See public data surfaces .
An impl in a source type’s defining module becomes available wherever that type is used. An impl for an imported source type is local to the declaring module and does not become visible through imports. The interface may be local or imported. Concrete and generic implementations follow the same coherence and visibility rules , including overlap rejection within the visible set and preservation of the selected implementation in explicit contract views.
Standard-library imports# Manuscript import { List, Map } from "@std/collections.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" @std is always available without an [aliases] entry and cannot be overridden. Importing one export does not bring its signature’s other type names into scope. For example, importing parallel permits matching its inferred result, but writing Result or ExecutionError in an annotation requires their own imports. Importing a contract supplies its interface. Separately imported host accessors return service values when called.
Optional aliases# A project-root ms.toml can define file and directory aliases. With @domain mapped to ./src/domain and @customers mapped to ./src/domain/customers.ms, either import selects the same exported type:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "@domain/customers.ms" Manuscript import CustomerId from "@customers" Each example is an alternative import spelling for the same CustomerId. Aliases change how a path is written; module identity and visibility still follow the resolved file. Relative imports and aliases that resolve to the same file refer to the same module.
Missing files, unknown aliases, missing exports, and cyclic module dependencies are compile errors. The project configuration defines alias resolution and filesystem identity.
See source structure and boundary contracts .
Next: Boundary contracts

title: Boundary contracts
content:
Boundary contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A module boundary tells callers which data and operations they may use. Keep those exported contracts explicit so a caller can see inputs, outputs, expected errors, and required access to external services.
Example: ordinary operations# The following uses application-defined Item, Stock, and OrderError types:
Manuscript interface Inventory: fn check(items: List[Item]) -> Result[Stock, OrderError] fn check_stock( inventory: Inventory, items: List[Item], ) -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return inventory.check(items: items) let first = fn() -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return check_stock(inventory: inventory, items: items) let [stock] = try parallel(tasks: [first]) The closure/call fragment belongs to an enclosing function returning Result[U, ExecutionError]. To propagate OrderError in the same function, first translate it explicitly with match; parallel gives a complete example.
The operation accepts its capability explicitly and returns the unchanged domain Result. The ordinary Inventory view can be captured without a sharing annotation; its implementation coordinates any shared mutable state. The caller chooses concurrent execution through an ordinary API. The outer try handles execution failure; stock still contains the inventory domain outcome.
Submitting work to a Background service instead chooses that service’s fixed lifetime. Passing a reference does not transfer cleanup or keep a scoped resource open.
See parallel operations , fixed work lifetimes , and derived effects .
Previous: Modules, exports, and imports · Next: Host services and capability values

title: Authority and effects
content:
Authority and effects# Guide index · Design index A capability gives a function access to an external service. An effect describes what the function can do through that access, including through other functions it calls. Read authority first, then the rules for inferred effect summaries.
Host services and capability values — Import standard host services or pass service values to helpers. Inferred effects and call relationships — Follow external behavior through a function and the functions it calls.

title: Contributing
content:
Contributing to Manuscript# Start with the repository architecture , then use the development workflow to build, test, and publish documentation. The implementation inventory distinguishes supported features from design work.
Read the repository’s AGENTS.md before changing language semantics or tooling. It routes to current design rules and remembered failure modes.

title: Host services and capability values
content:
Host services and capability values# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A capability is an object that lets a function use an external service, such as storage, networking, a clock, or a model client. A helper can receive that object as an ordinary parameter, making its dependency visible and allowing tests to supply a source implementation.
Applications can also import host accessors such as filesystem(), network(), or clock() from their standard modules. They return the services associated with the current execution; CLI hosts defines the complete accessor set and lifetime rules. Accessors do not require dependency declarations on the calling function. Importing a contract type alone does not obtain a service.
Manuscript does not enforce a per-function authority set or manifest permissions. Native host services provide their normal OS access. Explicit parameters are a composition and testing technique, rather than the only route to a service. Tooling cannot claim to enumerate all reachable authority from parameter names alone; callbacks and stored values can retain services as well.
Sharing an implementation# A network or storage implementation can receive concurrent calls. Its mutable internal state must be synchronized. References do not extend a resource’s open lifetime; methods coordinate active calls with close.
See resource sharing and the foreign-code trust boundary .
Previous: Boundary contracts · Next: Inferred effects and call relationships

title: Inferred effects and call relationships
content:
Inferred effects and call relationships# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An effect describes external behavior reachable from a function. If a function calls another function that writes to storage, that write is also part of the caller’s effect summary.
Transitive analysis# The compiler follows calls and combines their known effects. The vocabulary is read, write, external-call, and unknown.
Call target How it contributes to the summary Known source target Include its effects, including the effects of its callees. Several known targets Include the union of their effects. Unresolved function value or contract call Include unknown; do not treat it as having no effects. Foreign adapter Use its declared summary, which foreign code is trusted to honor. These summaries describe reachable behavior. Manuscript has no source syntax that promises static purity or restricts a function to an effect set.
Effects and cancellation# Cancellation can stop unfinished work and run cleanup. It cannot undo an external write that already completed. Review both a boundary’s returned errors and its external effects when deciding how to retry or recover.
See diagram views and architecture changes .
Previous: Explicit capability authority · Next: Adapter manifests

title: Foreign adapter contracts
content:
Foreign adapter contracts# Guide index · Design index Adapters connect Manuscript code to foreign implementations such as Go. These design contracts explain how an adapter declares its API, validates values, and cooperates with cancellation and cleanup. Check implementation coverage before relying on external adapters.
Adapter manifests — Declare a foreign adapter API and the facts the compiler trusts. Foreign values and the trust boundary — Validate foreign values before they enter Manuscript. Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition — Arrange for foreign calls and resource acquisition to respond to stopping.

title: Adapter manifests
content:
Adapter manifests# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Adapters are trusted Go implementations of operation contracts. Every exposed value must be safe for concurrent access. The standard API contract defines source semantics; a manifest binds implementations to those semantics.
Interface modules and package direction# A local adapter ships a .ms interface module containing exported data and contracts, with no function bodies, tests, or implementation blocks. It may import standard modules through @std/...ms and other registered interface modules. Signatures use intrinsic types, explicitly imported standard types, or public declarations in that interface graph, never application-defined types. Source imports interface declarations through ordinary .ms paths.
Each interface module generates a separate Go schema package. The native adapter imports schemas and runtime; the application imports schemas, adapters, and runtime. Schemas never import adapters or application packages. Standard schemas belong to the pinned standard-library/runtime distribution. This prevents Go import cycles. An application contract over application Money types can have source implementations or explicitly wrap an adapter interface using data conversion, but cannot directly bind a separately compiled native adapter to application types.
Native receivers remain opaque. The host creates them and exposes contract views. Source fakes implement the interface contract for their own concrete type under ordinary coherence. The standard CLI host supplies its enumerated roots through imported accessors; custom host construction still needs a concrete contract.
Manifest version 1# The manifest is UTF-8 TOML with closed fields; unknown keys, duplicate bindings, unsupported versions, missing fields, and signature mismatches are compile errors.
toml format = 1 interface = "./files.ms" go_package = "example.org/nativefiles" go_version = "v1.0.0" go_checksum = "h1:example-content-checksum" [[bindings]] contract = "Files" operation = "open" symbol = "Open" effects = ["read", "external-call"] cancellation = "cooperative" acquisition = "dispose-undelivered" disposer = "DisposeFile" This is a schema example; its package and checksum are placeholders. Interface paths resolve relative to the manifest, and the Go fields pin the native package.
Binding field Rule contract, operation, symbol Select an exported interface/standard contract operation and an exported Go symbol; bind each operation exactly once effects Explicit subset of read, write, external-call, and unknown; use [] for an empty summary cancellation cooperative, completion-only, or nonblocking acquisition none or dispose-undelivered disposer Required exported symbol for dispose-undelivered; forbidden for none Resource bindings include a matching close operation. All native receivers, results, and retained callback environments must be immutable or synchronize mutable state and lifecycle. This is a mandatory adapter obligation; there is no opt-out via a plain view. Wrapping an unsafe receiver in Synchronized does not make escaped aliases safe.
Generated bindings# Interface declarations determine parameter labels/order and result types; manifests do not duplicate them. Each Go operation receives the hidden execution context, opaque receiver, and generated parameters in declaration order, then returns the generated exact result type.
A disposer receives a shielded context and the acquired generated resource value. It completes release before returning. The fixed constructor New accepts runtime HostInputs and returns an opaque receiver token. Standard host packages follow the same convention.
The concrete Go declarations for HostInputs, receiver tokens, results, and disposers still need a pinned runtime ABI. Symbol/type mismatches must fail validation before linking; referring to an ABI alone does not define those declarations.
Wrappers enforce the foreign value invariants . Disposal of an undelivered acquisition finishes before unwind, and no wrapper returns with outstanding foreign work. Native code requires separate cancellation, sharing, conversion, and release tests.
Acceptance requires a minimal interface/native-adapter/application fixture whose Go builds without cycles, rejection of interface imports from the application, source fake implementations, and invalid-value/acquisition race fixtures.

title: Foreign values and the trust boundary
content:
Foreign values and the trust boundary# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An adapter must validate foreign values before exposing them as Manuscript values. For example, a Go string may contain invalid UTF-8, while a Manuscript String may not. Conversion must preserve every guarantee of the source type.
Adapters validate UTF-8, alternative tags and payloads, required non-nil values, and numeric ranges. They preserve value and reference behavior and copy immutable byte buffers unless exclusive ownership can be established. Mutable collection storage stays behind checked collection operations; unrestricted Go interfaces and runtime task internals are not exposed to Manuscript source. Raw Go dependencies may use ambient authority, so source capability checking is not a sandbox for adapter code.
Preserving invariants# A converted string must be valid UTF-8. An alternative must carry a valid tag. A buffer must not become mutable through a hidden Go alias after being exposed as immutable source data. Exclusive native buffer transfer is an optimization only when the adapter proves no mutable Go aliases remain; source code has no move or ownership checker.
An invalid foreign value is a programming fault with the operation, expected type, and value path in its diagnostic. It is not an expected input error: untrusted data should remain Bytes until explicitly decoded. The manifest binding defines wrapper validation and release obligations.
See Go representations and text and byte values .
Previous: Adapter manifests · Next: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition

title: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition
content:
Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A blocking adapter must pass cancellation to its underlying operation and wait until outstanding work actually ends. Returning early while a foreign call keeps running would break Manuscript’s join and cleanup guarantees.
Each blocking adapter defines how cancellation reaches the underlying operation and when cleanup completes. An uncancellable foreign call remains outstanding until it finishes; wrapping it in a goroutine and returning early violates joining guarantees. Host escalation is the final fallback. Adapters report acquired resources even when cancellation races with acquisition, so the runtime can close newly acquired undelivered resources.
An acquisition race# Suppose a connection is acquired just as cancellation is accepted. The acquisition adapter must close it if delivery loses the race. Once delivered into with, cleanup registration has no intervening cancellation checkpoint. This contract applies to newly acquired resources, not arbitrary result references that may alias existing objects.
See stable adapter contexts and result commitment .
Previous: Foreign values and the trust boundary

title: Compiler design
content:
Compiler design guide# Design index This chapter is for compiler contributors and readers who need to understand builds. Follow a program from parsing and checking to generated Go, then read how builds are pinned and tested. For ordinary application code, you can start with project configuration .
Reading order# 1. Parsing and checking # Compilation pipeline — Follow a program from project loading to the native executable. Type checking and source contracts Scope and capture checking Typed intermediate representation 2. Go lowering # Function and concurrency API lowering Source guarantees and Go representations Evaluation order and call preparation Cleanup and fault lowering 3. Builds and dependencies # Project configuration and module paths — Set the source directory, entry file, and import paths in ms.toml. Pinned dependencies and deterministic output — Record versions and inputs so builds use the intended distribution. Caching and Go package boundaries — Understand what can be cached and when Go must rebuild a package. 4. Conformance and scope # Core-language fixtures — Check complete modules and rejected variants.
Runtime binding fixtures — Check standard imports, sharing, and host bindings.
Semantic conformance tests — Test required behavior, including cancellation races and cleanup.
Complete-program conformance — Check that guarantees work together in complete applications.
Scope and implementation order — Find remaining decisions and the order in which work depends on them.

title: Parsing and checking
content:
Parsing and checking# Guide index · Design index Before generating Go, the compiler reads the source and checks names, types, scopes, and captured values. It records the checked facts in a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. These pages explain each stage.
Compilation pipeline — Follow a program from project loading to the native executable. Type checking and source contracts Scope and capture checking Typed intermediate representation

title: Compilation pipeline
content:
Compilation pipeline# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler turns Manuscript source into Go, then uses Go to build a native executable. Before generating code, it checks Manuscript’s own rules; Go accepting the generated program is not enough to prove the source is valid.
Following a program through compilation# Load the project. Read ms.toml, locate the entry .ms file, and follow imports. Resolve relative paths and aliases to canonical file identities so different spellings of one path identify the same module. Parse the source. Read declarations, expressions, and indented blocks. Each file is already a module; it needs no module declaration. Resolve imports and names. Find exported declarations and reject module dependency cycles. Check the program.
