Validate types, scopes, captured values, and source contracts. Record checked facts. Produce a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. It records evaluation order, closure captures, cleanup scopes, effects, and source locations. Generate Go and build. Translate those facts into Go and invoke the pinned Go toolchain with the versioned runtime and adapters. Package boundaries in the design# The compiler is written in Go. The backend design emits one application Go package and separate packages for adapter interface schemas. Schema packages cannot depend on the application package; see adapter bindings for the dependency direction.
This page defines required behavior. It does not prescribe a parser library, syntax-tree schema, or internal package layout. External adapters remain design work; implementation coverage identifies the working compiler’s limits.
Continue with project configuration , type checking , scope and capture checking , and typed IR .
Next: Type checking and source contracts

title: Type checking and source contracts
content:
Type checking and source contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The type checker decides whether source operations satisfy Manuscript’s rules before the compiler generates Go. The fact that a value can be represented in Go does not make every use of it legal in Manuscript.
Required checks# Accept source according to the normative grammar ; then resolve names and check the compatibility rules . Each rejected program must identify the violated source rule. Backend assignability and Go compiler acceptance are not substitutes for those checks.
Source rule Checker responsibility Explicit function signatures Check parameter and result types against calls and returns Names and scopes Collect module signatures, reject duplicate names, resolve locals in declaration order, and check assignments against fixed mutable binding types Operators Use the closed precedence and operand table; enforce Bool conditions and short-circuit evaluation without implicit numeric conversion Function values Preserve parameter labels/order and exact types; require explicit specialization of generic function values and explicit anonymous signatures Return completeness Allow Unit fallthrough/bare returns; reject reachable non-Unit fallthrough; track Never and function-local loop/return boundaries Argument labels Resolve an omitted label for a single-parameter function; require labels for multi-parameter functions and constructors; reject unknown labels, duplicate arguments, and missing required arguments, including function-value calls List literals Require the canonical standard List import; check homogeneous element types and use annotations or the expected parameter type for empty lists Parallel API packs Check zero-argument functions in literal tasks: [...] packs and preserve each position’s exact return type; see parallel operations Destructuring bindings Check positional arity, record fields, renaming, nesting, and duplicate bindings; infer each local’s type independently; see destructuring bindings Nominal records and tagged alternatives Preserve type identity and check declared fields and cases Expected types Propagate annotations/substituted constructor context through literals, fields, and parentheses; reject incomplete types and avoid result-context inference for generic calls Exhaustive match Check the scrutinee alternative, positional payload arity/bindings, exact qualified cases, missing alternatives, duplicate arms, and final nonredundant wildcard Generic bounds Check arity, invariant arguments, argument-only inference, every nested application’s bounds, and generic bodies under their declared assumptions Recursive types and specialization Reject inline storage cycles and expanding generic type/function specialization, including mutual calls and specialized function values; permit regular recursion guarded by collection storage Equality and hashing Derive only the specified properties; reject Float/collection keys and data containing ineligible components Explicit implementations Match substituted operation names/labels/order/types exactly, check generic bodies and receiver-determined parameters, reject overlap ignoring bounds, enforce module-local extension visibility, and require explicit contract views Standard bindings Resolve the minimal intrinsic prelude and explicit standard imports by canonical identity; check ordinary function signatures and exact contract views. Passing values requires no sharing bound; queue synchronization is the caller’s responsibility Public signatures Reject internal nominal types leaking through exported fields, signatures, bounds, or operation surfaces Iteration Admit List/Set/Map only, bind fixed iteration names for elements/MapEntry references, evaluate iterable once, and reject loop control outside the current function’s loops Result propagation Recognize the canonical standard Result identity; require the same exact error type at a try expression in the current function; do not infer missing operand type arguments backward String literals Validate escape/scalar syntax, support universal value conversion, and preserve left-to-right evaluation These requirements derive from the core language guide , with accepted and rejected modules in core conformance . The rules specify observable inference and compatibility; checker data structures and internal pass organization remain implementation choices. A module-level test body is a zero-parameter Unit function for static checking: ordinary local scopes, bare-return/fallthrough rules, and Result propagation restrictions apply. Test discovery and runner execution remain separate tooling contracts.
Type information feeds typed IR , generated representations , and structural tools .
Previous: Compilation pipeline · Next: Scope and capture checking

title: Implementation coverage
content:
Implementation coverage# This page tells you what the current compiler and runtime support and what remains design work. The compiler is written in Go and builds native executables through a Go backend. Release binaries embed reduced Go 1.25.1 build tools and references; source builds prepare them automatically with make build. WebSocket and public-suffix dependencies are pinned and vendored, so native builds need no package downloads.
Start with your first program for a walkthrough. Use the design book for language rules and the conformance fixtures for accepted and rejected examples.
Language and checking# UTF-8 source with original byte positions across BOM/CRLF normalization, ASCII identifiers, exact four-space suites, comments, delimiter continuation, numeric literals, escapes, universal toString(), and interpolation of every value. Exact intrinsic types, nominal mutable records and alternatives, typed field assignment and shallow data cloning, type records/alternatives, generic types/functions, interface operation contracts, explicit implementations with inherited generic parameters and bounds, contract views, signature and argument-label checking, module-local extensions for imported source types and overlap rejection, and universal sharing and structural equality/hashing eligibility. Calls with optional labels for single-parameter functions and mandatory labels for multi-parameter functions and constructors, per-call default argument expressions on source functions and methods, function values, suite closures, snapshot captures, and rejection of captured assignment. All function values may be shared through parameters, results, fields, collections, and generic forwarding. Local inference, contextual constructors, invariant generic applications, bounds, guarded recursive layouts, and finite generic call specialization. Generic inference uses independently typed arguments; an expected result does not supply missing type arguments. Bindings, name assignment, list/record destructuring, branching, loops, exhaustive alternative matching, returns, loop exits, lexical with, and exact-error try propagation. Return completeness includes Never and conservative loop rules. Explicit standard imports, exported-symbol visibility, relative imports and aliases, canonical module identity, root containment after symlink resolution, cycle rejection, and public type visibility. Conservative transitive effects (read, write, external-call, unknown), including implicit cleanup and nested closure bodies. Indirect calls remain unknown. These summaries do not claim to enumerate every capability retained by a value. syntax, lexer, parser, checker, and project are independent packages. Manifest and confined path resolution live in project; CLI orchestration lives in internal/cli. The architecture guide maps the package dependencies. Checked programs retain syntax, resolved types/operations, binding identities, captures, selected cleanup methods, and effects. Diagnostics have stable code families, phases, file/line/column, and original byte offsets. Failed checking produces no generated program.
Standard library and runtime# Facility Implemented behavior Numbers Checked signed 64-bit integers, IEEE binary64 floats, and 34-digit Decimal arithmetic with ties-to-even rounding and exact literal validation Data values List, insertion-ordered Map and Set, MapEntry, Bytes, UTF-8 conversion, Optional, and Result Time Duration construction/arithmetic, monotonic Clock/Instant domains, sleep, scoped after/every timers, and operation deadlines Cleanup Checker-selected contract dispatch, registration of delivered with values, reverse lexical release on every exit, shielded cleanup, primary/secondary fault preservation, and removal of completed cleanup actions Joined work Heterogeneous literal parallel packs, cancellation checkpoints, deadlines, sibling cancellation on faults, and joining before completion Background Bounded admission/history, fixed construction parent, cancellation, serialized reporting, bounded diagnostic fallback, optional drain, concurrent idempotent close, and nested-service joining Queues and synchronization Local FIFO queues with optional capacity, immediate full/empty results and explicit synchronization for shared use; Synchronized values with cancellable lock acquisition, scoped guards, atomic get/set, stale-alias checks, and reentry detection Pools and leases Fixed resource pools, cancellable acquisition, guarded contract views, stale-alias rejection, single capacity return, operation cancellation/joining, and reverse owned-resource release Builders Synchronized List/Map/Set/Bytes/String builders, sealed builder results, idempotent freeze, and rejection of mutation after sealing CLI capabilities Imported host arguments/environment, streams, read-only files, monotonic clock, network, commands, checked exit codes, signal cancellation, joined shutdown, and host-root cleanup HTTP Explicit Network authority; bounded buffered requests/responses, ordinary handlers, admission/body/output limits, timeout/disconnect cancellation, fault isolation, and grace/cancel/join shutdown Subprocesses Explicit Commands authority, joined execution, timeout, aggregate output bounds, captured bytes, exit status, and domain errors; process-group cancellation on platforms exposing that facility General-purpose packages Strict codecs/binary numbers, scalar text and bounded Unicode normalization, Float math/BigInt, exact JSON, CSV/URL/HTML, sequential collection algorithms, hashes/HMAC/PBKDF2/AES-GCM/Ed25519, compression and ZIP/TAR, bounded stream helpers, structured logging Additional CLI roots FileSystem read/write/copy/stat/list/directories/links, WallClock/Timestamp, System info/environment and cryptographic Entropy Network clients and sockets Buffered/streaming HTTP/1.1/HTTP/2 clients and servers, pooled transports/cookies/redirects, WebSocket sessions, TCP/Unix/TLS sockets and mutual TLS, bounded DNS record lookup, scoped resolver/policy and cancellation/close joining Native acquisition Undelivered files, lock guards, pool leases, and HTTP servers are disposed if cancellation wins before delivery The expanded package APIs and boundary behavior live in general-purpose packages ; their types and signatures live in pinned Manuscript source declarations, with native ABI validation. The original host/service APIs and boundary behavior live in the canonical queue , synchronization/pool , builder , HTTP , and subprocess pages. Source cannot manufacture native host authority.
After checking source, the backend translates functions and control flow into Go. Values use runtime representations rather than distinct concrete Go layouts for every source type. Generics use runtime type keys and coherent implementation dispatch; concrete Go layouts and machine-code monomorphization are not implemented. Map and Set use ordered linear storage. Pollable stream I/O supports cancellation/deadlines and concurrent close. Uncooperative native code or nonpollable I/O can still delay joining; forced termination does not constitute successful cleanup.
Commands, builds, and source tools# ms check, build, emit, run, test, inspect, and diagram accept a module or project ms.toml. Project configuration supports [project] and [aliases] with strict keys. Standalone modules use their containing directory as the import root. Applications export nongeneric fn main() -> Int.
Pins and artifact identity# ms lock ms.toml explicitly records compiler/frontend/runtime content and the selected Go toolchain/target in ms.lock. Native project builds reject missing or mismatched pins. Check/emit/source inspection do not need pins. Native artifacts have verified cache entries and <executable>.ms-build.json with source/configuration and executable hashes. Unchanged outputs are not rewritten. compiler.VerifyBuild checks binary/source identity. The compiler generates deterministic source and records artifact identity. Native binaries are not promised to be byte-identical across environments. Parsing and checking still run before an artifact cache hit.
Generated Go and debug builds# ms embeds a compressed build payload and atomically materializes it in the user cache under its content hash. It contains the Go build driver, compiler, linker, assembler, assembly headers, the runtime’s standard-library dependency closure for six targets, time-zone data, and licenses. Go tests, documentation, and unrelated tools are excluded. Pins and native builds share discovery with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOENV=off, and CGO_ENABLED=0, requiring no host Go or C compiler. MANUSCRIPT_GO explicitly overrides tool selection; direct developer binaries without an embedded payload retain a PATH fallback. make dist packages the single binary, examples, and licenses for Linux, macOS, and Windows on AMD64 and ARM64.
ms emit produces one Go file containing its runtime and imports of the pinned vendored dependencies. Native release builds use -trimpath using the embedded vendor source bundle without downloading dependencies. Generated source has Go line directives, and programming faults accumulate source function positions. --debug disables optimization/inlining while retaining native symbols and absolute source mappings. Debug build cache identities include the source root.
Formatting and source inspection# ms fmt file.ms validates syntax before atomically replacing a file and preserves comments and literal spellings. --check reports formatting drift without writing. ms check --json emits format-1 diagnostics. ms inspect emits checked entities, generated declaration and local names, source hashes, original-byte statement header spans, call sites, and effects. ms diagram emits their static Mermaid call graph, including implicit cleanup; neither command represents a runtime trace.
Editor, lint, debugger, and profiles# ms lint reports five advisory hygiene and semantic rules across the reachable local module graph, including project imports. Import usage follows resolved identities, so a shadowing local or field label does not conceal an unused import. ms lsp supplies typed completion, call snippets, signature help, navigation, project references, checked versioned rename, diagnostics and code actions. Editor-only recovery retains independently valid declarations; strict builds still reject malformed syntax. The VS Code extension includes source debugging through Delve and read-only views of records, collections, variants, locals, and execution/service state.
ms profile retains CPU/heap profiles, execution traces, executable/build metadata, and source inspection. Runtime work carries source/work/operation labels and cleanup/join trace regions without changing lifetime inheritance. See the tooling guide for commands and current limits.
Test execution# ms test executes test blocks in the reachable import graph in dependency/source order with file::name labels. Each test has a fresh execution lifetime; services join before the next test. Faults fail that test and remaining tests continue. Builds check test bodies but omit their execution code. Duplicate display names are allowed. Tests can import host service accessors; each test has fresh roots and an empty argument list. Declaration-only fixtures establish parse/check/build acceptance, not behavior of uncalled functions.
Remaining design work# The book’s outstanding decisions remain authoritative. The following parts are not implemented:
External native adapter manifests/ABI, [adapters] loading, custom host distributions, and adapter/dependency pins. HTTP/3 is excluded by explicit user instruction. Interactive subprocess streams and uniform cross-platform descendant supervision remain separate work. Grapheme segmentation, locale-sensitive text operations and legacy text codecs, timezone calendars, archive extraction and specialized formats. NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD normalization is implemented with bounded output. See the coverage map and built-in method guide for runnable equivalents and remaining gaps. Full incremental frontend/package compilation, concrete native generic layouts, precise retained-authority classification, and native adapter effect declarations. Transactional structural edits, rich diagnostic spans/related locations, architecture diffs, runtime trace transport, generalized structural value transformations. Test discovery globs, identity beyond display labels, authority injection, and expected-fault checks, which need the runner contract finalized. The language core, supplied standard APIs, compiler commands, and native conformance tests are usable now. The coverage above is not a claim that every future facility in the design book is complete.
Verification# sh make coverage make race make check make fuzz make book-check make dist-check Native end-to-end tests compile accepted syntax and execute test bodies; rejected cases cover typing, visibility, bounds, captures, and service boundaries. Observable tests cover evaluation order, numeric faults, cleanup exits, SIGTERM child-before-parent shutdown, HTTP, subprocesses, source tooling, and unusual module filenames. Runtime tests use barriers/channels for concurrent state transitions; cache tests exercise pin mismatches, corruption, stale sources, and unchanged outputs. CI runs formatting, vet, the complete suite, race tests, and the hello project.
Filesystem, OS, process, path, and timer expansion: Node.js 24 mapping and host limitations . Includes positional/vector file I/O and streams, typed metadata, filtered copy/glob, native/polling watches, scoped temporary directories, OS/process metrics and controls, explicit path dialects, and sleep and scoped after/every scheduling. Native helpers and dependencies are bundled for offline standalone builds.

title: Scope and capture checking
content:
Scope and closure checking# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler checks which names a closure captures and which cleanup actions each scope must run. It does not prove that every resource reference stays within its open lifetime. Runtime closed-state checks still matter.
Source operation Required check with initializer Require the concrete, contract-view, or generic-bound proof defined by Closeable ; register the resolved operation Scope exit Identify exited cleanup scopes for return, loop exits, errors, faults, and cancellation Closure creation Identify captured bindings and snapshot them once Assignment to captured outer local Reject implicit shared mutable cells Reassignment and branch scope Require initializers, enforce let/var, and keep branch-local names inside their scope Capturing a scoped resource is not a compile error merely because it may outlive its scope. Methods report closed state at runtime. Storing or returning a reference does not transfer a cleanup action. There are no moved-binding states, borrow lifetimes, partial-move restrictions, or source task-ownership checks.
See with scopes , closures , and typed IR .
All values may be captured and shared. parallel retains its direct-call literal-pack typing; Background.start, and HTTP serve methods are ordinary callable values. Constructors remain type constructors, not function values.

title: Typed intermediate representation
content:
Typed intermediate representation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index After checking source, the compiler stores the program in a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. It keeps the facts code generation and tooling need, rather than trying to rediscover them later.
Fact Why it remains explicit Types, comparison bounds, and resolved operations Preserve nominal contract identity and substituted generic implementation selection; select representations and validate API contracts Argument names and parameters Resolve omitted single-parameter labels and preserve checked parameter mapping and written evaluation order Lists and fixed positional packs Retain homogeneous element types or each position’s exact type Destructuring Retain shapes, field bindings, and extraction order Closure environments Record snapshot captures and receiver references with registration and cleanup scopes Resolve close() and unwind exited scopes Effects and concurrency API boundaries Derive host/service relationships and diagrams Source locations Connect generated behavior back to source There are no ownership-transfer instructions or affine states. Runtime operation IDs and fixed execution parents belong to the concurrency runtime; source IR records the API calls and contexts used to establish them.
See pipeline , evaluation lowering , and metadata .

title: Go lowering
content:
Go lowering# Guide index · Design index Lowering translates checked Manuscript into Go. The generated code must preserve evaluation order, closure captures, concurrency, and block-level cleanup. These pages describe how the compiler carries those guarantees across the translation.
Function and concurrency API lowering Source guarantees and Go representations Evaluation order and call preparation Cleanup and fault lowering

title: Function and concurrency API lowering
content:
Function and concurrency API lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler turns functions, closures, and contract methods into Go calls. Each generated call carries an internal execution context for cancellation, deadlines, and host service accessors. A closure also keeps its captured snapshots in an environment object. Source code still has one function kind; every function can wait for work.
Explicitly imported parallel, and Background methods lower as typed library calls. Scheduling, cancellation, joining, admission, and shutdown policy live in the standard library/runtime rather than an expanded source intrinsic list. Native runtime primitives start goroutines, signal cancellation, join completion, and synchronize state. The compiler checks the resolved standard API declarations and ordinary callback signatures; a same-spelled application declaration acquires none of that special typing. There is no special background class or task transfer. Go concurrency specification The hidden context carries the current operation, fixed cancellation parent, effective deadline, cleanup mode, and host roots. Parallel operations derive it from the caller; a background service supplies its stored construction-time context. Creating a closure does not capture the caller’s execution context as a hidden source dependency; invocation supplies the execution context. Each loop back-edge polls the context’s stop signal and unwinds through the iteration’s cleanup if it has stopped; cleanup contexts are shielded, so the poll never fires during cleanup.
The frontend implements the standard library’s fixed heterogeneous callable/result mapping , preserving inferred packs through locals, generic helpers, and Result matches. This is type-system/interop support for the API. General source pack syntax is unsupported; the standard mapping is normative and cannot be altered by an adapter manifest.
Policy can be implemented over native primitives. No goroutine-ID lookup, custom coroutine lowering, stack implementation, or memory collector is required. See parallel and background layering .

title: Source guarantees and Go representations
content:
Source guarantees and Go representations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A Go value must preserve the behavior promised by its Manuscript type. For example, generated Int arithmetic must detect overflow, and generated collections must prevent mutation through an alias. The compiler and runtime enforce guarantees that unrestricted Go values do not provide on their own.
The frontend enforces semantics that Go representations do not provide:
Source guarantee Go lowering Checked Int int64 with checked operations and conversions Decimal Versioned finite decimal implementation honoring the coefficient/exponent grid, exact literals, and per-operator rounding in the numeric contract Valid UTF-8 String Validated construction and conversion; no raw string escape Mutable records and collections Shared record field storage and pointer-backed collection headers; explicit shallow clone Immutable bytes Encapsulated storage; copies or exclusive adapter transfer Ordered maps and sets Ordered wrappers Tagged alternatives Generated typed tags and payloads; exhaustive frontend checking Guarded recursive data Records/alternatives with collection indirection; reject invalid layouts before Go emission Value equality and hashing Generated operations for eligible types Explicit contract implementation Frontend selection of a unique applicable concrete/generic implementation, then Go interfaces and wrappers Closures and resource references GC-retained environments, snapshot captures, and synchronized native closed-state checks Lexical cleanup Explicit with registrations, shielded Closeable.close(), and scope unwind operations Parallel results Typed positional packs preserving each exact return value Use Go generics where suitable; generated typed pack wrappers handle heterogeneous parallel results without exposing unchecked casts to source.
Representation boundaries# For example, emitting a raw int64 does not supply checked arithmetic. A raw Go slice does not establish immutable source bytes. The frontend and runtime cooperate with generated wrappers and operations to preserve those contracts.
Explicit view constructors create ordinary contract wrappers. There is one contract-view identity and no sharing proof in the frontend or IR. Native services synchronize their internals. Local queues rely on caller-managed Synchronized guards for concurrent access.
Contract wrappers and bound methods retain the selected implementation scope. Generic specialization carries that scope with each type argument, including nested receiver arguments; forwarding a bounded parameter must preserve its implementation evidence. Cleanup dispatch obeys the same scope rules.
Generic implementation bodies use checked substitutions; Go method selection cannot resolve overlapping source implementations. Function wrappers retain source labels/order in frontend identity even though Go erases labels. Check recursive storage rules before emission; a generated-Go error is not a source type check.
Int division/remainder overflow handling, Float non-finite outcomes, Decimal underflow/overflow, and checked truncation conversions follow runtime numeric outcomes , including parameterized runtime operands. Unchecked Go casts or a decimal package’s defaults do not establish these semantics.
See foreign conversions , type checking , and scope and capture checking .

title: Evaluation order and call preparation
content:
Evaluation order and call preparation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Named arguments can be written in a different order from the parameters in a declaration. Generated Go must still evaluate them in the order the caller wrote. Resolve the names first, including an omitted label on a single-parameter function. Evaluate each argument into a temporary value, then arrange those values for the Go call. Preserve short-circuit behavior too.
A tasks: [...] literal constructs a typed pack of function values in source order. Constructing closures snapshots their local captures; it does not invoke their bodies. If preparation fails, the concurrency API has not started work. Native acquisitions during preparation retain their explicit delivery/cleanup contracts.
Ordinary list elements evaluate left to right; an existing list argument evaluates once. Destructuring evaluates the initializer once and extracts bindings in written pattern order, retaining each positional result type.
A with initializer evaluates once, then registers the initialized object’s resolved close method before exposing another cancellation checkpoint. Later alias assignment does not change that receiver.
See source call order , operation preparation , and with scopes .

title: Cleanup and fault lowering
content:
Cleanup and fault lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler registers Closeable.close() after successful with initialization and generates cleanup for each block exit. A Go defer that runs only when a function returns is not enough for resources whose lifetime ends at a nested block or loop iteration.
The backend implements scope-exit order and fault selection as follows:
Use private tagged Go panics for nonlocal language faults and cancellation. Give each function with active registrations a local scope stack and one deferred unwind handler. Normal block exits drain and pop explicitly; panic paths drain the remaining stack. Pop an action before invoking it, and recover each close separately so a secondary panic cannot skip later cleanup. Give cleanup a context without the initiating cancellation or expired work deadline, retaining authority and cleanup mode. Rethrow the selected fault or cancellation after draining, until its operation or host boundary handles it. Recoverable unexpected adapter panics become programming faults; concurrency boundaries report them as Crashed. Active parallel APIs join before the caller’s cleanup begins. Ordinary values and captures are never recursively disposed. Process-fatal out-of-memory or stack exhaustion has no cleanup guarantee.
Resources acquired but not delivered require cleanup from the acquisition adapter or factory. Returned references do not suppress an existing with registration. See exit order , fault selection , and acquisition races .

title: Builds and dependencies
content:
Builds and dependencies# Guide index · Design index These pages explain how the compiler locates source files, records the versions used by a build, and reuses cached work. Start with the project manifest if you are setting up an application.
Project configuration and module paths — Set the source directory, entry file, and import paths in ms.toml. Pinned dependencies and deterministic output — Record versions and inputs so builds use the intended distribution. Caching and Go package boundaries — Understand what can be cached and when Go must rebuild a package.

title: Project configuration and module paths
content:
Project configuration and module paths# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A project has an ms.toml file at its root. The compiler reads this file to locate source and the entry file and to resolve optional import aliases. Each .ms file is one module; no source-level module declaration is required or accepted.
A project manifest# toml [project] name = "store" source = "./src" entry = "./src/main.ms" [aliases] "@domain" = "./src/domain" "@customers" = "./src/domain/customers.ms" project.name names the project. project.source identifies its source directory, and project.entry identifies its entry .ms file. All filesystem paths in the manifest resolve relative to the directory containing ms.toml, including the entry path; the entry path is not relative to project.source.
Commands and module discovery# Command Behavior ms check <ms.toml> Check the program and its entry signature ms build <ms.toml> Check, generate Go, and build the executable A relative manifest argument resolves from the invocation directory. Its containing directory then becomes the project root for configuration paths. The entry follows the CLI main contract .
The compiler discovers application modules by following imports from entry. The manifest does not enumerate them. Only [project] and [aliases] are implemented; unknown tables, unknown project keys, duplicate tables, and duplicate keys are rejected. Values must be double-quoted strings. Comments begin with # outside a quoted string.
External [adapters] entries and adapter bindings remain design work. The current compiler rejects those tables.
The compiler supplies the minimal intrinsic prelude and the standard modules under @std. Third-party Manuscript packages are unsupported; native dependencies follow build pinning .
Resolving an import# Imports name an exported symbol and a path:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms" import Order from "@domain/orders.ms" For an import in src/main.ms, the first path resolves to src/domain/customers.ms. The second expands @domain using the manifest and resolves to src/domain/orders.ms.
A path beginning with ./ or ../ resolves relative to the importing file’s directory. A path beginning with @std/ resolves within the compiler-supplied standard-library directory. @std alone selects no module. The [aliases] key @std is rejected, so an application cannot override standard identities. Other paths beginning with @ resolve through the importing project’s aliases. Alias keys consist of @ followed by one identifier, such as @domain. A directory alias matches its complete first path segment and appends the remaining path. @domain does not match @domain_extra. A directory alias alone does not select a module. A file alias selects exactly its target .ms file and accepts no appended path segments. Alias targets are filesystem paths relative to ms.toml; aliases do not expand other aliases. Direct paths and paths appended to directory aliases must include .ms. Resolution does not infer extensions or search for directory entry files. A file alias can omit the extension in the import because its configured target supplies it. Bare logical module names and absolute filesystem paths are not import forms. Paths use / as the separator. [aliases] is optional. Ordinary relative imports work without it. Missing source directories or entry files, invalid alias definitions, unknown aliases, and imports that do not resolve to an existing .ms file are compile errors. Import checking also rejects missing or internal symbols, wildcard imports, and cyclic module dependencies.
Module identity and configuration scope# The compiler normalizes resolved paths, including . and .., and resolves symbolic links to establish one canonical file identity within a build. Importing the same file through a relative path, a file alias, or a directory alias does not create separate modules. Cycle detection and module caching use this identity, so alternate path spellings cannot bypass cycle checks. Stable build metadata records paths relative to the owning project root rather than checkout-specific absolute paths.
Application paths, source directories, user aliases, adapter manifests, and interface modules must resolve inside the project root after symlink resolution. Escapes are compile errors. @std/...ms is the sole exception: paths resolve inside the pinned standard-library directory, and normalization/symlinks cannot escape that directory or reach application files. Standard module identity is its distribution version/content identity plus canonical distribution-relative path, independent of its installation location. Standard modules cannot import application modules.
Interfaces may use intrinsic types and import standard declarations or other registered interfaces, never application modules. Native Go dependencies are pinned adapter inputs. External Manuscript dependency projects and package acquisition syntax are unsupported.
Changes to source roots, entry files, aliases, or the pinned standard-library distribution can change the resolved module graph. The compiler includes relevant manifest settings in build and analysis cache identity, alongside source and dependency identities.
See module exports and imports , the compilation pipeline , and incremental compilation .

title: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output
content:
Pinned dependencies and deterministic output# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A reproducible build records which inputs and tool versions produced it. Those inputs include source, relevant ms.toml settings, the compiler and runtime, the Go toolchain, adapters, and dependencies. The project manifest chooses the entry file, source directory, and import aliases.
Pin the Go toolchain, compiler-supplied standard-library modules and their content identity, runtime, native adapters, and their dependencies. @std resolves only to that pinned distribution; a build does not fetch or silently substitute a newer library. Include this identity in module, analysis, and generated-code caches. Debug builds also pin the supported Delve version.
Generate deterministic symbol names and declaration order; do not rewrite unchanged output. This promises stable generated source for the same inputs. Byte-identical binaries need a separate toolchain and environment contract.
Details still needed# ms lock ms.toml explicitly creates or updates project-root ms.lock, a JSON object with closed fields: format: 1, compiler: "0.1.0", implementation_sha256, and toolchain. The implementation digest covers sorted compiler/frontend and embedded runtime source contents, excluding tests and checkout paths. Toolchain records Go version, OS/architecture, CGO, experiments, and architecture tuning from the embedded build payload, or an explicit MANUSCRIPT_GO override. Pins and builds share toolchain selection. The payload is extracted into a cache identified by its content hash and supplies its own GOROOT. Native commands use GOENV=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, and CGO_ENABLED=0; they need no system Go or C compiler and cannot automatically download another Go version. Pinned builds require empty GOFLAGS and use explicit -trimpath; --debug additionally disables optimization and inlining.
Project build, run, and test reject missing or mismatched pins and instruct the caller to explicitly run lock. Check/format/inspect/emit do not require a native toolchain pin. Standalone module builds record the selected toolchain without claiming a project lock. There are no third-party native dependencies in the supplied runtime. External adapter dependency pins and Delve remain separate future distribution contracts.
Native artifacts are cached under project .ms-cache/ by generated source, original module/configuration hashes, implementation content, target/toolchain, and debug flags. Cache hits verify metadata and binary content hashes; corruption rebuilds. A matching output is not rewritten. <executable>.ms-build.json carries source/configuration hashes and executable identity. compiler.VerifyBuild rejects mismatched binaries or supplied source/configuration snapshots before source interpretation. This pins source generation and artifact identity; byte-identical binary reproducibility across environments is not promised.
Pinning Delve keeps the native transport contract aligned with debugger integration .
Build identity and source hashes must travel with debug and trace metadata . See incremental compilation for caching and package boundaries.
Previous: Project configuration and module paths · Next: Caching and Go package boundaries

title: Caching and Go package boundaries
content:
Caching and Go package boundaries# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Caching can save the compiler from repeating parsing and checking. It cannot always save Go from rebuilding an application package. This page separates those two boundaries and explains what must be included in a cache key.
Cache parsing, checking, and module summaries by source, relevant project configuration, and dependency identity. Use canonical resolved file identity for modules; imports through different path spellings or aliases share a module summary.
Runtime, adapter schemas, and native adapters compile as separate packages. Native adapters and the application import schemas; schemas never import either. Adapter interfaces cannot use application types. Changing application code rebuilds its package; multiple generated files do not create independent compilation units. Go build documentation See project configuration , the pipeline , and deterministic generation .
Previous: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output · Next: Semantic conformance tests

title: Conformance and scope
content:
Conformance and scope# Guide index · Design index Conformance tests check whether the implementation follows the language rules. Some fixtures check that source is accepted or rejected; others must execute code and check observable behavior. Use the scope page to see remaining work and its dependencies.
Core-language conformance fixtures Runtime binding acceptance cases Semantic conformance tests — Test required behavior, including cancellation races and cleanup. Complete-program conformance — Check that guarantees work together in complete applications. Scope and implementation order — Find remaining decisions and the order in which work depends on them.

title: Core-language conformance fixtures
content:
Core-language conformance fixtures# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These fixtures check whether the compiler accepts or rejects core-language programs and whether executed expressions behave as specified. They complement the semantic test plan . Host behavior, resource lifetimes, and concurrency have separate fixtures.
Each fenced accepted fixture is an independent .ms module, with its application types and helper functions included. Its module-level test body has the ordinary Unit return contract. A rejected variant replaces or removes exactly the indicated text in that fixture, leaving the rest unchanged. If a variant introduces a standard declaration, add its individual import unless missing-import rejection is the behavior under test. Test each variant independently: combining unrelated errors makes the expected diagnostic ambiguous.
The expected stage identifies the violated contract: parse for invalid source structure; resolution for an unknown or ambiguous symbol; type for incompatible types, shapes, labels, bounds, or control flow after parsing and resolution. A checker may combine its resolution and type passes, but must identify the specified cause at the offending source span. Diagnostic wording and internal pass layout are implementation choices. Accepted fixtures must satisfy the stated checks, rather than merely generate Go that compiles.
CL-01: Layout and named-call syntax# Contract: source syntax and declarations and calls .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn subtract(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction test "named multiline call": let remaining = subtract( deduction: 2, amount: 9, ) if not (remaining == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") This accepts trailing commas and multiline calls while mapping labels to declared parameters. Reordering the written labels does not change the parameter mapping.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the call with subtract(amount: 9, deduction: 2) Accept; remaining is Int and equals 7 Replace it with subtract(9, 2) Type rejection: multi-parameter functions require argument labels Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, amount: 2) Type rejection: duplicate supplied argument and missing deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9) Type rejection: missing required deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, discount: 2) Type rejection: unknown argument name discount Replace return amount - deduction with return missing Resolution rejection: unknown binding missing Remove the indentation before the function’s return Parse rejection: missing function block/module-level return Add lexical rejection fixtures for tabs, inconsistent dedentation, and unterminated delimiters as specified by the syntax chapter. Preserve the error’s actual cause rather than reporting a later missing return.
CL-02: Arithmetic grouping and Boolean short-circuiting# Contract: expressions and operators and numeric operations .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn invalid_division(zero: Int) -> Bool: return 1 / zero == 0 test "grouping and short circuit": if not (2 + 3 * 4 == 14): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ((2 + 3) * 4 == 20): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (10 - 3 - 2 == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (true or invalid_division(zero: 0)): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (not (false and invalid_division(zero: 0))): return panic(message: "check failed") Both short-circuit checks must complete without invoking the invalid division. This observes control flow, not only operator result types.
